Why Charts Behave Differently by Session

lessons.title: Reading Volume Bars
lessons.celebration: You understand volume bars!

screens.title: A Bar for Every Candle
screens.text: Most charts show a volume bar beneath each candle. Its height reflects how many shares traded during that period. Reading volume alongside price is a core intermediate skill.

screens.question: A volume bar's height reflects...
options: How many shares traded during that period.
screens.explanation: Volume bar height specifically shows shares traded in that period.

screens.question: Volume bars are typically read alongside the price candle above them, not in isolation.
screens.explanation: Volume adds context to the price action it sits beneath.

screens.question: A taller volume bar means [___] shares traded that period.
screens.explanation: Height directly reflects the amount traded.

screens.question: Match the volume bar height to its meaning.
pairs: A visual count of shares traded per period
screens.explanation: Bar height is a direct, visual read of trading activity.

screens.question: Why read volume alongside price, rather than price alone?

options.label: Volume adds context about how much participation was behind a price move
Volume guarantees the next price move
options.wrong_explanation: Volume is descriptive context, not a guarantee.

options.label: Volume replaces the need to look at price entirely
options.wrong_explanation: Volume is read alongside price, not instead of it.

screens.explanation: Volume adds participation context to a price move. It doesn't replace or guarantee anything.

screens.scenario: Someone reads volume bars completely separately, without ever looking at the price candles above them.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Volume should always be read alone.
Volume is commonly read alongside price for context, not in total isolation from it.
Volume has no relationship to price at all.
screens.explanation: Volume and price are read together for a fuller picture.

lessons.title: High vs. Low Volume
lessons.celebration: You can classify high vs. low volume!

screens.title: Compared to What's Typical
screens.text: "High" or "low" volume is judged relative to what's typical for that asset, a big bar for one stock might be an ordinary bar for another.

screens.question: Volume is commonly judged as "high" or "low" relative to...
options: What's typical for that specific asset.
A single universal number for all stocks.
screens.explanation: High/low volume is a relative judgment, compared to that asset's own typical activity.

screens.question: A volume level that's "high" for one stock could be perfectly ordinary for a much more actively traded stock.
screens.explanation: Volume is judged relative to each asset's own typical activity level, not a single universal threshold.

screens.question: High or low volume is a [___] judgment, not a fixed universal number.
screens.explanation: Comparing to what's typical for that specific asset is the relative approach.

screens.question: Why might comparing volume to recent history matter?
options: It only matters for the very first candle on a chart.
It has no bearing on reading volume at all.
It helps judge whether current activity is unusually high or low for that asset.
screens.explanation: Comparing to recent history gives a relative baseline for judging current volume.

screens.question: How should "high volume" be judged?

options.label: Relative to what's typical for that specific asset
options.detail: A comparison, not a fixed number

options.label: Ignoring recent history entirely
options.wrong_explanation: Recent history is exactly the baseline used for comparison.

options.label: Using one single universal volume number for every stock
options.wrong_explanation: Typical volume varies widely between assets.

screens.explanation: Volume is judged relative to that asset's typical activity, not a fixed universal figure.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes any stock trading 1 million shares must have "high" volume, without checking that stock's typical activity.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Without comparing to that stock's typical volume, there's no way to know if 1 million shares is high or low for it.
Any large-sounding number is automatically high volume.
Volume never needs a comparison point.
screens.explanation: A single number means nothing without comparing it to that asset's own typical activity.

lessons.title: Volume on Breakouts
lessons.celebration: You understand volume's role in breakouts!

screens.title: Does the Move Have Backing?
screens.text: A breakout on higher-than-typical volume is commonly read as having more participation behind it than one on quiet, typical volume.

screens.question: A breakout on unusually high volume is commonly read as...
options: Having more participation behind the move.
Identical in meaning to a low-volume breakout.
screens.explanation: Higher volume on a breakout is commonly read as more participation, without guaranteeing success.

screens.question: A breakout on very low, quiet volume is commonly read the same way as one on high volume.
screens.explanation: Volume level is commonly read as a meaningful difference between the two, not identical.

screens.question: A breakout with strong volume behind it is commonly described as having more [___].
screens.explanation: Higher volume reflects more participants involved in that move.

screens.question: Match the breakout volume scenario to its commonly cited read.
pairs: Less participation, commonly read with more caution
A commonly cited form of confluence
screens.explanation: Volume is commonly combined with a breakout as a form of confluence.

screens.question: Which best describes reading volume on a breakout?

options.label: Higher volume suggests more participation, adding confluence to the breakout
Volume has no relationship to breakouts
options.wrong_explanation: Volume is commonly read as added context on breakouts.

options.label: High volume on a breakout guarantees it continues
options.wrong_explanation: Even high-volume breakouts can still fail.

screens.explanation: Volume adds confluence to a breakout read, without guaranteeing the outcome.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a low-volume breakout is exactly as convincing as a high-volume one.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: All breakouts are read identically regardless of volume.
Volume level is commonly read as a meaningful difference, a low-volume breakout is commonly treated with more caution.
screens.explanation: Volume is commonly used to gauge how much participation is behind a breakout.

lessons.title: Volume on Reversals
lessons.celebration: You understand volume's role in reversals!

screens.title: A Surge at the Turn
screens.text: A reversal accompanied by a surge in volume is commonly read as more significant than one on quiet, typical volume.

screens.question: A reversal on unusually high volume is commonly read as...
options: Potentially more significant, given the added participation.
Identical in meaning to a quiet-volume reversal.
screens.explanation: Higher volume at a reversal is commonly read as adding significance, without guaranteeing anything.

screens.question: A reversal on very quiet volume is commonly read the same as one with a volume surge.
screens.explanation: Volume level is commonly read as a meaningful difference at reversal points too.

screens.question: A volume surge at a turning point is commonly read as adding [___] to that reversal.
screens.explanation: More participation at the turn is commonly read as more meaningful, not certain.

screens.question: Match the reversal volume scenario to its commonly cited read.
pairs: Commonly read as potentially more significant
Another commonly cited form of confluence
screens.explanation: Volume is commonly combined with reversal patterns as a form of confluence, same idea as with breakouts.

screens.question: Which best describes reading volume on a reversal?

options.label: A volume surge adds confluence to a reversal read, without guaranteeing it
High volume at a reversal guarantees the trend has permanently turned
options.wrong_explanation: Even high-volume reversals can fail.

options.label: Volume has no relationship to reversals
options.wrong_explanation: Volume is commonly read as added context at reversals.

screens.explanation: Volume adds confluence to a reversal read, without guaranteeing the outcome.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every reversal, regardless of volume, is equally significant.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Volume level is commonly used to gauge how significant a reversal might be, treating them all as identical ignores that context.
All reversals are read identically regardless of volume.
screens.explanation: Volume is commonly read as meaningful added context at a reversal point.

lessons.title: Climactic Volume
lessons.celebration: You understand climactic volume!

screens.title: An Extreme Volume Spike
screens.text: Climactic volume describes an extreme, sudden spike in volume, commonly noted near the end of a strong move, though not a guaranteed signal of an ending.

screens.question: "Climactic volume" describes...
options: A perfectly steady, average volume level.
An extreme, sudden spike in trading activity.
The complete absence of any trading.
screens.explanation: Climactic volume is specifically an extreme spike, not steady or absent activity.

screens.question: Climactic volume is commonly noted near the end of a strong move, though it doesn't guarantee an ending.
screens.explanation: It's a commonly cited observation, not a guaranteed signal of an ending.

screens.question: Climactic volume describes an extreme, sudden [___] in activity.
screens.explanation: A spike, not an absence or an average level, defines climactic volume.

screens.question: Match the volume type to its description.
pairs: An extreme, sudden spike in activity
Ordinary, expected activity for that asset
screens.explanation: Climactic volume specifically describes an extreme spike, distinct from typical activity.

screens.question: Why treat climactic volume as a clue rather than a certainty?

options.label: Because a spike is commonly noted near move-endings, but doesn't guarantee one
Because climactic volume has no relationship to move-endings at all
options.wrong_explanation: It IS commonly cited context, just not certain.

options.label: Because climactic volume always guarantees the move ends immediately
options.wrong_explanation: It's a commonly cited tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Like other volume reads, climactic volume is descriptive context, not a guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every climactic volume spike guarantees the current move is about to end.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Every volume spike guarantees an immediate ending.
Climactic volume is commonly noted near endings, but it doesn't guarantee one. The move can still continue.
Climactic volume never relates to move-endings at all.
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited tendency, not a certainty.

lessons.title: Dry-Up Volume
lessons.celebration: You understand dry-up volume!

screens.title: When Activity Fades
screens.text: "Dry-up" volume describes an unusually quiet period, often noted during consolidation or a pause, commonly read as reduced participation, not any specific direction.

screens.question: "Dry-up" volume describes...
options: Trading that has completely and permanently stopped.
An unusually quiet period of trading activity.
screens.explanation: Dry-up volume specifically describes unusually low, quiet activity.

screens.question: Dry-up volume is commonly noted during consolidation or a pause in the move.
screens.explanation: Quiet volume commonly accompanies sideways, pausing price action.

screens.question: Dry-up volume reflects reduced [___], not a specific price direction.
screens.explanation: It describes lower participation, without implying up or down on its own.

screens.question: Match the volume type to its description.
pairs: An extreme spike, often near a strong move's end
Unusually quiet activity, often during a pause
screens.explanation: Climactic and dry-up volume are commonly discussed as opposite extremes.

screens.question: What does dry-up volume suggest, on its own?

options.label: A guarantee that a big move is about to happen
options.wrong_explanation: Dry-up volume describes quietness, not a guaranteed next move.

options.label: That trading has permanently stopped altogether
options.wrong_explanation: Trading continues, just at reduced levels.

options.label: Reduced participation during that period, without indicating a specific direction

screens.explanation: Dry-up volume describes reduced activity, not a guaranteed next direction.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes dry-up volume always precedes a big upward move.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Dry-up volume always means a crash is coming.
Dry-up volume always means a big rally is coming.
Dry-up volume describes reduced participation generally. It doesn't specify or guarantee an upward move.
screens.explanation: Dry-up volume is descriptive of quietness, not a directional guarantee either way.

lessons.title: Comparing Candles and Volume
lessons.celebration: You can combine candle and volume reads!

screens.title: Two Reads Together
screens.text: Combining a candle's shape with its volume gives a fuller picture, a big-bodied candle on high volume reads differently than the same shape on quiet volume.

screens.question: A large-bodied candle on unusually high volume is commonly read as...
options: More significant, given the added participation behind it.
Identical in meaning to the same candle on quiet volume.
screens.explanation: Combining candle shape with volume level adds confluence to the read.

screens.question: The same candle shape can carry a different reading depending on the volume behind it.
screens.explanation: Volume adds context that can change how a candle's shape is interpreted.

screens.question: Combining candle shape with volume is an example of [___] from an earlier unit.
screens.explanation: This is the same confluence idea, multiple agreeing factors, applied to candles and volume.

screens.question: Match the combination to its commonly cited read.
screens.explanation: Combining body size and volume gives a richer, more nuanced read than either alone.

screens.question: Why combine candle shape with volume, rather than reading candles alone?

options.label: Combining them guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: Combining factors is still descriptive, not a guarantee.

options.label: Volume always contradicts what the candle shows
options.wrong_explanation: Volume can agree with or add nuance to the candle, not just contradict it.

options.label: Volume adds participation context that can strengthen or weaken the candle's read

screens.explanation: Volume and candle shape together give a fuller, more confluent read.

screens.scenario: Someone reads a big-bodied candle as equally significant regardless of the volume behind it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Volume never changes how a candle should be read.
Volume level can meaningfully change how significant a candle's shape is read to be.
Candle shape is the only thing that ever matters.
screens.explanation: Combining the two factors (confluence) gives a fuller picture than shape alone.

lessons.title: Volume Analysis Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Volume Analysis unit!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of reading volume bars, high vs. low volume, volume on breakouts/reversals, climactic and dry-up volume, and combining candles with volume.

screens.question: Volume is commonly read alongside price and candle shape, not in isolation.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every lesson in this unit.

screens.question: High or low volume is judged [___] to what's typical for that asset.
screens.explanation: Reviewing the relative-judgment idea from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do climactic and dry-up volume have in common?
options: Both are extremes (high or low) commonly noted at certain points, without guaranteeing an outcome.
Neither has any relationship to price action.
Both guarantee the exact same future price move.
screens.explanation: Both are descriptive extremes, read as context rather than guarantees.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: An extreme spike, often near a move's end
Unusually quiet activity, often during a pause
Combining reads for a fuller, more confluent picture
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.template: Volume adds [__1__] to price reads, functioning as a form of [__2__] when combined with candles or levels.
screens.explanation: Volume is context that can add confluence, not a standalone guarantee.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Volume adds participation context to price reads, descriptive, and stronger in combination
Volume has no relationship to price action
options.wrong_explanation: Volume is a core, descriptive companion to price.

options.label: Volume guarantees every price outcome
options.wrong_explanation: This contradicts the whole unit.

screens.explanation: Descriptive, confluence-adding volume reading is the throughline of this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts treating every high-volume move as a guaranteed success.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Volume has no relationship to move quality at all.
Volume adds context and confluence. It never guarantees a move's success.
screens.explanation: This unit consistently frames volume as descriptive context, never a guarantee.

lessons.title: Swing Highs & Swing Lows
lessons.celebration: You understand swing highs and lows!

screens.title: The Turning Points
screens.text: A swing high is a peak where price turned down; a swing low is a trough where price turned up. These turning points are the raw building blocks behind trend and structure.

screens.question: A "swing high" is...
options: Any random candle on the chart.
A trough where price turned up afterward.
A peak where price turned down afterward.
screens.explanation: A swing high specifically marks a turning point where price reversed downward.

screens.question: A swing low is a trough where price turned up afterward.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of a swing low.

screens.question: Swing highs and lows are the raw building blocks behind [___] and structure.
screens.explanation: These turning points are what trend/structure classification is built from.

screens.question: Tap the swing high on this chart.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle's peak, right before the pullback, is a swing high.

screens.question: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: A peak where price turned down
A trough where price turned up
The general term for either one
screens.explanation: These are the basic vocabulary for describing price's ups and downs.

screens.question: Why are swing highs and lows described as "raw building blocks"?

options.label: They have no relationship to trend classification
options.wrong_explanation: Trend classification is built directly from comparing these points.

options.label: They only apply to downtrends
options.wrong_explanation: Swing highs/lows apply to any market condition.

options.label: Trend and structure classifications are built by comparing sequences of them

screens.explanation: Comparing sequences of swing highs/lows is literally how trend structure gets classified.

screens.scenario: Someone tries to classify a trend without ever identifying any swing highs or lows.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Swing highs and lows are unnecessary for trend reading.
Trend classification is built from comparing swing highs and lows, skipping them removes the basis for the read.
Any single candle can replace a full swing sequence.
screens.explanation: Swing highs/lows are the foundational vocabulary trend classification relies on.

lessons.title: Impulses & Corrections
lessons.celebration: You understand impulses and corrections!

screens.title: The Push and the Pause
screens.text: An impulse is a strong, decisive move in the trend's direction. A correction is the smaller counter-move that follows, the same idea as a pullback, named differently.

screens.question: An "impulse" is...
options: A small counter-move against the trend.
A strong, decisive move in the trend's direction.
A single candle with no body.
screens.explanation: Impulse describes the strong, decisive leg of a trend.

screens.question: A correction is the same basic idea as a pullback, just a different name.
screens.explanation: "Correction" and "pullback" both describe a temporary counter-move within a trend.

screens.question: An impulse moves [___] with the trend; a correction moves against it.
screens.explanation: Impulse legs align with the trend direction; corrections move against it temporarily.

screens.question: Match the term to its role.
pairs: The strong, decisive leg in the trend's direction
The repeating pattern that builds a trend
screens.explanation: Trends are commonly described as a repeating cycle of impulses and corrections.

screens.question: How does an impulse differ from a correction?

options.label: Impulses only happen in downtrends
options.wrong_explanation: Impulses occur in either direction, aligned with whichever trend is in play.

options.label: An impulse is the strong move with the trend; a correction is the smaller pause against it
They are exactly the same thing
options.wrong_explanation: One moves with the trend, the other against it.

screens.explanation: Direction (with vs. against the trend) is what separates an impulse from a correction.

screens.scenario: Someone labels every single candle in an uptrend as an "impulse," including the pullbacks.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Corrections don't exist as a separate concept.
Only the strong, trend-aligned legs are impulses. The counter-trend dips are corrections, not impulses.
Impulses and corrections are the same label for everything.
screens.explanation: Impulses and corrections describe two distinct, alternating phases within a trend.

lessons.title: Compression & Expansion
lessons.celebration: You understand compression and expansion!

screens.title: Squeezing and Releasing
screens.text: Compression describes price ranges narrowing (like inside a triangle or tight consolidation). Expansion describes ranges widening out again, often after a squeeze.

screens.question: "Compression" describes...
screens.explanation: Compression specifically describes a narrowing price range.

screens.question: Expansion describes price ranges widening, often after a period of compression.
screens.explanation: Expansion is commonly described as the release that follows a compressed, narrowing range.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle is a chart example of [___].
screens.explanation: The narrowing, converging structure of a triangle is a form of compression.

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price ranges widening, often after compression
screens.explanation: These terms describe the narrowing-then-widening rhythm commonly seen in price.

screens.question: What commonly follows a period of compression?

options.label: Expansion, the range widening out again
Nothing ever follows compression
options.wrong_explanation: Expansion is the commonly cited follow-through.

options.label: Compression always continues forever
options.wrong_explanation: Compression is commonly described as temporary, resolving eventually.

screens.explanation: Compression is commonly read as a temporary squeeze that resolves into expansion.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a compressed, narrowing range will stay narrow forever.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Compression never resolves into anything else.
Compression is commonly described as temporary, eventually resolving into expansion.
Expansion has no relationship to compression.
screens.explanation: The narrowing-then-widening rhythm is a commonly cited pattern, not a permanent state.

lessons.title: Rejection & Acceptance
lessons.celebration: You understand rejection and acceptance!

screens.title: Testing a Level
screens.text: Rejection describes price testing a level and getting pushed back (like a long wick). Acceptance describes price testing a level and then holding there, trading through it comfortably.

screens.question: "Rejection" at a level describes...
options: Price testing the level and comfortably holding there.
A candle with no wicks at all.
Price testing the level and getting pushed back.
screens.explanation: Rejection specifically describes a failed test that gets pushed back.

screens.question: "Acceptance" describes price testing a level and then comfortably holding or trading through it.
screens.explanation: Acceptance is the opposite of rejection, the level is absorbed rather than pushed back from.

screens.question: A long wick at a level is commonly read as a sign of [___].
screens.explanation: A long wick shows a level was tested and pushed back from, rejection.

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price tested a level and got pushed back
Price tested a level and comfortably held there
Ways of describing how price behaves at a tested level
screens.explanation: Rejection and acceptance are two contrasting ways price can behave at the same level.

screens.question: How would you describe price that breaks a level and then holds calmly above it?

options.label: Acceptance, the level was tested and comfortably held through
Neither term applies here
options.wrong_explanation: Acceptance specifically describes this calm-holding behavior.

options.label: Rejection, the level pushed price back
options.wrong_explanation: Rejection describes a push-back, not a calm hold.

screens.explanation: Calmly holding through a level, rather than being pushed back, is acceptance.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a long-wick rejection candle an example of "acceptance."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A long wick shows price was pushed back. That's rejection, not the calm holding that defines acceptance.
Rejection and acceptance mean the same thing.
Wick length has no relationship to rejection or acceptance.
screens.explanation: A pushed-back wick is rejection; acceptance describes a level being calmly held or traded through instead.

lessons.title: Continuation & Exhaustion
lessons.celebration: You understand continuation and exhaustion!

screens.title: Keep Going or Run Out of Steam
screens.text: Continuation describes a move persisting in its existing direction. Exhaustion describes signs a move may be running out of steam, like shrinking bodies or rejected pushes.

screens.question: "Continuation" describes...
options: A move persisting in its existing direction.
screens.explanation: Continuation specifically describes the existing direction persisting.

screens.question: Exhaustion describes signs a move may be running out of steam.
screens.explanation: Shrinking bodies or rejected pushes are commonly cited exhaustion signs.

screens.question: Shrinking candle bodies late in a move are a commonly cited sign of [___].
screens.explanation: Smaller bodies suggest weakening momentum, a commonly cited exhaustion sign.

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Signs the move may be running out of steam
Contrasting reads of an ongoing trend's health
screens.explanation: Continuation and exhaustion are contrasting ways to read whether a move still has strength.

screens.question: How should exhaustion signs be read?

options.label: As proof continuation is impossible from here
options.wrong_explanation: The move can still continue despite exhaustion signs.

options.label: As a guarantee the move ends immediately
options.wrong_explanation: Exhaustion signs are clues, not guarantees.

options.label: As a descriptive clue the move may be weakening, not a guaranteed end

screens.explanation: Exhaustion signs are descriptive clues about weakening momentum, not a certain ending.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a single small-bodied candle as guaranteed proof the whole trend is over.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Exhaustion signs never mean anything at all.
A single candle always ends a trend for certain.
One candle is a clue, not a guarantee. Exhaustion signs describe a possibility, not a certainty.
screens.explanation: Exhaustion signs are descriptive context, read alongside everything else, not a standalone guarantee.

lessons.title: Reading Context
lessons.celebration: You understand reading context!

screens.title: The Same Vocabulary, Different Meaning
screens.text: Context, where a candle or move sits relative to the broader trend, level, and recent structure, changes how every term in this unit should be read.

screens.question: Why does "context" matter so much in price action reading?
options: The same shape or move can mean different things depending on the surrounding trend and levels.
Context never changes how anything should be read.
Context only matters for the very first candle on a chart.
screens.explanation: The surrounding trend and levels can change the meaning of an identical shape or move.

screens.question: An impulse in an uptrend and an impulse in a downtrend describe the same underlying idea, just in different directions.
screens.explanation: Impulse describes a strong, trend-aligned move regardless of which direction the trend runs.

screens.question: Reading price action well means combining vocabulary with [___].
screens.explanation: Context is what turns raw vocabulary into a meaningful read.

screens.question: Match the price-action term to why context matters for it.
pairs: Reads differently depending on the level it happens at
Depends on where the move sits in its overall structure
Read differently depending on the broader trend surrounding it
screens.explanation: Every term in this unit changes meaning depending on the surrounding context.

screens.question: Which best captures why context matters in price action reading?

options.label: Context never affects how a term should be read
options.wrong_explanation: This lesson's whole point is that it does.

options.label: Only the exact vocabulary word matters, never the surroundings
options.wrong_explanation: The surroundings are what make the vocabulary meaningful.

options.label: The same term or shape means different things depending on the surrounding trend and levels

screens.explanation: Combining vocabulary with context is what makes price-action reading useful.

screens.scenario: Someone memorizes every term in this unit but never once considers the surrounding trend or level.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Memorizing terms is the only skill that matters here.
Vocabulary without context misses the surrounding trend and levels that actually give each term its meaning.
Context has no relationship to price-action vocabulary.
screens.explanation: Context is what turns raw vocabulary into a meaningful, applied reading skill.

lessons.title: Price Action Vocabulary Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Price Action Vocabulary unit!

screens.title: Bringing the Vocabulary Together
screens.text: A final review of swing highs/lows, impulses/corrections, compression/expansion, rejection/acceptance, continuation/exhaustion, and context.

screens.question: Every term in this unit describes price action descriptively, not as a guaranteed signal.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every lesson in this unit.

screens.question: A peak where price turned down is called a swing [___].
screens.explanation: Reviewing the term from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do impulse/correction and compression/expansion have in common?
options: Neither has any relationship to price behavior.
Both are pairs of contrasting price-action phases.
Both describe the exact same single idea.
screens.explanation: Each pair describes two contrasting phases within price's ongoing rhythm.

screens.question: Match each term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: The strong move and its counter-pause
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.template: Price-action vocabulary is most useful when combined with [__1__], since the same term can mean different things depending on [__2__].
screens.explanation: Context is what gives meaning to this vocabulary, as covered in the previous lesson.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: A set of guaranteed trading signals
options.wrong_explanation: This contradicts the whole unit.

options.label: Vocabulary unrelated to earlier units in the course
options.wrong_explanation: This vocabulary describes ideas already covered, just named precisely.

options.label: A shared vocabulary for describing price behavior, most useful combined with context

screens.explanation: Shared, context-dependent vocabulary is the throughline of this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts using these terms as guaranteed trade signals.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: This vocabulary has no practical use at all.
These terms guarantee specific trading outcomes.
This vocabulary is descriptive, useful for communication and reading charts, not a guaranteed signal system.
screens.explanation: Like the rest of this course, this vocabulary supports descriptive reading, not guaranteed signals.

lessons.title: Uptrend Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand uptrends!

screens.title: Climbing Step by Step
screens.text: An uptrend is commonly described as a series of higher swing highs and higher swing lows.

screens.question: An uptrend is commonly described as higher swing highs and higher swing lows over time.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of an uptrend's structure.

screens.question: In an uptrend, each pullback often finds a [___] low than the one before.
screens.explanation: Higher lows stepping up is part of the classic uptrend description.

screens.question: What would commonly lead a chart reader to classify a chart as an uptrend?
options: A single green candle appearing anywhere on the chart.
The asset's name containing a positive-sounding word.
A pattern of higher swing highs and higher swing lows.
screens.explanation: Classification is based on the pattern of swings, not one candle or the name.

screens.question: Match the trend feature to its role in an uptrend.
pairs: Each rally reaches further than the last
Each pullback holds above the prior low
screens.explanation: These features together build the descriptive picture of an uptrend.

screens.template: An uptrend is a [__1__] label describing a pattern that has already [__2__] happened.
screens.explanation: Trend labels describe the past and present pattern, not a guaranteed future.

screens.question: A simple way to classify a chart as an uptrend:
items: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally rising
Assign the "uptrend" label if so
correct_order: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally rising
Assign the "uptrend" label if so
screens.explanation: This turns raw swing points into a simple, consistent classification process.

screens.question: Which best describes what "uptrend" means as a term?

options.label: A guarantee that price will keep rising forever
options.wrong_explanation: A trend describes the past pattern, not a certain future.

options.label: A description of a pattern of rising swing highs and lows
A specific single candlestick shape
options.wrong_explanation: Trend describes multiple candles together, not one shape.

screens.explanation: "Uptrend" is a useful descriptive shorthand, not a promise about what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a chart "can't" be in an uptrend just because one single candle closed red.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have ignored the red candle's existence entirely.
They should have switched to a totally different asset.
One candle within an overall uptrend doesn't change the broader classification by itself.
screens.explanation: Trend classification is based on the broader swing pattern, not any single candle.

screens.question: Both the highs and the lows in an uptrend generally move [___] together.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows rising together is the defining structure.

screens.question: A single lower low automatically disqualifies an otherwise clear uptrend.
screens.explanation: One isolated swing doesn't override the broader pattern; classification looks at the overall sequence.

lessons.title: Downtrend Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand downtrends!

screens.title: Stepping Down
screens.text: A downtrend is commonly described as a series of lower swing highs and lower swing lows.

screens.question: A downtrend is commonly described as lower swing highs and lower swing lows over time.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a downtrend's structure.

screens.question: In a downtrend, each rally often reaches a [___] high than the one before.
screens.explanation: Lower highs stepping down is part of the classic downtrend description.

screens.question: What would commonly lead a chart reader to classify a chart as a downtrend?
options: A pattern of lower swing highs and lower swing lows.
The asset's name containing a negative-sounding word.
A single red candle appearing anywhere on the chart.
screens.explanation: Classification is based on the pattern of swings, not one candle or the name.

screens.question: Match the trend feature to its role in a downtrend.
pairs: Each decline reaches further than the last
Each rally fails to reach the prior high
screens.explanation: These features together build the descriptive picture of a downtrend.

screens.template: A downtrend is a [__1__] label, not a [__2__] of what happens next.
screens.explanation: Trend labels describe the past and present, not a certain future.

screens.question: A simple way to classify a chart as a downtrend:
items: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally falling
Assign the "downtrend" label if so
correct_order: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally falling
Assign the "downtrend" label if so
screens.explanation: This turns raw swing points into a simple, consistent classification process.

screens.question: Which best describes what "downtrend" means as a term?

options.label: A description of a pattern of falling swing highs and lows
A guarantee that price will keep falling forever
options.wrong_explanation: A trend describes the past pattern, not a certain future.

options.label: A specific single candlestick shape
options.wrong_explanation: Trend describes multiple candles together, not one shape.

screens.explanation: "Downtrend" is a useful descriptive shorthand, not a promise about what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone says a chart "can't" be in a downtrend just because one single candle closed green.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: One candle within an overall downtrend doesn't change the broader classification by itself.
They should have ignored the green candle's existence entirely.
They should have switched to a totally different asset.
screens.explanation: Trend classification is based on the broader swing pattern, not any single candle.

screens.question: Both the highs and the lows in a downtrend generally move [___] together.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows falling together is the defining structure.

screens.question: A single higher high automatically disqualifies an otherwise clear downtrend.
screens.explanation: One isolated swing doesn't override the broader pattern; classification looks at the overall sequence.

lessons.title: Sideways Markets
lessons.celebration: You can spot sideways price action!

screens.title: Going Nowhere (For Now)
screens.text: A sideways market bounces between a rough high and low without a clear overall direction.

screens.question: A sideways market shows a clear upward direction.
screens.explanation: A sideways market describes a lack of clear direction, bouncing within a band instead.

screens.question: Price moving back and forth between a rough ceiling and floor is often called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Range" (or sideways/consolidation) describes this kind of bounded movement.

screens.question: What generally characterizes a sideways market?
options: Swing highs and lows both falling steadily.
Swing highs and lows staying within a similar band over time.
Swing highs and lows both rising steadily.
screens.explanation: A lack of clear directional progress in the swings is the hallmark of sideways action.

screens.question: Match the market phase to its swing description.
pairs: Swing highs and lows both rising
Swing highs and lows both falling
Swing highs and lows staying roughly similar
screens.explanation: Comparing all three side by side highlights what makes sideways distinct.

screens.template: During a range, price tends to stay between a rough [__1__] and a rough [__2__].
screens.explanation: This floor/ceiling description matches the earlier support/resistance concept.

screens.question: A simple way to identify a sideways market:
items: Look for a period without clear higher highs or lower lows
Note the rough high and low it's bouncing between
Confirm price has touched each side more than once
Label it as sideways/range for that period
correct_order: Look for a period without clear higher highs or lower lows
Note the rough high and low it's bouncing between
Confirm price has touched each side more than once
Label it as sideways/range for that period
screens.explanation: Multiple touches on both sides is what distinguishes a range from a brief pause.

screens.question: Which best describes a chart currently moving sideways?

options.label: Falling to zero without pause
options.wrong_explanation: That would be an extreme downtrend, not sideways action.

options.label: Bouncing between a rough high and low without a clear direction
options.detail: The standard description of sideways action

options.label: Making new all-time highs every single candle
options.wrong_explanation: That would describe a strong uptrend, not sideways action.

screens.explanation: Sideways action specifically describes bounded, directionless movement.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a sideways market will stay sideways forever.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Sideways periods are commonly followed by a move in one direction or another. They don't last forever.
They should have only looked at a shorter timeframe.
They should have widened their definition of the range instead.
screens.explanation: Treating any market phase as permanent overstates what is really just a temporary description.

screens.question: A sideways market is sometimes also called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Range" is a common alternate term for sideways price action.

screens.question: A sideways market can eventually break into either an uptrend or a downtrend.
screens.explanation: Ranges are commonly described as temporary, eventually resolving in one direction or another.

lessons.title: Higher Highs & Higher Lows
lessons.celebration: You can spot the building blocks of an uptrend!

screens.title: The Uptrend's Signature
screens.text: "Higher highs and higher lows" is the specific swing pattern behind every uptrend classification.

screens.question: "Higher highs and higher lows" describes the swing pattern behind an uptrend.
screens.explanation: This phrase is the standard descriptive shorthand for uptrend structure.

screens.question: A swing high that is higher than the previous swing high is called a [___] high.
screens.explanation: "Higher high" specifically means it exceeds the prior swing high.

screens.question: Why does a rising sequence of swing lows matter for an uptrend?
options: It shows pullbacks are holding at progressively higher levels.
It has no relationship to trend classification.
It shows the asset is about to be delisted.
screens.explanation: Rising swing lows are part of the defining structure of an uptrend.

screens.question: Match the swing sequence to its label.
pairs: Each low holds above the last
screens.explanation: These two sequences combined are what define uptrend structure.

screens.template: If either swing highs or swing lows stop [__1__], the uptrend structure may be starting to [__2__].
screens.explanation: A break in this rising pattern is commonly noted as an early sign structure may be shifting.

screens.question: A simple way to check for higher-highs-and-higher-lows structure:
items: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high exceeds the last
Check that each low holds above the last
correct_order: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high exceeds the last
Check that each low holds above the last
screens.explanation: Confirming both sequences together is what verifies uptrend structure.

screens.question: Which best describes what "higher highs and higher lows" means?

options.label: Each new swing high and swing low both exceed the prior ones
Only the lows need to rise; highs don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows rising together define this structure.

options.label: Only the highs need to rise; lows don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows rising together define this structure.

screens.explanation: Both sequences rising together is what the phrase specifically describes.

screens.scenario: Someone claims a chart has "higher highs and higher lows" after checking only the swing highs.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should ignore swing lows entirely from now on.
Confirming this structure requires checking both the swing highs AND the swing lows, not just one.
They should check the swing highs twice instead.
screens.explanation: Both sequences need to be checked together to properly confirm this structure.

screens.question: Which best completes an uptrend's structure alongside higher highs?
screens.explanation: Higher highs paired with higher lows together define the uptrend structure.

screens.question: Checking only swing highs is enough to confirm an uptrend.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows need to be checked together.

options.label: Each new swing high and swing low both fall below the prior ones
Only the lows need to fall; highs don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows falling together define this structure.

options.label: Only the highs need to fall; lows don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows falling together define this structure.

screens.explanation: Both sequences falling together is what the phrase specifically describes.

screens.scenario: Someone claims a chart has "lower highs and lower lows" after checking only the swing lows.

options: Confirming this structure requires checking both the swing highs AND the swing lows, not just one.
They should check the swing lows twice instead.

screens.explanation: Lower highs paired with lower lows together define the downtrend structure.

lessons.title: Trend Strength
lessons.celebration: You can gauge how strong a trend looks!

screens.title: Steep vs. Gradual
screens.text: Trends aren't just "up" or "down". They can look stronger or weaker depending on how steadily price is moving.

screens.question: All uptrends move at exactly the same speed and steepness.
screens.explanation: Trends can vary widely in steepness and consistency, even when sharing the same overall direction.

screens.question: A trend with large, consistent moves in one direction is often described as [___].
screens.explanation: "Strong" commonly describes a trend with consistent, sizable moves in one direction.

screens.question: What might commonly suggest a trend is weakening?
options: Swings becoming smaller or less consistent than before.
The chart changing to a different color scheme.
The asset's name being mentioned in the news.
screens.explanation: Smaller, less consistent swings are commonly read as a sign of weakening momentum.

screens.question: Match the trend description to its common reading.
pairs: Large, consistent swings in one direction
Often read as a stronger trend
Often read as a weaker or fading trend
Often read as declining trend conviction
screens.explanation: These descriptions offer a rough, non-certain way to gauge trend strength.

screens.template: Trend strength is a matter of [__1__], not a simple [__2__] label.
screens.explanation: Trends exist on a spectrum from very strong to very weak, not just "on" or "off."

screens.question: A simple way to informally gauge trend strength:
items: Compare the size of recent swings to earlier ones
Note how consistently price is moving in one direction
Note whether pullbacks are getting larger or smaller
Form a general (not certain) sense of trend strength
correct_order: Compare the size of recent swings to earlier ones
Note how consistently price is moving in one direction
Note whether pullbacks are getting larger or smaller
Form a general (not certain) sense of trend strength
screens.explanation: These comparisons together give a rough sense of how strong a trend currently looks.

screens.question: Which best describes a "weakening" trend, as commonly read?

options.label: Swings becoming smaller and less consistent than before

options.label: Swings becoming larger and more consistent

screens.scenario: Someone assumes trend strength is either "fully strong" or "fully weak," with nothing in between.
screens.question: What is the mistake?

They should only ever describe trends as weak.
They should only ever describe trends as strong.
screens.explanation: Treating strength as binary oversimplifies what's actually a matter of degree.

screens.question: Trend strength is commonly judged by comparing swing size to what's [___] for that chart.

screens.question: A trend can remain in the same direction while getting weaker over time.

lessons.title: Momentum Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand basic momentum!

screens.title: How Fast, Not Just Which Way
screens.text: Momentum describes how quickly and forcefully price is moving in its current direction.

screens.question: Momentum describes how quickly and forcefully price is currently moving.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive meaning of momentum in this context.

screens.question: A market with fast, forceful moves in one direction is often described as having strong [___].
screens.explanation: "Momentum" describes the speed and force of a current move.

screens.question: How does momentum generally differ from trend?
options: They are exactly the same concept with different names.
Momentum describes the current speed/force of movement; trend describes overall direction over time.
Momentum only applies to downtrends, never uptrends.
screens.explanation: Trend and momentum describe related but distinct ideas, direction versus speed/force.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: Overall direction over a period of time
Current speed and force of movement
Size and speed of price swings generally
screens.explanation: These related terms each describe a slightly different angle on price behavior.

Note how quickly price is covering distance
Note whether pullbacks are shallow or deep
Form a general (not certain) sense of current momentum

Note how quickly price is covering distance
Note whether pullbacks are shallow or deep
Form a general (not certain) sense of current momentum
screens.explanation: These comparisons together give a rough sense of how forceful the current move looks.

screens.question: Which best describes "momentum" as used here?

options.label: The current speed and force behind a price move
options.detail: A description of intensity, not direction alone

options.label: A level guaranteed to hold on the sixth touch
options.wrong_explanation: More touches don't guarantee the next reaction.

options.label: A more established, closely watched level, though not a guarantee
options.detail: More touches, more notability, still no certainty

options.label: A level that's now meaningless due to overuse
options.wrong_explanation: More touches are commonly viewed as adding notability, not removing it.

screens.explanation: More touches add notability in how a level is commonly discussed, without guaranteeing what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a level touched five times is now mathematically guaranteed to hold a sixth time.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: More touches can add notability, but they never guarantee the level will hold again.
They should stop counting touches entirely.
They should wait for even more touches before considering it at all.
screens.explanation: Notability from repeated touches is not the same as a guarantee about future behavior.

screens.question: Touch count is one simple way to compare the relative [___] of levels.
screens.explanation: Comparing touch counts is a simple, descriptive way to judge relative notability.

screens.question: A level with many touches is mathematically certain to hold on the next test.
screens.explanation: More touches add notability but never guarantee the next reaction.

lessons.title: Breakouts
lessons.celebration: You understand breakouts through levels!

screens.title: Leaving the Level Behind
screens.text: A breakout describes price clearly moving beyond a prior support or resistance level.

screens.question: A breakout always guarantees the new direction will continue indefinitely.
screens.explanation: A breakout describes what just happened; it doesn't guarantee what happens next.

screens.question: When price clearly moves above a prior resistance level, it's often called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Breakout" is the standard term for clearing a prior ceiling.

screens.question: What does the term "breakdown" commonly describe?
options: Any red candle appearing on the chart.
Price clearly moving below a prior support level.
A chart that has stopped updating.
screens.explanation: "Breakdown" is the downside counterpart to "breakout."

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price clearly moves above a prior resistance level
Price clearly moves below a prior support level
Price returns to test a broken level from the other side
screens.explanation: These three terms are commonly used together when describing this kind of event.

screens.template: A breakout happens to the [__1__] of a level, while a breakdown happens to the [__2__].
screens.explanation: Direction is what distinguishes the two terms.

screens.question: A simple way to describe a breakout after the fact:
items: Identify the prior support or resistance level
Note that price closed clearly beyond that level
Check whether it stayed beyond that level afterward
Describe it as a breakout (or a failed one, if it didn't hold)
correct_order: Identify the prior support or resistance level
Note that price closed clearly beyond that level
Check whether it stayed beyond that level afterward
Describe it as a breakout (or a failed one, if it didn't hold)
screens.explanation: Confirming the move held is part of how chart readers describe breakouts after the fact.

screens.question: Which best describes what a breakout tells you, on its own?

options.label: Proof that the prior level was drawn incorrectly
options.wrong_explanation: A breakout doesn't mean the level was wrong.

options.label: A guarantee that price will keep moving in that direction forever
options.wrong_explanation: Breakouts can fail and reverse.

options.label: A description that price has moved clearly past a prior level

screens.explanation: A breakout is a description of a past event, not a certainty about the future.

screens.scenario: Someone treats every single breakout as guaranteed to keep going in that direction.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have picked a totally different asset instead.
Breakouts sometimes fail and reverse, treating them as guaranteed outcomes overstates certainty.
They should have used a shorter timeframe only.
screens.explanation: Not every breakout continues, some reverse back, commonly called a "false breakout."

screens.question: A breakout is described [___] the fact, based on what actually happened.
screens.explanation: Confirming the move held is part of how breakouts are described in hindsight.

screens.question: A breakdown is the same concept as a breakout, just in the opposite direction.
screens.explanation: Breakdown is simply the downside counterpart to breakout.

lessons.title: Fakeouts
lessons.celebration: You can recognize a false breakout!

screens.title: When the Breakout Fails
screens.text: A fakeout (false breakout) happens when price briefly moves past a level, then reverses back, the opposite of a confirmed break.

screens.question: A false breakout means price moved past a level and then reversed back, instead of continuing.
screens.explanation: That reversal back into the prior range is what defines a false breakout.

screens.question: A breakout that quickly reverses back is often called a [___] breakout.
screens.explanation: "False" describes the failed follow-through.

screens.question: Why do chart readers commonly pay attention to false breakouts?
options: They guarantee a certain outcome every time they occur.
They're a commonly cited reason why waiting for confirmation matters, rather than reacting instantly.
They mean the chart's data is inaccurate.
screens.explanation: False breakouts are simply one commonly described risk of reacting to a level break too early.

screens.question: Match the outcome to its label.
pairs: Price breaks a level and keeps moving that direction
Price breaks a level then quickly reverses back
Price returns to test a broken level from the other side
screens.explanation: These are standard descriptive labels for different outcomes after a level is broken.

screens.template: A false breakout is described [__1__] the fact, once price has already [__2__] back.
screens.explanation: You can only classify a breakout as "false" once you've seen what happened next.

screens.question: A cautious way to think about a fresh breakout:
items: Note that price has just moved past a level
Recognize the move could continue or reverse
Wait to see whether the move holds over subsequent candles
Only then describe it as confirmed or false
correct_order: Note that price has just moved past a level
Recognize the move could continue or reverse
Wait to see whether the move holds over subsequent candles
Only then describe it as confirmed or false
screens.explanation: Patience before labeling a breakout is a commonly cited way to reduce being misled by an early false move.

screens.question: Which best describes a false breakout?

options.label: Price moved past a level and kept going for months
options.wrong_explanation: That would be a confirmed breakout.

options.label: A candle with a small body and long wicks
options.wrong_explanation: That describes a doji, not a false breakout.

options.label: Price moved past a level but then reversed back into the range
options.detail: The definition of a false breakout

screens.explanation: The reversal back is the defining feature of a false breakout.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every breakout must be false and never trusts one at all.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Some breakouts do continue, treating every single one as false is just as much an overstatement as treating every one as guaranteed.
They should have used a completely different chart type.
They should have only looked at longer wicks.
screens.explanation: Both extremes, assuming every breakout works, or assuming none do, overstate certainty in either direction.

screens.question: A false breakout can only be labeled [___] price has already reversed back.
screens.explanation: You need to see the reversal happen before calling it a false breakout.

screens.question: False breakouts are a reason many chart readers wait for confirmation before reacting.
screens.explanation: The risk of a false breakout is commonly cited as a reason to wait for confirmation.

lessons.title: Retests
lessons.celebration: You understand retests of broken levels!

screens.title: Coming Back for a Second Look
screens.text: After a level breaks, price sometimes returns to that same level from the other side before continuing, commonly called a retest.

screens.question: A retest means price returns to a broken level from the other side.
screens.explanation: That's the definition, revisiting the level after it was already broken.

screens.question: Old resistance that gets broken is sometimes described as becoming new [___].
screens.explanation: A commonly cited idea is that a broken ceiling can act as a new floor, and vice versa.

screens.question: What is a retest, in simple terms?
options: A chart with no candles at all.
Price returning to touch a previously broken level before (potentially) continuing.
screens.explanation: A retest is specifically about revisiting a level that was already broken.

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price returns to touch that same level again
A commonly cited idea about broken ceilings
screens.explanation: These terms are frequently used together when describing this kind of price sequence.

screens.template: A retest happens [__1__] the original breakout, when price revisits the [__2__] level.
screens.explanation: The order matters, a retest only makes sense once a level has already broken.

screens.question: A simple way to describe a breakout-and-retest sequence:
items: Price breaks clearly past a level
Price pulls back to touch that same level again
Price either holds there and continues, or breaks back through
The sequence is described based on what actually happened
correct_order: Price breaks clearly past a level
Price pulls back to touch that same level again
Price either holds there and continues, or breaks back through
The sequence is described based on what actually happened
screens.explanation: Like breakouts, retests are described after the fact based on how price actually behaved.

screens.question: Which best matches the idea that "old resistance can become new support"?

options.label: A rule enforced by exchanges
options.wrong_explanation: This is informal chart-reading terminology, not an official rule.

options.label: A guarantee that every broken level will hold on retest
options.wrong_explanation: Retests can also fail and break back through.

options.label: A broken ceiling sometimes acts as a floor on a later retest

screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited pattern, not a guaranteed rule.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every retest of a broken level will always hold and bounce.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Retests sometimes fail and price breaks back through. It isn't guaranteed to hold.
They should have used a shorter timeframe only.
They should have ignored the retest entirely.
screens.explanation: Like other chart concepts here, a retest describes a common pattern, not a certainty.

screens.question: A retest only makes sense once a level has already [___].
screens.explanation: Retesting implies revisiting a level after it was already broken.

screens.question: A retest is guaranteed to hold and never break back through.
screens.explanation: Retests can also fail, with price breaking back through the level.

lessons.title: Range Trading (Intro)
lessons.celebration: You understand the basic idea of a trading range!

screens.title: Bouncing Between the Lines
screens.text: A trading range describes a period where price bounces between a fairly consistent support and resistance level.

screens.question: A trading range describes price bouncing between a fairly consistent support and resistance level.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a trading range.

screens.question: The upper boundary of a trading range is commonly the level acting as [___].
screens.explanation: Resistance forms the upper boundary in a typical range description.

screens.question: What commonly happens at the edges of an established trading range?
options: Price has commonly reacted (bounced or rejected) at those edges before.
Price is guaranteed to break out immediately.
The chart data resets at each edge.
screens.explanation: The edges of a range are, by definition, levels where price has reacted previously.

screens.question: Match the range concept to its description.
pairs: The support side of the range
The resistance side of the range
Price clearly leaving the established range
screens.explanation: These terms describe the basic structure of a trading range.

screens.template: A trading range is bounded by a [__1__] level below and a [__2__] level above.
screens.explanation: Support and resistance together form the floor and ceiling of a range.

screens.question: A simple way to identify a trading range:
items: Look for repeated reactions near a similar low
Look for repeated reactions near a similar high
Confirm price has bounced between these levels more than once
Label that zone as a trading range
correct_order: Look for repeated reactions near a similar low
Look for repeated reactions near a similar high
Confirm price has bounced between these levels more than once
Label that zone as a trading range
screens.explanation: Multiple touches on both sides is what distinguishes a range from a brief pause.

screens.question: Which best describes a trading range, as commonly used?

options.label: A guarantee price will break out imminently
options.wrong_explanation: Ranges can persist for a long time before resolving.

options.label: Price bouncing between a fairly consistent support and resistance level
The exact same thing as a single candlestick pattern
options.wrong_explanation: A range spans many candles, not one shape.

screens.explanation: A trading range specifically describes bounded, repeated bouncing between two levels.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes an established trading range will hold forever and never resolve into a breakout.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Ranges are commonly followed eventually by a breakout in one direction or another. They don't last forever.
They should have widened the range indefinitely instead.
They should have only looked at a shorter timeframe.
screens.explanation: Treating any market phase as permanent overstates what is really just a temporary description.

screens.question: A trading range is bounded by consistent support [___] resistance levels.
screens.explanation: Both a floor (support) and a ceiling (resistance) together define a range.

screens.question: A trading range can persist for a long time before finally breaking out.
screens.explanation: Ranges are commonly described as lasting a while before eventually resolving.

lessons.title: Combining Levels with Trend
lessons.celebration: You can combine levels and trend context together!

screens.title: Reading Levels in Context
screens.text: Support and resistance are commonly read alongside the broader trend, not in isolation from it.

screens.question: Support and resistance levels should always be read completely independently of the overall trend.
screens.explanation: Levels are commonly read alongside trend context for a fuller picture, not in total isolation.

screens.question: A support level within an established uptrend is sometimes described as aligning with the [___] trend.
screens.explanation: Levels are commonly discussed in relation to the broader trend they sit within.

screens.question: Why might a support level be viewed differently during an uptrend versus a downtrend?
options: The broader trend context can add to how a level is commonly interpreted.
Trend and support have no relationship to each other at all.
Support only exists during uptrends and never during downtrends.
screens.explanation: Combining level and trend context is commonly described as giving a fuller picture than either alone.

screens.question: Match the combined context to a commonly cited description.
pairs: Sometimes read as aligning with the broader upward structure
Sometimes read as aligning with the broader downward structure
Read with extra caution, given the conflicting context
screens.explanation: These are common (not certain) ways trend and levels are discussed together.

screens.template: Combining [__1__] and [__2__] together is commonly described as giving a fuller picture than either alone.
screens.explanation: Neither concept alone captures everything; combining them is the commonly cited habit.

screens.question: A simple way to combine levels and trend context:
items: Identify the broader trend direction first
Identify nearby support or resistance levels
Note whether the level aligns with or goes against the trend
Factor both pieces into your overall description
correct_order: Identify the broader trend direction first
Identify nearby support or resistance levels
Note whether the level aligns with or goes against the trend
Factor both pieces into your overall description
screens.explanation: This habit builds a fuller, combined read rather than relying on just one concept.

screens.question: Which best reflects a balanced way to combine trend and levels?

options.label: Considering both together for a fuller descriptive picture
options.detail: Neither alone tells the whole story

options.label: Only ever considering levels, ignoring trend entirely
options.wrong_explanation: This ignores useful context the trend can add.

options.label: Only ever considering trend, ignoring levels entirely
options.wrong_explanation: This ignores useful context levels can add.

screens.explanation: Combining both is more descriptive than relying on either one alone.

screens.scenario: Someone reads a resistance level the exact same way regardless of whether the chart is in an uptrend or downtrend.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Ignoring the broader trend context misses useful information that's commonly combined with level analysis.
They should ignore resistance levels entirely instead.
They should only ever look at trend, never levels.
screens.explanation: Combining trend and level context together is more descriptive than looking at either alone.

screens.question: Combining levels with trend gives a [___] picture than either alone.
screens.explanation: Together, levels and trend context are commonly described as more complete than either alone.

screens.question: A level that goes against the broader trend is commonly read with extra caution.
screens.explanation: Conflicting context (level vs trend) is commonly treated as worth extra caution.

lessons.title: Levels Drill, Support or Resistance?
lessons.celebration: You can classify levels across a mixed set of charts!

screens.title: Practice Round
screens.text: Practice identifying where support and resistance levels sit relative to price.

screens.question: Where is the support level in this chart, in relation to price?
options: There is no support shown in this chart
Above, where price hasn't yet traded
Below, where price has bounced more than once
screens.explanation: Support is the price floor where a chart has previously had trouble falling below.

screens.question: Where is the resistance level in this chart, in relation to price?
options: There is no resistance shown in this chart
Above, where price has struggled to close beyond
Below, where price has never traded
screens.explanation: Resistance is the price ceiling where a chart has previously had trouble rising above.

screens.question: What does the final candle in this chart illustrate about the nearby level?
options: Price staying entirely within the prior range
A breakout clearing above the prior level on strong momentum
Price falling below the prior level
screens.explanation: The final candles here clear the prior level and hold above it, matching a breakout.

screens.question: A support level and a resistance level can be the exact same price, just viewed from different sides.
screens.explanation: A broken resistance level commonly becomes a new support level from the other side, and vice versa.

screens.question: Match the level type to its position relative to price.
pairs: Below current price, acting as a floor
Above current price, acting as a ceiling
Can act as the opposite type after being broken
screens.explanation: A quick recap of how these levels relate to price position.

screens.question: What is the main goal of practicing level identification like this?

options.label: Replacing the need to look at the trend entirely
options.wrong_explanation: Levels are read alongside trend, not instead of it.

options.label: Guaranteeing exactly where price will react next
options.wrong_explanation: Levels are historical references, not guarantees.

options.label: Building a consistent habit for spotting these zones on any chart

screens.concern: Understanding the purpose of this drill
screens.explanation: This drill builds a consistent, descriptive habit, not predictive certainty.

screens.question: These drills build a consistent, [___] habit for spotting levels.
screens.explanation: The goal is descriptive skill, not predictive certainty.

screens.question: Support and resistance can each act as the other after a level breaks.
screens.explanation: A broken resistance can become support (and vice versa), this flip is commonly discussed.

screens.question: Match the drill focus to its skill.
screens.explanation: These are the three core skills this drill practices together.

lessons.title: Support & Resistance Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Support & Resistance unit!

screens.title: Bringing It All Together
screens.text: A final review of support, resistance, breakouts, fakeouts, and retests, all descriptive tools for reading key price zones.

screens.question: Everything covered in this unit describes historical price behavior, not guaranteed future outcomes.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every concept in this unit.

screens.question: A price floor where declines have previously struggled is called [___].
screens.explanation: Reviewing the basic definition from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do support, resistance, and breakouts all have in common as terms?
options: They all describe patterns in price history around key levels, not certainties about the future.
They only apply to one specific asset.
They all refer to a single specific candlestick shape.
screens.explanation: Each is a descriptive label for behavior around price levels.

screens.question: Match the concept to its one-line summary.
pairs: Price areas where reactions have happened before
Price clearly moving past a level
Ways a level break can play out afterward
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the core vocabulary from this unit.

screens.template: Reading levels well means combining [__1__] with a healthy dose of [__2__] about certainty.
screens.explanation: Useful chart reading pairs descriptive skill with realistic expectations.

screens.question: The general path this unit followed:
items: Learn the basic definitions of support and resistance
Learn why levels are commonly thought to form
Learn about breakouts, fakeouts, and retests
Practice combining levels with trend, while staying skeptical of guarantees
correct_order: Learn the basic definitions of support and resistance
Learn why levels are commonly thought to form
Learn about breakouts, fakeouts, and retests
Practice combining levels with trend, while staying skeptical of guarantees
screens.explanation: Each lesson built on the one before it toward a fuller picture.

screens.question: Which best summarizes the overall theme of this unit?

options.label: Support and resistance are meaningless and should be ignored
options.wrong_explanation: They're useful descriptive tools, just not guarantees.

options.label: Support and resistance always predict the future with certainty
options.wrong_explanation: This directly contradicts what every lesson covered.

options.label: Support and resistance are descriptive tools, not predictive guarantees

screens.explanation: This balanced view has been the throughline of every lesson in this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and claims they can now predict every future price reaction with certainty.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have skipped straight to more advanced lessons.
They should have only studied one single chart.
Nothing in this unit was about certainty. It was about describing key price zones more clearly.
screens.explanation: This unit builds reading literacy, not a predictive guarantee, that distinction matters.

screens.question: This unit treats levels as [___] tools, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Descriptive, not predictive, framing has been the throughline of this unit.

screens.question: Fakeouts and retests are both ways a level break can play out after the fact.
screens.explanation: Both describe possible outcomes once a level has been broken.

lessons.title: What Is a Double Top?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a double top on a chart!

screens.title: Two Peaks at the Same Level
screens.text: A double top is commonly described as price rising to a level, pulling back, rising to about the same level again, then turning down, an "M" shape. It's read as a possible reversal after an up-move.

screens.question: The chart above shows two peaks stalling at about the same price. This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same level forming an "M" is the double top shape.

screens.question: A double top is commonly described as forming after an up-move, at resistance.
screens.explanation: The two peaks stall at the same resistance level after price has risen into it.

screens.question: The two peaks of a double top reach roughly the [___] price level.
screens.explanation: The defining feature is two peaks at about the same level.

screens.question: Match each part of the double top to what it is.
pairs: Highs that stall at the same resistance
A pullback before the second attempt
Price failing to break higher a second time
screens.explanation: These three parts together make the "M" shape.

screens.question: What does a double top describe, on its own?

options.label: That both peaks are green candles
options.wrong_explanation: Candle color isn't what defines the pattern.

options.label: A guaranteed crash from here
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee the next move.

options.label: Price tested a level twice and failed to break above it
options.detail: A descriptive read, not a guarantee
