lessons.title: Reading Momentum From Bodies
lessons.celebration: You can read momentum off a chart!

screens.title: Big Bodies, Strong Moves
screens.text: A large candle body reflects momentum, price moved decisively one way. Reading body size is a quick read of how strong a move is.

screens.question: The big, near-wickless candle highlighted above reflects...
screens.explanation: A large body (marubozu) reflects decisive momentum.

screens.question: Tap the strong-momentum candle (the big body).
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle is the big-bodied momentum candle.

screens.question: A [___] body reflects stronger momentum.
screens.explanation: Bigger bodies reflect stronger, more one-sided moves.

screens.question: A large candle body reflects a decisive, one-sided move.
screens.explanation: The full body shows price pushed one way and held.

screens.question: A large candle body reflects [___] in that period.
screens.explanation: A large body shows price moved decisively one way. That's momentum.

screens.question: Reading body size is a quick way to gauge how strong a move looks.
screens.explanation: Body size is a simple, descriptive read of a period's momentum.

screens.question: What does a large, decisive candle body suggest?
options: Strong momentum in one direction that period.
screens.explanation: A large body reflects a decisive, one-sided move, momentum.

lessons.title: Exhaustion: Long Wicks
lessons.celebration: You can read exhaustion from wicks!

screens.title: Pushed, Then Rejected
screens.text: A long wick shows a push that got rejected, a sign a move may be running out of steam (exhaustion) at that extreme.

screens.question: The long upper wick highlighted above shows...
options: an up-push that got rejected back down.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick shows buyers were rejected at the highs.

screens.question: Tap the rejection candle (the long upper wick).
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle's long upper wick shows the rejected push up.

screens.question: A long wick is commonly read as a sign of possible [___] at that extreme.
screens.explanation: A rejected push suggests the move may be running out of steam there.

screens.question: A long lower wick shows a down-push that got rejected (buyers stepped in).
screens.explanation: A long lower wick shows sellers were rejected and buyers recovered price.

screens.question: A long wick shows a push that got [___].
screens.explanation: The wick marks a level price touched but couldn't hold, a rejection.

screens.question: A long wick can be a sign a move is running out of steam at that extreme.
screens.explanation: Rejection at an extreme is commonly read as a possible sign of exhaustion there.

screens.question: What does a long wick suggest, descriptively?
options: A push to an extreme that was rejected before the close.
screens.explanation: A long wick describes a rejected push, not a guarantee of what's next.

lessons.title: Indecision: Doji & Spinning Top
lessons.celebration: You can read indecision candles!

screens.title: Neither Side Wins
screens.text: Small-bodied candles like the doji and spinning top reflect indecision, momentum stalling, with neither side in control.

screens.question: The tiny-bodied candle highlighted above reflects...
screens.explanation: A doji's tiny body reflects a balance, indecision.

screens.question: The small-bodied candle with wicks on both sides above reflects...
screens.explanation: A spinning top's small body and balanced wicks reflect indecision.

screens.question: A doji reflects strong one-directional momentum.
screens.explanation: A doji reflects balance/indecision, the opposite of strong momentum.

screens.question: Small-bodied candles reflect momentum [___], not a strong move.
screens.explanation: A small body means neither side pushed decisively, momentum stalling.

screens.question: A doji or spinning top reflects [___], not decisive momentum.
screens.explanation: Small bodies on both these shapes reflect a balanced, indecisive period.

screens.question: A doji and a spinning top both have relatively small bodies.
screens.explanation: Small body size is what both shapes share, reflecting indecision.

screens.question: What do doji and spinning top candles have in common?
options: Both reflect indecision through a small body.
screens.explanation: Small bodies on both shapes point to indecision, not decisive momentum.

lessons.title: Strong vs. Weak Candles
lessons.celebration: You can compare candle strength!

screens.title: Decisive or Hesitant?
screens.text: Comparing candles: a big body = decisive momentum; a tiny body = hesitation. Reading relative strength is descriptive context.

screens.question: Which reflects more momentum: a big-bodied marubozu or a tiny-bodied doji?
screens.explanation: A big body reflects far more momentum than a tiny doji body.

screens.question: Tap the more decisive candle on this chart.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied 2nd candle is the more decisive, higher-momentum one.

screens.template: A big body reflects [__1__]; a tiny body reflects [__2__].
screens.explanation: Body size is a quick read of momentum vs hesitation.

screens.question: Reading candle strength is descriptive context, not a guaranteed prediction.
screens.explanation: Strength informs the read; it doesn't guarantee what comes next.

screens.question: Comparing candles helps read [___] strength between them.
screens.explanation: Comparing body sizes is about relative, descriptive strength, not certainty.

screens.question: A strong (large-bodied) candle guarantees the next candle will also be strong.
screens.explanation: Reading strength is descriptive context for that period. It doesn't guarantee the next one.

screens.question: Comparing a marubozu to a doji, which reflects more momentum?
screens.explanation: A marubozu's large body reflects far more momentum than a doji's tiny one.

lessons.title: Momentum Into a Level
lessons.celebration: You can read momentum meeting a level!

screens.title: When a Push Meets Resistance
screens.text: Momentum into a level can either break it or get rejected. A strong push that then rejects (long wick) at resistance is a common exhaustion read.

screens.question: The chart above pushes up into resistance, then gets rejected. This is commonly read as...
screens.explanation: A rejected push at resistance is a common exhaustion read, descriptive.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the push was rejected at.
screens.explanation: The level where the push got rejected is the resistance.

screens.question: A rejection at resistance guarantees price falls.
screens.explanation: A rejection is a descriptive clue about exhaustion, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A strong push that rejects at a level is a common [___] read.
screens.explanation: A rejected push at a level commonly reads as exhaustion there.

screens.question: A strong push into resistance that then rejects is a common [___] read.
screens.explanation: A rejected push at a level is commonly read as possible exhaustion there.

screens.question: A rejection at resistance guarantees price will fall from there.
screens.explanation: A rejection is descriptive context about that push, not a guarantee of what follows.

screens.question: What does momentum meeting resistance and getting rejected commonly suggest?
options: Possible exhaustion of that push at the level.
screens.explanation: A rejected push at a level is commonly read as a possible exhaustion signal.

lessons.title: Momentum Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered momentum & exhaustion!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of momentum (bodies), exhaustion (wicks), and indecision (small bodies).

screens.question: Match each candle read to what it reflects.
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's candle reads.

screens.question: What do momentum and exhaustion reads have in common?
options: Both are descriptive context from candles, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Both read the candles descriptively; neither guarantees the outcome.

screens.template: A big body reflects [__1__]; a long wick reflects a rejected push and possible [__2__].
screens.explanation: Bodies read momentum; wicks read rejection/exhaustion.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Candle shape tells you nothing
options.wrong_explanation: Shape reflects momentum and exhaustion.

options.label: Candle shape guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.label: Read momentum, exhaustion, and indecision from candle shape, descriptively

screens.explanation: Descriptive candle-strength reading is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together momentum (bodies), exhaustion (wicks), and [___] (small bodies).
screens.explanation: All three core reads from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: Reading momentum and exhaustion from candles is descriptive context, not a guarantee.
screens.explanation: This has been the throughline, descriptive candle reads, never certainties.

screens.question: What is the single most useful habit from this unit?
options: Only ever looking at candle color.
Reading body size and wick length together for momentum and exhaustion clues.
screens.explanation: Combining body and wick reads is the core skill from this unit.

lessons.title: What Is Confluence?
lessons.celebration: You understand confluence!

screens.title: When Signals Line Up
screens.text: Confluence is when two or more readings point the same way at the same spot, for example, a support level AND a bounce candle together. More agreement makes a stronger read (still not a guarantee).

screens.question: Confluence means...
options: a single reading on its own.
two or more readings lining up at the same spot.
screens.explanation: Confluence is multiple factors agreeing at once.

screens.question: More confluence makes a read stronger, but still not guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Agreement strengthens the read; it doesn't make it a certainty.

screens.question: Confluence is when [___] or more readings agree at the same spot.
screens.explanation: Confluence requires at least two agreeing factors.

screens.question: Why is confluence useful to read?

options.label: Several readings agreeing is stronger evidence than one alone
It replaces reading the chart
options.wrong_explanation: Confluence IS reading several chart factors together.

options.label: It guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: More agreement isn't a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Confluence stacks evidence, stronger, but never a guarantee.

screens.question: Confluence is [___] or more readings agreeing at the same spot.
screens.explanation: Confluence requires at least two agreeing factors at one spot.

screens.question: More agreeing factors make a read stronger, but never guarantee the outcome.
screens.explanation: Agreement strengthens the read; it doesn't make it a certainty.

screens.question: What is confluence, in simple terms?
options: Multiple readings pointing the same way at once.
screens.explanation: Confluence describes multiple agreeing factors, not a lone signal or a certainty.

lessons.title: Level + Candle Signal
lessons.celebration: You can read level-plus-candle confluence!

screens.title: A Bounce at Support
screens.text: One common confluence: price reaches a support level AND prints a bounce (like a long lower wick) there. The level and the candle agree.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support where price bounced.
screens.explanation: The level price bounced from is the support, one half of the confluence.

screens.question: "Support level + a bounce candle there" is an example of...
screens.explanation: The level and the candle agreeing is confluence.

screens.question: A bounce candle right at a support level is stronger evidence than a bounce with no level nearby.
screens.explanation: The level plus the candle agreeing (confluence) is stronger than the candle alone.

screens.question: A support level and a bounce candle together is an example of [___].
screens.explanation: Two agreeing factors at one spot is confluence.

screens.question: A support level plus a bounce candle together is an example of [___].
screens.explanation: Two agreeing factors (level + candle) at one spot is confluence.

screens.question: A bounce candle at a support level is stronger evidence than the same candle with no nearby level.
screens.explanation: The level and the candle agreeing (confluence) is stronger than the candle alone.

screens.question: What two factors combine in "level + candle signal" confluence?
options: A support/resistance level and a candle signal like a bounce wick.
The account balance and the time of day.
screens.explanation: A level plus a candle signal agreeing is this specific type of confluence.

lessons.title: Level + Pattern
lessons.celebration: You can read level-plus-pattern confluence!

screens.title: A Pattern at a Level
screens.text: Another confluence: a pattern forming right at a key level, like a double top forming at resistance. The pattern and the level reinforce each other.

screens.question: A double top forming right at a resistance level is an example of...
screens.explanation: The pattern and the level agreeing at the same spot is confluence.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this double top is testing.
screens.explanation: The resistance the two peaks test is the level reinforcing the pattern.

screens.question: Tap both peaks that make up the pattern half of this confluence.
screens.explanation: Candles 2 and 4 are the double top's two peaks, the pattern reinforcing the resistance level.

screens.question: A pattern at a key level is stronger evidence than the same pattern in empty space.
screens.explanation: The pattern plus the level (confluence) is stronger than the pattern alone.

screens.question: A double top at resistance combines a pattern with a [___].
screens.explanation: The resistance level plus the double top pattern is confluence.

screens.question: A pattern forming at a key level is an example of [___] confluence.
screens.explanation: The pattern and the level reinforcing each other is this type of confluence.

screens.question: A pattern in empty space (with no nearby level) is generally weaker evidence than the same pattern at a level.
screens.explanation: A pattern reinforced by a level (confluence) is stronger than the pattern alone.

screens.question: What two factors combine in "level + pattern" confluence?
options: A key level and a chart pattern forming there.
screens.explanation: A pattern reinforced by a level is this specific type of confluence.

lessons.title: Trend + Pullback
lessons.celebration: You can read trend-plus-pullback confluence!

screens.title: A Pullback in a Trend
screens.text: Confluence also shows up as a healthy pullback within a trend, the trend direction and the higher-low pullback agree on the up-bias.

screens.question: Tap the higher-low pullback that agrees with the uptrend.
screens.explanation: The higher-low pullback within the uptrend is the two factors (trend + pullback) agreeing.

screens.question: An uptrend plus a higher-low pullback is an example of...
screens.explanation: The trend and the pullback both pointing up is confluence.

screens.question: A higher-low pullback within an uptrend is [___] with the trend.
screens.explanation: The pullback and the trend agree. They're aligned (confluence).

screens.question: A pullback that agrees with the trend adds confluence to an up-bias read.
screens.explanation: Trend plus an aligned pullback is two factors agreeing, confluence.

screens.question: A healthy pullback within a trend is an example of [___] confluence.
screens.explanation: The trend direction and the pullback's structure agreeing is this type of confluence.

screens.question: A pullback that breaks the trend's structure would NOT add confluence to the trend's bias.
screens.explanation: Only an aligned, structure-preserving pullback adds confluence; a broken one doesn't.

screens.question: What two factors combine in "trend + pullback" confluence?
options: The overall trend direction and an aligned, healthy pullback.
screens.explanation: Trend direction plus an aligned pullback is this specific type of confluence.

lessons.title: More Confluence, Stronger Read
lessons.celebration: You can weigh confluence honestly!

screens.title: Stronger, Not Certain
screens.text: The more independent readings that agree, the stronger the read. But even lots of confluence is never a guarantee. It stacks probability, not certainty.

screens.question: Stacking more agreeing readings makes a read...
screens.explanation: More agreement strengthens the read without guaranteeing it.

screens.question: Enough confluence eventually makes an outcome guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Confluence stacks probability, never certainty. Nothing is guaranteed.

screens.question: Confluence stacks [___], not certainty.
screens.explanation: More agreeing factors raise the odds in the read, not a guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone finds three agreeing signals and bets everything, sure it "can't fail."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Even strong confluence isn't a guarantee, treating it as "can't fail" overstates the read.
screens.explanation: Confluence improves the read's odds but never removes uncertainty.

screens.question: Confluence stacks [___], not certainty.
screens.explanation: More agreeing factors raise the odds in the read, never guaranteeing an outcome.

screens.question: Enough confluence can eventually make an outcome fully guaranteed.
screens.explanation: No amount of confluence removes uncertainty entirely. It only stacks probability.

screens.question: What is the honest limit of confluence, even with many agreeing factors?
options: It has no effect on the read at all.
It strengthens the read but never guarantees the outcome.
screens.explanation: Confluence improves the odds of a read without ever making it certain.

lessons.title: Confluence Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered confluence!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of confluence, stacking agreeing readings for a stronger (not certain) view.

screens.question: Match each example to the factors it combines.
screens.explanation: Each is two factors agreeing, confluence.

screens.question: What is the honest limit of confluence?
options: It guarantees the outcome once you have enough.
It has no effect on a read.
It stacks probability but never guarantees an outcome.
screens.explanation: Confluence strengthens the read without ever making it certain.

screens.template: Confluence combines [__1__] agreeing readings for a [__2__] read, never a guarantee.
screens.explanation: Multiple agreeing factors make a stronger, not certain, read.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Confluence means ignoring the chart
options.wrong_explanation: It's reading several chart factors together.

options.label: Confluence guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.label: Stacking agreeing readings makes a stronger, still-uncertain read

screens.explanation: Stronger-but-never-certain, from agreeing factors, is the throughline.

screens.scenario: Someone treats one signal alone as if it were full confluence.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Confluence needs two or more agreeing readings, a single signal on its own isn't confluence.
One signal is always full confluence.
The number of factors doesn't matter.
screens.explanation: Confluence requires multiple agreeing factors, not a lone signal.

screens.question: This review ties together the idea of stacking [___] readings.
screens.explanation: Stacking multiple agreeing readings is the throughline of this unit.

screens.question: Confluence is about combining chart factors, not ignoring them.
screens.explanation: Confluence specifically means reading several chart factors together, not skipping analysis.

screens.question: What is the single most useful habit from this unit?
options: Ignoring levels, patterns, and trend entirely.
Looking for multiple agreeing factors before treating a read as stronger.
Acting on a single isolated signal as if it were certain.
screens.explanation: Seeking agreement across factors (without assuming certainty) is the core skill here.

lessons.title: What Is a Gap?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a gap!

screens.title: A Jump With No Trading
screens.text: A gap is a jump in price where one candle opens well away from the previous candle, leaving an empty space with no trading in between. It often happens between sessions or on news.

screens.question: The chart above shows a candle opening well above the previous candle, leaving empty space. This is a...
screens.explanation: A jump leaving empty space between candles is a gap.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle (the one that jumped away from the previous candle).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens above the prior candle's high, the gap candle.

screens.question: A gap leaves an empty space with no [___] in between.
screens.explanation: Price jumped, so no trades happened across the gap.

screens.question: A gap up opens above the previous candle's high.
screens.explanation: A gap up jumps above the prior candle, leaving space below the new open.

screens.question: A gap leaves an empty space with no [___] in between.
screens.explanation: Price jumped, so no trades happened across the gap.

screens.question: A gap can occur between one candle's close and the next candle's open.
screens.explanation: That jump between close and next open is the defining feature of a gap.

screens.question: What best describes a gap?
options: A jump where price opens well away from the prior candle, leaving empty space.
A level tested twice by price.
A candle with a tiny body and long wicks.
screens.explanation: A gap is specifically about a jump in price, leaving no trading in between.

lessons.title: Gap Up vs. Gap Down
lessons.celebration: You can tell gap direction!

screens.title: Which Way Did It Jump?
screens.text: A gap up opens above the prior candle's high; a gap down opens below the prior candle's low. Direction is just which way the jump went.

screens.question: The chart above opens well below the previous candle's low. This is a...
screens.explanation: Opening below the prior low is a gap down.

screens.question: Tap the gap-down candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens below the prior candle's low, the gap down.

screens.question: A gap down opens below the previous candle's low.
screens.explanation: A gap down jumps below the prior candle.

screens.template: A gap [__1__] opens above the prior high; a gap [__2__] opens below the prior low.
screens.explanation: Up = above prior high; down = below prior low.

screens.question: A gap up opens [___] the prior candle's high.
screens.explanation: Opening above the prior high is what defines a gap up.

screens.question: A gap down opens below the prior candle's low.
screens.explanation: Opening below the prior low is what defines a gap down.

screens.question: What separates a gap up from a gap down?
options: The direction of the jump, above the prior high, or below the prior low.
screens.explanation: Direction of the jump is what separates the two gap types.

lessons.title: Why Gaps Happen
lessons.celebration: You understand why gaps form!

screens.title: News and Session Breaks
screens.text: Gaps commonly form when price can't trade continuously, overnight between sessions, or when news hits and the next available price is far from the last.

screens.question: Gaps commonly form because of...
options: session breaks or news, when trading isn't continuous.
screens.explanation: When price can't trade continuously (overnight, news), the next price can be far away, a gap.

screens.question: Gaps commonly appear between sessions or around news.
screens.explanation: Non-continuous trading (overnight/news) is a common cause of gaps.

screens.question: A gap forms when trading isn't [___], so the next price is far from the last.
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading lets price jump, forming a gap.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes gaps only appear randomly for no reason.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Gaps commonly have causes, session breaks or news, not pure randomness.
Gaps only depend on candle color.
screens.explanation: Gaps usually reflect non-continuous trading (sessions/news), not randomness.

screens.question: Gaps commonly form when trading isn't [___].
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading (overnight/news) lets price jump, forming a gap.

screens.question: News released while the market is closed is a commonly cited cause of gaps.
screens.explanation: Overnight or weekend news is a commonly cited reason for the next open to jump.

screens.question: Why do gaps commonly form between trading sessions?
options: Trading isn't continuous, so news can shift sentiment before the next open.
screens.explanation: Non-continuous trading is the commonly cited reason gaps form between sessions.

lessons.title: The Gap Fill
lessons.celebration: You understand gap fills!

screens.title: Returning to the Gap
screens.text: A "gap fill" is when price later returns to trade back through the empty gap space. It happens often but not always, a tendency, never a guarantee.

screens.question: A "gap fill" is when price...
options: returns to trade back through the gap's empty space.
screens.explanation: Filling the gap means price comes back through the empty space.

screens.question: Every gap is guaranteed to fill.
screens.explanation: Gaps fill often but not always. It's a tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A gap fill happens [___], not always.
screens.explanation: Gap fills are a common tendency, not a certainty.

screens.question: How should you read "gaps often fill"?

options.label: As a common tendency, not a guarantee
As a certainty every time
options.wrong_explanation: Not every gap fills.

options.label: As something that never happens
options.wrong_explanation: Gap fills are common, just not guaranteed.

screens.explanation: "Often fills" is a descriptive tendency, never a guarantee.

screens.question: A gap fill happens [___], not always.
screens.explanation: Gap fills are a common tendency, not a certainty.

screens.question: Every gap is guaranteed to eventually fill.
screens.explanation: Gaps fill often but not always. It's a tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.question: What is a "gap fill," in simple terms?
options: Price later trading back through the gap's empty space.
A gap that never gets touched again.
screens.explanation: A gap fill specifically describes price retracing back through the skipped range.

lessons.title: Gaps Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered gaps!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of gaps, direction, causes, and gap fills.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Opens above the prior candle's high
Opens below the prior candle's low
Price returning through the gap's empty space
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the one that gapped away from the previous candle.

screens.question: What causes most gaps?
options: Non-continuous trading, session breaks or news.
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading is the common cause of gaps.

screens.question: Which best summarizes gaps?

options.label: Random marks with no cause
options.wrong_explanation: Gaps usually have a cause.

options.label: Gaps that always fill immediately
options.wrong_explanation: Not every gap fills.

options.label: Jumps leaving empty space, from discontinuous trading, that often (not always) fill

screens.explanation: Cause + a fill tendency (not guarantee) is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together gap direction, causes, and [___].
screens.explanation: All three core ideas from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: Even after this review, a gap fill should be read as a tendency, not a certainty.
screens.explanation: This remains true throughout, a common tendency, never a guarantee.

screens.question: What is the single most useful habit from this unit?
options: Reading gap direction and cause, without assuming a fill is guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Reading gaps descriptively, without assuming a guaranteed fill, is the core skill here.

lessons.title: What Is a Timeframe?
lessons.celebration: You understand timeframes!

screens.title: Each Candle's Duration
screens.text: A timeframe is how much time each candle represents, a 1-minute candle, an hourly candle, a daily candle. The same market looks different on different timeframes.

screens.question: A "timeframe" describes...
options: how much time each candle represents.
screens.explanation: Timeframe is the duration each candle covers (1m, 1h, 1d, …).

screens.question: The same market can look different on different timeframes.
screens.explanation: A move that's a blip on a daily chart can be a whole trend on a 1-minute chart.

screens.question: A daily candle represents [___] time than a 1-minute candle.
screens.explanation: Each daily candle covers a full day, far more than a minute.

screens.question: Which is a "higher" timeframe?
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes cover more time per candle (daily > hourly > 1-minute).

screens.question: A timeframe describes how much [___] each candle represents.
screens.explanation: Timeframe defines the duration each candle covers.

screens.question: The same market can look different across different timeframes.
screens.explanation: A move that's a blip on a daily chart can look like a full trend on a 1-minute chart.

screens.question: What determines what a single candle represents?
screens.explanation: Timeframe determines the duration each candle summarizes.

lessons.title: Higher vs. Lower Timeframe
lessons.celebration: You can compare timeframes!

screens.title: Zoomed Out vs. Zoomed In
screens.text: A higher timeframe (daily) is the zoomed-out big picture; a lower timeframe (1-minute) is the zoomed-in detail. Both describe the same market at different scales.

screens.question: The higher timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes are the big-picture, zoomed-out view.

screens.question: The lower timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Lower timeframes zoom in on fine detail within the bigger move.

screens.template: A higher timeframe is more [__1__]; a lower timeframe is more [__2__].
screens.explanation: Higher = zoomed out (big picture); lower = zoomed in (detail).

screens.question: Higher and lower timeframes describe the same market at different scales.
screens.explanation: They're the same price data viewed zoomed out vs zoomed in.

screens.question: A higher timeframe shows the [___] picture.
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes compress more history into each candle, the big picture.

screens.question: A lower timeframe shows more fine-grained detail over a shorter period.
screens.explanation: Lower timeframes zoom in, offering finer detail over less total time.

screens.question: What do higher and lower timeframes have in common?
options: Both describe the same market, just at different scales.
They describe two entirely unrelated markets.
Only one of them is ever accurate.
screens.explanation: They're the same underlying price data, viewed at different zoom levels.

lessons.title: Trends Can Differ by Timeframe
lessons.celebration: You can read trends across timeframes!

screens.title: Up Here, Down There
screens.text: A market can be in an uptrend on the higher timeframe while showing a short-term downtrend on a lower one. A pullback on the daily can look like a full downtrend on the 1-minute.

screens.question: The chart above is a higher-timeframe uptrend with a dip. On a lower timeframe, that dip might look like a...
screens.explanation: A higher-timeframe pullback can appear as a full downtrend when zoomed in.

screens.question: A pullback on a higher timeframe can look like a downtrend on a lower timeframe.
screens.explanation: Zooming into a pullback can show a complete small downtrend.

screens.question: A market can trend one way on a higher timeframe and [___] on a lower one.
screens.explanation: Trends can differ across timeframes for the same market.

screens.scenario: Someone reads only the 1-minute chart and ignores the daily trend entirely.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Ignoring the higher timeframe misses the big-picture trend the short-term move sits inside.
screens.explanation: The higher-timeframe context frames what the lower-timeframe move means.

screens.question: A pullback on a higher timeframe can look like a full [___] on a lower one.
screens.explanation: Zooming into a higher-timeframe pullback can reveal what looks like a complete small downtrend.

screens.question: Trend direction can differ depending on which timeframe you're viewing.
screens.explanation: The same market can trend one way on one timeframe and differently on another.

screens.question: Why might a chart look like it's trending down on a 1-minute chart but up on the daily?
options: Timeframes never affect how a trend appears.
The two timeframes are showing completely different assets.
The lower timeframe may just be showing a pullback within the larger uptrend.
screens.explanation: A higher-timeframe pullback can appear as its own trend when zoomed in.

lessons.title: Top-Down Reading
lessons.celebration: You understand top-down reading!

screens.title: Big Picture First
screens.text: "Top-down" reading means checking the higher timeframe first for the big-picture trend and key levels, then zooming into a lower one for detail. Context first, detail second.

screens.question: Top-down reading starts with the...
screens.explanation: Top-down means big-picture (higher timeframe) first, then detail.

screens.question: A top-down reading process:
items: Check the higher timeframe for the big-picture trend
Note the higher-timeframe key levels
Zoom into a lower timeframe for detail
Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context
correct_order: Check the higher timeframe for the big-picture trend
Note the higher-timeframe key levels
Zoom into a lower timeframe for detail
Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context
screens.explanation: Context first (higher timeframe), then zoom in. That's top-down.

screens.question: Top-down reading checks the big-picture timeframe before the detail one.
screens.explanation: Big picture first, then detail, is the top-down idea.

screens.question: Top-down reading sets [___] from the higher timeframe first.
screens.explanation: The higher timeframe provides the context to read the detail within.

screens.question: Top-down reading checks the [___] timeframe first.
screens.explanation: Top-down means starting with the big picture (higher timeframe) before zooming in.

screens.question: Top-down reading means checking the lower timeframe before the higher one.
screens.explanation: Top-down specifically means higher timeframe first, then lower for detail.

screens.question: What is the point of checking a higher timeframe before a lower one?
options: It replaces the need to ever look at a lower timeframe.
It sets big-picture context before looking at fine detail.
screens.explanation: Context from the higher timeframe frames how the lower-timeframe detail is read.

lessons.title: Timeframe Alignment
lessons.celebration: You can read timeframe alignment!

screens.title: When They Agree
screens.text: When multiple timeframes point the same way, say, an uptrend on both the higher and lower timeframe, that agreement is a form of confluence. It's stronger, but still not a guarantee.

screens.question: When the higher and lower timeframe both trend up, that agreement is a form of...
screens.explanation: Agreement across timeframes is confluence, a stronger read.

screens.question: Timeframe agreement makes a read stronger but not guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Alignment stacks evidence (confluence), which is stronger but never certain.

screens.question: When timeframes agree, it adds [___] to the read.
screens.explanation: Agreeing timeframes are another agreeing factor, confluence.

screens.scenario: Someone sees both timeframes agree and assumes the trade "can't lose."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Timeframe agreement is stronger evidence but never a guarantee, "can't lose" overstates it.
screens.explanation: Even aligned timeframes only stack probability, not certainty.

screens.question: Timeframes agreeing with each other is a form of [___].
screens.explanation: Multiple timeframes pointing the same way is an example of confluence.

screens.question: Timeframe alignment guarantees the trade idea will work out.
screens.explanation: Alignment strengthens the read but never guarantees the outcome.

screens.question: What happens when the higher and lower timeframe both point the same direction?
options: That agreement is read as a stronger, more confluent signal.
It has no added meaning at all.
screens.explanation: Agreement across timeframes adds confluence, stronger, but not certain.

lessons.title: Multi-Timeframe Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered multi-timeframe basics!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of timeframes, higher vs lower, top-down reading, and alignment.

screens.question: Match each idea to its meaning.
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's ideas.

screens.template: Read the [__1__] timeframe for context, then the [__2__] one for detail.
screens.explanation: Higher for context, lower for detail, top-down.

screens.question: Why check more than one timeframe?
options: The big picture frames what the short-term move means.
Because lower timeframes are the only ones that matter.
To make the chart more colorful.
screens.explanation: Context from the higher timeframe frames the lower-timeframe detail.

screens.question: Which best summarizes multi-timeframe reading?

options.label: Read big-picture context first, then detail, alignment adds confluence, not certainty
Timeframe agreement guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: Alignment isn't a guarantee.

options.label: Only the lowest timeframe matters
options.wrong_explanation: Context comes from higher timeframes.

screens.explanation: Context-first reading with alignment as confluence (not certainty) is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together timeframes, higher vs lower, and [___].
screens.explanation: All the core ideas from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: Even after this review, timeframe alignment should be read as added confluence, not a guarantee.
screens.explanation: This remains true throughout, stronger evidence, never a certainty.

screens.question: What is the single most useful habit from this unit?
options: Only ever looking at one single timeframe forever.
Reading the higher timeframe for context before zooming into the lower one.
screens.explanation: Top-down, context-first reading across timeframes is the core skill here.

lessons.title: Pattern Speed Round
lessons.celebration: You can name any pattern fast!

screens.title: Name What You See
screens.text: Rapid-fire identification across everything you've learned. Read each chart and name it.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same resistance is a double top.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle is a head & shoulders.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Flat top with rising lows is an ascending triangle.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A strong up pole with a small downward flag is a bull flag.

screens.question: Which structure is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Falling and converging is a falling wedge.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three troughs with a lower middle is an inverse head & shoulders.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A flat bottom with falling highs is a descending triangle.

screens.question: The chart above shows a symmetrical triangle.
screens.explanation: Lower highs and higher lows converging, with no flat side, is a symmetrical triangle.

lessons.title: Level Reading Round
lessons.celebration: You can mark levels anywhere!

screens.title: Find the Level
screens.text: Read the key level on each chart and mark it.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance on this chart.
screens.explanation: The level the highs were rejected at is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support on this chart.
screens.explanation: The level the lows bounced from is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance of this triangle.
screens.explanation: The flat top of the ascending triangle is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the range's support.
screens.explanation: The floor of the range is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the two troughs of the head & shoulders.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support in this range.
screens.explanation: The floor of the range is its support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this breakout chart.
screens.explanation: The level price cleared with momentum is the resistance being broken out of.

screens.question: Drag across every candle in this range's consolidation.
screens.explanation: All six candles here stay bounded between the support and resistance.

screens.question: Marking a level is a matter of judgment, not an exact science.
screens.explanation: Support and resistance are estimated zones based on past reactions, not precise fixed lines.

lessons.title: Candle Reading Round
lessons.celebration: You can read any candle!

screens.title: Tap the Candle
screens.text: Read each chart and tap the candle described.

screens.question: Tap the doji.
screens.explanation: The middle candle's tiny body with wicks both sides is the doji.

screens.question: Tap the hammer.
screens.explanation: The last candle, small body up top, long lower wick, is the hammer.

screens.question: Tap the shooting star.
screens.explanation: The last candle, small body down low, long upper wick, is the shooting star.

screens.question: Tap the engulfing candle.
screens.explanation: The larger down candle covering the prior up candle is the bearish engulfing.

screens.question: Tap the big-momentum candle.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied, near-wickless candle is the momentum (marubozu) candle.

screens.question: Tap the spinning top.
screens.explanation: The small body with even wicks on both sides is the spinning top.

screens.question: Tap the inverted hammer.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick with a small low body after a decline is the inverted hammer.

screens.question: Reading candles well means considering both body and wicks together.
screens.explanation: Body and wicks together tell the fuller story of a candle's period.

lessons.title: Multi-Candle Round
lessons.celebration: You can tap groups of candles!

screens.title: Tap All That Match
screens.text: Some reads need more than one candle. Tap every candle that matches.

screens.question: Tap BOTH peaks of the double top.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two peaks at resistance.

screens.question: Tap BOTH troughs of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two troughs at support.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders of the head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat resistance.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push into the flat resistance.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat support in this descending triangle.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push down into the flat support.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form this head & shoulders' neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head.

screens.question: Drag across the candles that make up this bull flag's pause.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole.

screens.question: Multi-select questions ask you to identify more than one matching candle at once.
screens.explanation: That's the defining feature of this question type, unlike single tap-the-candle questions.

lessons.title: Reversal or Continuation?
lessons.celebration: You can classify the setup type!

screens.title: Turn or Keep Going?
screens.text: Classify each chart as a reversal shape (a possible turn) or a continuation shape (a likely resume), descriptively.

screens.question: Is a head & shoulders commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn after an up-move).
screens.explanation: Head & shoulders is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Is a bull flag commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Continuation (a pause that often resumes up).
screens.explanation: Flags are continuation patterns.

screens.question: Is a double bottom commonly read as a reversal or continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn up after a down-move).
screens.explanation: A double bottom is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Match each to its usual category.
screens.explanation: Reversal shapes suggest a turn; continuation shapes suggest a resume.

screens.question: Every reversal shape guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: Categories describe tendencies; nothing is guaranteed.

screens.question: Is a triangle commonly read as continuation, reversal, or either?
options: Either. It can break in either direction, though flat sides add a bias.
screens.explanation: Triangles can break either way, though ascending/descending triangles carry a directional bias.

screens.question: Wedges are commonly read as reversal shapes despite their sloped direction.
screens.explanation: A rising wedge (despite rising) and falling wedge (despite falling) are both commonly read as reversal-biased.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together
lessons.celebration: You can read a full chart!

screens.title: Everything at Once
screens.text: Combine pattern, level, and candle reads on each chart, the whole intermediate skillset.

screens.question: On the chart above, two peaks stall at resistance and roll over. Best read?

options.label: A double top at resistance, a reversal shape at a level (confluence)
A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: Confluence isn't a guarantee.

options.label: A bull flag
options.wrong_explanation: This is two peaks at resistance, not a pole-and-flag.

screens.explanation: Pattern + level agreeing is a confluent, descriptive read, not a guarantee.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this double top.
screens.explanation: The two peaks mark the resistance being tested.

screens.question: Tap the second peak.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the second peak at resistance.

screens.question: A pattern that lines up with a key level is stronger evidence than the pattern alone.
screens.explanation: Pattern-plus-level is confluence, stronger than either alone.

screens.scenario: Someone reads one perfect pattern and ignores the level, the trend, and the candles around it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A full read combines pattern, level, trend, and candles, not one factor in isolation.
screens.explanation: The strongest reads combine several agreeing factors, not a lone signal.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the two troughs framing the head.

screens.question: Combining pattern, level, and candle reads gives a fuller picture than any one alone.
screens.explanation: This unit's core lesson is that combining reads (confluence) is stronger than a single factor.

lessons.title: Intermediate Mastery Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Intermediate level!

screens.title: You Can Read Charts
screens.text: You've learned patterns, levels, candles, structure, and confluence, and to read them all descriptively, never as guarantees. A final check.

screens.question: What ties this whole level together?
options: Reading charts descriptively, patterns, levels, and candles as clues, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Descriptive, context-aware chart reading is the throughline of the level.

screens.question: Match each skill to what it reads.
pairs: Shapes like double tops, triangles, flags
screens.explanation: A recap of the three core reading skills.

screens.template: The strongest reads combine [__1__] agreeing factors, but are still [__2__] guarantees.
screens.explanation: Confluence is stronger but never a guarantee.

screens.question: Which best summarizes the Intermediate level?

options.label: Read patterns, levels, and candles together, descriptively, as probabilities, not certainties
A list of shapes with no context
options.wrong_explanation: Context and confluence are the point.

options.label: A system of guaranteed signals
options.wrong_explanation: Nothing here is guaranteed.

screens.explanation: Context-aware, descriptive, probability-minded reading is what this level built.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this level and starts treating every pattern as a guaranteed trade.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Everything here is a descriptive clue read with context, never a guaranteed trade.
Context stops mattering after this level.
screens.explanation: The whole level teaches probability-minded, descriptive reading, not guarantees.

screens.question: This level's core skill is combining pattern, level, and candle reads through [___].
screens.explanation: Confluence, combining multiple agreeing factors, has been the throughline of this level.

screens.question: Everything in the Intermediate level stays descriptive, never a guaranteed signal.
screens.explanation: This has been true across every unit in this level, description, not guarantees.

screens.question: What's the single biggest skill gained across this entire level?
options: Memorizing one guaranteed rule for every situation.
Reading charts by combining patterns, levels, and candles as descriptive, probability-based clues.
screens.explanation: Combining multiple descriptive reads is the core Intermediate-level skill.

lessons.title: Market Sessions Overview
lessons.celebration: You understand the basic session structure!

screens.title: Pre-Market and the Open
screens.text: Before the standard session, "pre-market" trading happens with thinner liquidity. "The open" is the first stretch of the standard session, commonly the most active part of the day.

screens.question: "Pre-market" refers to...
options: A period when markets are fully closed.
Trading before the standard session begins.
screens.explanation: Pre-market is the extended session before the standard open.

screens.question: Pre-market trading commonly has thinner liquidity than the standard session.
screens.explanation: Fewer participants are commonly active during pre-market hours.

screens.question: "The open" refers to the first stretch of the [___] session.
screens.explanation: "The open" describes the beginning of the standard trading session.

screens.question: Match the session period to its common trait.
pairs: Commonly the most active part of the day
The main trading hours most participants use
screens.explanation: Each session period commonly has a distinct liquidity and activity profile.

screens.question: Why is "the open" commonly considered especially active?

options.label: Trading is impossible during the open
options.wrong_explanation: The open is trading, just often the busiest part.

options.label: The open has no relationship to activity level
options.wrong_explanation: The open is commonly one of the most active periods.

options.label: Many participants who were waiting through pre-market act once standard hours begin

screens.explanation: Pent-up activity from pre-market commonly concentrates right at the open.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes pre-market liquidity is always identical to the standard session's.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Pre-market commonly has thinner liquidity than the standard session, treating them as identical ignores that difference.
Pre-market always has more liquidity than standard hours.
screens.explanation: Liquidity commonly varies a lot by session, a pattern worth being aware of.

lessons.title: Midday Lull and Power Hour
lessons.celebration: You understand the midday lull and power hour!

screens.title: The Quiet Middle, the Busy End
screens.text: Midday ("lunch") is commonly a quieter stretch with reduced activity. "Power hour" is the final hour of the standard session, commonly picking activity back up.

screens.question: The midday period is commonly described as...
options: Quieter, with reduced activity compared to the open or close.
The single busiest period of the entire day.
A period when the market is fully closed.
screens.explanation: Midday is commonly a lull in activity between the open and the close.

screens.question: "Power hour" refers to the final hour of the standard session.
screens.explanation: That's the standard meaning of the term.

screens.question: Power hour commonly sees activity [___] compared to the midday lull.
screens.explanation: Activity commonly increases again heading into the close.

screens.question: Match the session period to its common activity level.
pairs: Busy-quiet-busy across open, midday, and close
screens.explanation: Standard sessions commonly follow this busy-quiet-busy activity pattern.

screens.question: Why might power hour commonly see increased activity?

options.label: Power hour has no relationship to activity level
options.wrong_explanation: It's commonly one of the more active periods.

options.label: Participants commonly position or adjust ahead of the session's close
The market briefly reopens during power hour
options.wrong_explanation: Power hour is part of the same standard session, not a reopening.

screens.explanation: End-of-day positioning is a commonly cited reason for power hour's added activity.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes midday is always the busiest part of the trading day.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Session timing has no effect on typical activity level.
Midday is commonly the quieter lull, not the busiest period. That's more commonly the open or power hour.
Midday is always busier than the open.
screens.explanation: The open and power hour are more commonly cited as the busier periods, not midday.

lessons.title: After-Hours Trading
lessons.celebration: You understand after-hours trading!

screens.title: After the Bell
screens.text: "After-hours" trading happens once the standard session ends, commonly with thinner liquidity, similar in spirit to pre-market, just on the other side of the day.

screens.question: "After-hours" trading refers to...
options: A period when no trading of any kind occurs.
Trading only during the standard session.
Trading after the standard session has ended.
screens.explanation: After-hours describes the extended session following the standard close.

screens.question: After-hours trading commonly has thinner liquidity, similar to pre-market.
screens.explanation: Both extended sessions commonly see reduced participation compared to standard hours.

screens.question: After-hours is the [___]-session counterpart to pre-market.
screens.explanation: Both are extended sessions, just on opposite sides of the standard hours.

screens.question: Match the extended session to its position relative to standard hours.
pairs: Commonly thinner liquidity than standard hours
screens.explanation: Pre-market and after-hours are the two extended sessions bookending the standard day.

screens.question: Why might a large order have a bigger price impact after-hours?

options.label: Order size never affects price impact
options.wrong_explanation: With thinner liquidity, size matters even more.

options.label: After-hours liquidity always exceeds standard-hours liquidity
options.wrong_explanation: The reverse is more commonly true.

options.label: Thinner liquidity commonly means the same order size has more relative price impact

screens.explanation: This connects the liquidity idea from earlier units to the after-hours session specifically.

screens.scenario: Someone expects an after-hours fill to behave identically to a standard-hours fill.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Liquidity has no relationship to fill behavior.
After-hours fills always match standard-hours fills exactly.
Thinner after-hours liquidity can commonly lead to bigger gaps between expected and actual fill prices.
screens.explanation: As covered in the Orders & Execution unit, thinner liquidity commonly affects fill behavior.

lessons.title: Earnings Reports
lessons.celebration: You understand earnings reports!

screens.title: A Scheduled Information Event
screens.text: An earnings report is a company's scheduled release of financial results, commonly associated with sharply increased volatility around the release.

screens.question: An "earnings report" is...
options: A company's scheduled release of financial results.
screens.explanation: Earnings reports are scheduled releases of a company's financial performance.

screens.question: Earnings reports are commonly associated with increased volatility around the release.
screens.explanation: New information hitting the market at once commonly produces sharper price swings.

screens.question: Earnings reports are commonly [___] in advance, unlike random news.
screens.explanation: Being scheduled in advance is what distinguishes earnings from random breaking news.

screens.question: Match the event to its commonly cited trait.
pairs: Scheduled, often volatile around the release
A commonly cited example of a scheduling-driven gap
A commonly cited effect around the release
screens.explanation: Earnings connect directly back to the gaps and volatility concepts from earlier units.

screens.question: Why are earnings reports commonly linked to gaps?

options.label: Gaps only happen for reasons unrelated to earnings
options.wrong_explanation: Earnings are a commonly cited gap driver.

options.label: New information released while the market is closed can shift the next open sharply
Earnings reports never affect price at all
options.wrong_explanation: They're commonly linked to some of the largest volatility events.

screens.explanation: This ties the earlier Gaps unit directly to a commonly cited real-world cause.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes earnings reports have no relationship to price volatility.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Only random, unscheduled news can affect volatility.
Earnings reports are commonly associated with some of the sharpest volatility spikes around their release.
Earnings reports never affect price behavior.
screens.explanation: Scheduled information events like earnings are commonly cited volatility drivers.

lessons.title: Economic Releases
lessons.celebration: You understand economic releases!

screens.title: Broader Information Events
screens.text: Economic releases (like employment or inflation data) are scheduled reports about the broader economy, commonly associated with volatility across many assets at once, not just one company.

screens.question: Economic releases commonly affect...
options: Many assets at once, since they describe the broader economy.
Nothing at all in the markets.
screens.explanation: Broader economic data commonly moves many assets simultaneously, unlike company-specific earnings.

screens.question: Economic releases are commonly scheduled in advance, similar to earnings reports.
screens.explanation: Both are commonly known events with a set release time.

screens.question: Economic releases commonly affect [___] assets at once, unlike single-company earnings.
screens.explanation: Broad economic data is commonly linked to market-wide moves, not one company alone.

screens.question: Match the event type to its commonly cited scope.
pairs: Many assets across the broader market
Scheduled events commonly linked to volatility
screens.explanation: Scope (one company vs. the broader market) is the key difference between these two event types.

screens.question: Why might economic releases commonly cause broader market volatility?

options.label: They have no relationship to market behavior
options.wrong_explanation: They're commonly cited as broad volatility drivers.

options.label: They describe the broader economy, which can affect sentiment across many assets at once
They only ever affect a single company
options.wrong_explanation: That describes earnings, not economic releases.

screens.explanation: Broad economic data commonly shifts sentiment market-wide, unlike a single company's earnings.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes economic releases only affect the specific company mentioned in the report.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Economic releases and earnings reports describe the same scope.
Economic releases commonly affect many assets across the market, not just one specific company.
Economic releases always affect only one company.
screens.explanation: Economic releases are commonly cited as broader, market-wide events.

lessons.title: Why Volatility Spikes Around News
lessons.celebration: You understand why volatility spikes around news!

screens.title: New Information Hits at Once
screens.text: Volatility commonly spikes around scheduled news because a lot of new information gets absorbed by the market all at once, rather than gradually.

screens.question: Why does volatility commonly spike around scheduled news?
options: New information gets absorbed by the market all at once, rather than gradually.
News releases always calm the market down.
Volatility has no relationship to news timing.
screens.explanation: A sudden burst of new information commonly produces sharper, faster price swings.

screens.question: Volatility spikes around news are commonly temporary, not a permanent state.
screens.explanation: Volatility commonly settles back down after the initial reaction to new information.

screens.question: Volatility spikes because information is absorbed all at [___], not gradually.
screens.explanation: A sudden burst of information, rather than a gradual release, is what commonly drives the spike.

screens.question: Match the concept to its commonly cited connection to news.
pairs: Common sources of sudden new information
A commonly cited effect of that sudden information
Another commonly cited effect around scheduled news
screens.explanation: These concepts connect back to ideas from Gaps and Market Mechanics earlier in the course.

screens.question: Which best explains why news-driven volatility is commonly temporary?

options.label: News-driven volatility never settles back down
options.wrong_explanation: It's commonly described as temporary, not permanent.

options.label: Once the market absorbs the new information, activity commonly settles back toward typical levels
Volatility has no relationship to how information gets absorbed
options.wrong_explanation: This lesson's core point is that connection.

screens.explanation: Volatility spikes are commonly read as a temporary reaction, not a lasting new state.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes volatility around a news event will stay permanently elevated forever.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: News has no relationship to volatility at all.
News-driven volatility is commonly temporary, settling back down once the information is absorbed.
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited temporary pattern, not a permanent shift.

lessons.title: Trading Around News
lessons.celebration: You understand the cautious approach to trading around news!

screens.title: Extra Caution, Not a Guarantee
screens.text: Because of the added volatility and wider spreads commonly seen around news, many traders commonly apply extra caution, like reduced size or wider stops, rather than a rigid rule.

screens.question: A commonly cited approach around scheduled news is to...
options: Always dramatically increase size right before news.
Ignore risk management entirely during news.
Apply extra caution, like reduced size or wider stops.
screens.explanation: Extra caution around the added volatility is a commonly cited approach, not a guaranteed rule.

screens.question: Spreads commonly widen around major scheduled news.
screens.explanation: Increased uncertainty commonly widens the bid/ask spread around news events.

screens.question: Extra caution around news is a commonly cited [___], not a rigid universal rule.
screens.explanation: Different traders commonly apply this idea differently. It's a general approach, not one fixed rule.

screens.question: Match the news-related risk factor to its commonly cited behavior.
pairs: Commonly reduced by some traders around news
screens.explanation: These three factors are commonly discussed together when planning around news events.

screens.question: Why might someone reduce position size around scheduled news?

options.label: Because news guarantees a losing trade
options.wrong_explanation: News doesn't guarantee an outcome, it adds uncertainty.

options.label: Because added volatility and wider spreads can increase risk per trade around news
Because position size never matters around news
options.wrong_explanation: Size is exactly the risk lever some traders adjust.

screens.explanation: This connects the Risk Management unit's ideas directly to a real-world scenario.

screens.scenario: Someone dramatically increases their position size right before a major scheduled news release, assuming it's the same as any other moment.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: News commonly brings added volatility and wider spreads. Many traders apply extra caution, not more size, around it.
News has no relationship to typical risk levels.
Increasing size before news always leads to bigger profits.
screens.explanation: This ignores the commonly cited added risk around scheduled news events.

lessons.title: Why Charts Behave Differently by Session
lessons.celebration: You understand session-based differences in chart behavior!

screens.title: Same Asset, Different Rhythm
screens.text: The same chart can behave differently depending on the session, thinner, choppier moves in pre/after-hours; different rhythms across the open, midday, and power hour.

screens.question: Why might a chart look different during pre-market versus the standard open?
options: Liquidity and participation commonly differ by session, changing the chart's rhythm.
Session timing has no relationship to chart behavior.
Charts are always identical no matter the session.
screens.explanation: Session-specific liquidity differences are commonly cited as changing how a chart behaves.

screens.question: The open, midday, and power hour commonly have different typical rhythms within the same day.
screens.explanation: Each session period commonly carries its own typical activity level, as covered earlier in this unit.

screens.question: Session context is one more form of [___] to combine with everything else you've read.
screens.explanation: Like other context factors in this course, session timing adds to (not replaces) the full read.

screens.question: Match the session to a commonly cited chart trait.
pairs: Often the most active, sometimes sharpest moves
screens.explanation: A recap of the session-based rhythm differences covered across this unit.

screens.question: Why combine session awareness with everything else you've learned?

options.label: Because it's one more piece of context that can change how a chart's move should be read
Because session timing has no bearing on reading a chart
options.wrong_explanation: This whole unit shows it commonly does.

options.label: Because session timing replaces the need for any other analysis
options.wrong_explanation: It's one added factor, not a replacement for everything else.

screens.explanation: Session context is one more descriptive factor to combine with the rest of your reading skills.

screens.scenario: Someone reads a choppy, thin pre-market move exactly the same way as an identical-looking move during the standard open.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Pre-market and the standard open always behave identically.
Session timing never matters for reading a chart.
Session context (liquidity, participation) commonly changes how the same-looking move should be read.
screens.explanation: The same shape can carry different meaning depending on which session it happened in.

lessons.title: Trading Sessions & News Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Trading Sessions & News unit!

screens.title: Bringing It All Together
screens.text: A final review of market sessions, earnings, economic releases, news-driven volatility, and reading session context.

screens.question: Every session and news concept in this unit adds context, rather than guaranteeing an outcome.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every lesson in this unit.

screens.question: After-hours is the extended-session counterpart to [___].
screens.explanation: Reviewing the pairing from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do earnings reports and economic releases have in common?
options: Both are scheduled information events commonly linked to increased volatility.
Neither has any relationship to price behavior.
Both are completely random and unscheduled.
screens.explanation: Both are scheduled events commonly tied to volatility, differing mainly in scope.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Extended sessions with commonly thinner liquidity
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.template: News commonly brings [__1__] volatility and [__2__] spreads, calling for extra caution.
screens.explanation: Higher volatility and wider spreads are the commonly cited reasons for added caution around news.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Session and news timing are irrelevant to reading a chart
options.wrong_explanation: This unit's whole point is that they matter.

options.label: Session and news context shape how charts behave, descriptive factors, not guarantees
Sessions and news guarantee specific price outcomes
options.wrong_explanation: This contradicts the whole unit.

screens.explanation: Descriptive, context-adding session and news awareness is the throughline of this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts treating news events as guaranteed trading opportunities.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: News adds volatility and context, but never a guaranteed outcome. This unit has framed it as added risk to manage, not a guaranteed opportunity.
Session and news context never matter after this unit.
screens.explanation: This unit consistently frames news as added context and risk, never a guaranteed opportunity.
