lessons.title: What Is Risk Per Trade?
lessons.celebration: You understand risk per trade!

screens.title: How Much Is on the Line
screens.text: Risk per trade describes how much of your capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.

screens.question: Risk per trade describes how much capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of risk per trade.

screens.question: Risking a larger portion of your account on one trade is generally considered [___] risk.
screens.explanation: A bigger portion of capital at stake means a larger risk for that trade.

screens.question: Why is thinking about risk per trade useful, in general terms?
options: It helps quantify how much a single loss could realistically cost.
It guarantees the trade will be profitable.
It removes the need for a stop-loss entirely.
screens.explanation: Quantifying potential loss is the whole point of thinking about risk per trade.

screens.question: Match the risk framing to its description.
pairs: How much could be lost on one specific trade
The combined risk across all open positions
How much loss someone is generally comfortable with
screens.explanation: These related concepts together build a fuller risk picture.

screens.template: Risking 10% of an account on one trade is generally considered a [__1__] risk than risking [__2__]%.
screens.explanation: A larger percentage risked per trade means a bigger potential impact from one loss.

screens.question: A simple way to think through risk before placing a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
screens.explanation: This process turns an abstract risk tolerance into a concrete plan.

screens.question: Which best describes "risk per trade"?

options.label: The total amount of money in your account
options.wrong_explanation: That's your total account size, not the risk on one trade.

options.label: How much of your capital could be lost if a single trade goes against you
A guarantee of how much you will actually lose
options.wrong_explanation: It's the potential loss if things go against you, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.explanation: Risk per trade specifically describes the potential loss on a single position.

screens.scenario: Someone risks 50% of their account on a single trade because they feel very confident about it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have felt even more confident before risking that much.
They should have risked their entire account instead.
Risking such a large portion of an account on one trade exposes it to severe damage from a single loss.
screens.explanation: Confidence in an outcome doesn't remove risk, a single loss at that size could be very damaging.

screens.question: Risk per trade is commonly kept [___] and consistent across trades.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade is a commonly recommended habit.

screens.question: Risking a large percent of the account on one trade is generally considered lower risk than a small percent.
screens.explanation: A larger percentage at risk is generally considered higher, not lower, risk.

lessons.title: Position Sizing Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand position sizing!

screens.title: How Much to Put In
screens.text: Position sizing is the process of deciding how much capital to allocate to a single trade, commonly derived from your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop-loss level.
screens.explanation: A sound position size is commonly calculated backward from how much you're willing to risk.

screens.question: The amount of capital allocated to a single trade is commonly called its [___].
screens.explanation: "Position size" describes how much of your capital a single trade uses.

screens.question: What is a commonly cited way to calculate an appropriate position size?
options: Start from your maximum acceptable dollar risk, then work out the size that keeps a stop-loss hit within that amount.
Randomly pick a size that feels right in the moment.
Always use the same position size regardless of the stop-loss distance.
screens.explanation: Working backward from acceptable risk is a commonly cited, methodical approach.

screens.question: Match the risk concept to its description.
pairs: How much capital is allocated to a single trade
How far price can move before the risk limit is hit
The most you're willing to lose on that trade
screens.explanation: These three concepts together determine an appropriate position size.

screens.template: A wider stop-loss distance generally calls for a [__1__] position size, to keep the same dollar [__2__].
screens.explanation: If the stop is further away, a smaller size keeps the total dollar risk the same.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate position size before a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
screens.explanation: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop level, not chosen randomly.

screens.question: Which of these two hypothetical trades has the better risk-to-reward ratio, as described?

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $100 (1:1)
options.wrong_explanation: Reward here is equal to risk, not more favorable.

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $300 (1:3)
options.detail: Reward is three times the risk

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $50 (2:1 against)
options.wrong_explanation: This risks more than it could potentially gain.

screens.explanation: A higher reward relative to the risk taken is generally considered a more favorable ratio, on paper.

screens.scenario: Someone uses the exact same position size on every trade, regardless of how far away their stop-loss is.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A fixed position size regardless of stop distance means dollar risk varies unpredictably between trades.
They should remove stop-losses to simplify things.
They should always use an even bigger position size instead.
screens.explanation: Adjusting position size to the stop-loss distance is how consistent dollar risk is commonly maintained.

screens.question: Position size is commonly derived from your risk amount and [___] distance.
screens.explanation: Position size is worked backward from your dollar risk and stop distance.

screens.question: A wider stop generally calls for a larger position size to keep the same dollar risk.
screens.explanation: A wider stop calls for a SMALLER position size to keep the same dollar risk, not larger.

lessons.title: Risk/Reward Ratio
lessons.celebration: You understand risk/reward ratios!

screens.title: What You Could Lose vs. Gain
screens.text: A risk/reward ratio compares the potential loss on a trade to its potential gain, pure math, not a signal.

screens.question: A "2:1 risk-to-reward ratio" means the potential reward is twice the potential risk.
screens.explanation: That's the standard meaning of a 2:1 (or similarly stated) risk/reward ratio.

screens.question: A trade risking $100 to potentially make $200 has a risk/reward ratio of [___].
screens.explanation: $100 of risk against $200 of potential reward is a 1:2 ratio (risk:reward).

screens.question: What does a favorable risk/reward ratio generally describe?
options: A guarantee that the trade will be profitable.
Potential reward that is larger than the potential risk taken.
The exact number of shares being traded.
screens.explanation: Risk/reward describes the relationship between potential loss and gain, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: Match the risk/reward description to its general reading.
pairs: Generally considered a more favorable ratio
Generally considered a less favorable ratio
screens.explanation: Comparing potential reward to potential risk is the core of this concept.

screens.template: A [__1__] risk/reward ratio means more potential reward for the same [__2__] taken.
screens.explanation: A higher ratio means a larger potential payoff relative to the risk.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate a trade's risk/reward ratio before entering:
items: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
correct_order: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
screens.explanation: This calculation can be done in advance, before a trade is even placed.

screens.question: Which best describes what risk/reward ratio measures, on its own?

options.label: The total dollar amount in your account
options.wrong_explanation: That's your account size, not a per-trade ratio.

options.label: A guarantee of how the trade will actually turn out
options.wrong_explanation: It's a ratio of possibilities, not a guaranteed outcome.

options.label: The relationship between potential loss and potential gain on a trade
options.detail: A math comparison, not a certainty

screens.explanation: Risk/reward is a mathematical comparison, not a prediction of the outcome.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a favorable risk/reward ratio guarantees the trade will be profitable.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should look for an even higher ratio to be sure.
A favorable ratio describes the potential payoff structure, not a guarantee that the trade succeeds.
They should ignore risk/reward ratios entirely.
screens.explanation: Risk/reward is about the shape of possible outcomes, not a certainty about which one happens.

screens.question: A higher risk/reward ratio means more potential reward for the same [___] taken.
screens.explanation: A higher ratio means a bigger potential payoff relative to the risk.

screens.question: A 1:3 risk/reward ratio means the potential reward is three times the potential risk.
screens.explanation: 1:3 (risk:reward) means the reward is three times the risk.

lessons.title: Stop-Loss Placement Logic
lessons.celebration: You understand where stop-losses are commonly placed!

screens.title: Not Just a Random Number
screens.text: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific reason, like a nearby support/resistance level, rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: A stop-loss level is commonly chosen completely at random, with no specific reasoning.
screens.explanation: Stop-loss levels are commonly tied to a specific reason, like a nearby support or resistance level.

screens.question: Placing a stop-loss just beyond a nearby support or resistance level is a commonly cited [___].
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited approach, among several, for placing a stop-loss with a clear reason behind it.

screens.question: Why might a stop-loss be placed just beyond a nearby support level?
options: It has no relationship to the trade's original reasoning.
It guarantees the stop will never be triggered.
If that level breaks, it may suggest the original reason for the trade no longer holds.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable reason.

screens.question: Match the stop-loss placement idea to its reasoning.
pairs: Tied to a level that would invalidate the original idea
Tied to a consistent risk amount regardless of chart structure
Commonly cited as being triggered by normal price noise
screens.explanation: These are different commonly discussed approaches to stop-loss placement.

screens.template: A stop-loss placed too [__1__] may get triggered by normal price [__2__], not a meaningful shift.
screens.explanation: A stop set with too little room can be triggered by ordinary fluctuations rather than a real change in the picture.

screens.question: A simple way to think through stop-loss placement:
items: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
correct_order: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
screens.explanation: This ties the stop-loss to a specific reason rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: Which best describes a stop-loss placed "just beyond a nearby support level"?

options.label: A completely random number with no logic behind it
options.wrong_explanation: This approach is specifically about having a clear reason.

options.label: A guarantee the position will never lose money
options.wrong_explanation: A stop-loss limits risk; it doesn't guarantee no loss ever occurs.

options.label: Tied to a level that would suggest the original trade idea no longer holds

screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable rationale.

screens.scenario: Someone sets a stop-loss extremely close to their entry price, with no particular reasoning behind the distance.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should remove the stop-loss entirely instead.
A stop placed too close with no reasoning can get triggered by normal price noise rather than a meaningful shift.
They should place it even closer for extra safety.
screens.explanation: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific, reasoned level rather than an arbitrarily tight distance.

screens.question: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific [___], not a random number.
screens.explanation: A reasoned placement (like just beyond a level) is commonly recommended over an arbitrary stop.

screens.question: A stop-loss placed too close to entry can get triggered by normal price noise.
screens.explanation: A too-tight stop risks getting hit by ordinary fluctuations, not a meaningful shift.

lessons.title: Overleveraging Danger
lessons.celebration: You understand the danger of overleveraging!

screens.title: Amplifying Both Directions
screens.text: Leverage amplifies both potential gains and potential losses, overleveraging describes using more than a comfortable, risk-appropriate amount.

screens.question: Leverage only amplifies potential gains, never potential losses.
screens.explanation: Leverage amplifies both directions, potential gains and potential losses alike.

screens.question: Using more leverage than is appropriate for your risk tolerance is commonly called [___].
screens.explanation: "Overleveraging" describes taking on leverage beyond what fits your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Why is overleveraging commonly cited as a significant danger?
options: It guarantees larger profits with no added risk.
It amplifies losses, potentially causing much larger damage from a single adverse move.
It has no effect on the size of potential losses.
screens.explanation: Amplified losses are the commonly cited core danger of overleveraging.

screens.question: Match the leverage concept to its description.
pairs: A tool that amplifies both potential gains and losses
Using more leverage than fits one's risk tolerance
Sized to fit an individual's risk tolerance and plan
screens.explanation: Leverage itself is a neutral tool; overleveraging describes misusing it relative to one's own risk tolerance.

screens.template: Leverage can [__1__] both potential gains and potential [__2__] from the same price move.
screens.explanation: This dual amplification is the core mechanism behind leverage's risk.

screens.question: A simple way to think through leverage before using it:
items: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
correct_order: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
screens.explanation: This keeps leverage decisions tied to individual risk tolerance rather than chasing amplified gains alone.

screens.question: Which best describes "overleveraging"?

options.label: Using any leverage at all, under any circumstances
options.wrong_explanation: Leverage itself isn't inherently overleveraging; it's about fit with risk tolerance.

options.label: A guarantee of larger losses no matter what
options.wrong_explanation: It raises risk, but exact outcomes still depend on what actually happens.

options.label: Using more leverage than fits your own risk tolerance
options.detail: A mismatch between leverage and personal risk capacity

screens.explanation: Overleveraging specifically describes a mismatch between leverage used and one's own risk tolerance.

screens.scenario: Someone uses very high leverage because "it worked out fine last time."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should assume high leverage always works out.
Past luck with high leverage doesn't reduce the risk of amplified losses on a future adverse move.
They should use even higher leverage next time to be consistent.
screens.explanation: One favorable past outcome doesn't change the underlying amplified risk that leverage carries.

screens.question: Leverage amplifies both potential gains and potential [___].
screens.explanation: Leverage cuts both ways, bigger potential gains AND bigger potential losses.

screens.question: Overleveraging means using leverage that fits your risk tolerance well.
screens.explanation: Overleveraging specifically means using MORE leverage than fits your risk tolerance.

lessons.title: Drawdowns
lessons.celebration: You understand drawdowns!

screens.title: The Dip From a Peak
screens.text: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from a prior peak value, a normal part of any trading account's history.

screens.question: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from its prior peak value.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of a drawdown.

screens.question: The percentage decline from an account's highest value to a subsequent low point is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Drawdown" is the standard term for this kind of decline.

screens.question: Why is understanding drawdowns commonly considered useful?
options: It only applies to accounts that have never had any losses.
It guarantees an account will never decline again.
It helps set realistic expectations that account value doesn't move in a straight line.

screens.question: Breakout trading expects price to reverse the instant it clears a range.
screens.explanation: Breakout trading expects continuation, not an immediate reversal.

lessons.title: Range Trading
lessons.celebration: You understand range trading!

screens.title: Between the Boundaries
screens.text: Range trading is commonly described as an approach expecting price to stay between established support and resistance boundaries.

screens.question: Range trading is commonly described as expecting price to stay between established boundaries.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of range trading.

screens.question: An approach expecting price to stay between established support and resistance boundaries is commonly called [___].
screens.explanation: "Range trading" is the standard term for this boundary-based approach.

screens.question: What commonly characterizes a range-trading approach?
options: Ignoring any concept of support or resistance.
Expecting price to move between established support and resistance boundaries, rather than break beyond them.
Expecting price to clear its boundaries and continue in one direction indefinitely.
screens.explanation: Range trading is commonly described around bouncing between boundaries, not clearing beyond them.

screens.question: Match the approach to its commonly described core idea.
pairs: Expecting price to stay between established boundaries
Expecting continuation after a range is cleared
Staying aligned with a sustained directional move
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited core ideas distinguishing several strategy types.

screens.template: Range trading commonly expects price to [__1__] between boundaries rather than [__2__] beyond them.
screens.explanation: This captures the core contrast between range trading and breakout trading.

screens.question: A commonly described general process for a range-trading approach:
items: Identify established support and resistance boundaries
Watch for price approaching one of those boundaries
Consider an entry aligned with an expected bounce within the range
Plan an exit if price instead clears the boundary
correct_order: Identify established support and resistance boundaries
Watch for price approaching one of those boundaries
Consider an entry aligned with an expected bounce within the range
Plan an exit if price instead clears the boundary
screens.explanation: This reflects the commonly described boundary-based logic of range trading.

screens.question: Which best describes "range trading," as commonly defined?

options.label: Expecting price to break through every boundary and keep going
options.detail: This describes breakout trading, not range trading
options.wrong_explanation: That's closer to a breakout-trading idea.

options.label: Expecting price to stay between established support and resistance boundaries
A guarantee that price will never leave the range
options.wrong_explanation: Range trading describes an expectation within an approach, not a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Range trading specifically describes an expectation of staying within boundaries, not a guaranteed certainty.

screens.scenario: Someone describes "expecting price to break every boundary and keep moving in one direction" as an example of range trading.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should expect it to break through even more boundaries to match the description.
They should assume range trading has no relationship to support or resistance.
Range trading is commonly described as expecting price to stay within boundaries, not break through them repeatedly.
screens.explanation: This description contradicts the commonly cited core idea behind range trading.

screens.question: Range trading expects price to stay [___] established boundaries.
screens.explanation: Range trading expects price to bounce within its boundaries, not break beyond them.

screens.question: Range trading expects price to break through every boundary and keep going.
screens.explanation: That describes breakout trading, range trading expects price to stay bounded instead.

lessons.title: Risk Per Trade
lessons.celebration: You understand risk per trade!

screens.title: A Percent of the Account
screens.text: Risk per trade is commonly expressed as a percent of the account you're willing to lose on one trade, often a small figure like 1%. Keeping it small and consistent is a common risk approach.

screens.question: Risk per trade is commonly expressed as a...
screens.explanation: Risk per trade is commonly set as a small percent of the account.

screens.question: Keeping risk per trade [___] and consistent is a common approach.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade is commonly recommended.

screens.question: Risking a huge percent of the account on one trade is commonly considered high risk.
screens.explanation: A large percent at risk on one trade exposes the account to big damage from one loss.

screens.question: Why keep risk per trade small and consistent?

options.label: So you never have to use a stop
options.wrong_explanation: Sizing works with a stop, not instead of one.

options.label: So a single loss can't do outsized damage to the account
So every trade is guaranteed to win
options.wrong_explanation: Sizing doesn't change win odds.

screens.explanation: Small consistent risk limits the damage any one loss can do.

screens.question: Risk per trade is commonly expressed as a [___] of the account.
screens.explanation: Risk per trade is commonly set as a small, consistent percent of the account.

screens.question: Keeping risk per trade small and consistent is a commonly recommended habit.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade limits damage from any single loss.

screens.question: Why keep risk per trade small?
options: So position size never has to be calculated.
So a single loss can't do outsized damage to the account.
So every trade is guaranteed to win.
screens.explanation: Small risk per trade limits the impact of any one loss, without guaranteeing outcomes.

lessons.title: Calculating Dollar Risk
lessons.celebration: You can calculate dollar risk!

screens.title: Percent Into Dollars
screens.text: To turn a risk percent into dollars: multiply the account size by the percent. On a $10,000 account, 1% risk = $100.

screens.question: On a $10,000 account, risking 1% means risking...
On a $5,000 account, risking 2% means risking...
To get dollar risk, multiply account size by the risk [___].
screens.explanation: Dollar risk = account size × risk percent.

screens.question: On a $20,000 account, risking 1% means risking...
A larger account risking the same percent risks more dollars.
screens.explanation: The same percent of a bigger account is a bigger dollar amount.

screens.question: Dollar risk equals account size multiplied by risk [___].
screens.explanation: Multiplying account size by the risk percent gives the dollar risk amount.

screens.question: A larger account risking the same percent risks more dollars in absolute terms.
screens.explanation: The same percent of a bigger account is a larger dollar amount.

lessons.title: What Is 1R?
lessons.celebration: You understand R!

screens.title: R = The Amount Risked
screens.text: "R" is shorthand for the amount you risked on a trade. If you risk $100, then 1R = $100. Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes.

screens.question: If you risk $100 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R is simply the amount risked, here, $100.

screens.question: "R" stands for the amount you [___] on the trade.
screens.explanation: R is the risk amount; results are measured in multiples of it.

screens.question: If you risk $250 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R = the amount risked = $250.

screens.question: Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different dollar sizes.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results, so a "2R win" means the same regardless of position size.

screens.question: "R" is shorthand for the amount [___] on a trade.
screens.explanation: R specifically represents the risk amount, used to measure results.

screens.question: Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes fairly.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results across different position sizes.

lessons.title: Reward in R
lessons.celebration: You can measure reward in R!

screens.title: Wins as Multiples of Risk
screens.text: A win is measured in R too. If you risk $100 (1R) and gain $200, that's a +2R result. A loss of the full risk is −1R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade gains $200. That result is...
screens.explanation: A $200 gain on $100 risk is twice the risk, +2R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade loses the full risk. That result is...
screens.explanation: Losing the full amount risked is −1R.

screens.question: A gain of three times your risk is a [___] result.
screens.explanation: Three times the risk gained is +3R.

screens.question: You risk $200 and gain $600. That result is...
screens.explanation: $600 gain on $200 risk is three times the risk, +3R.

screens.question: A full loss is −1R, since you lost exactly the amount you risked.
screens.explanation: Losing the whole risked amount is by definition −1R.

screens.question: A gain of twice the amount risked is a [___] result.
screens.explanation: Twice the risk gained is +2R, by definition.

screens.question: A full loss of the entire risked amount is described as -1R.
screens.explanation: Losing exactly what was risked is, by definition, -1R.

lessons.title: Position Size From Risk & Stop
lessons.celebration: You understand position sizing!

screens.title: Size to Fit the Risk
screens.text: Position size is commonly worked backward from your dollar risk and stop distance: choose a size so that if the stop is hit, the loss equals your planned dollar risk.

screens.question: Position size is commonly calculated from your...
screens.explanation: Size is derived from how much you'll risk and how far the stop is.

screens.question: If your stop is further away, to keep the same dollar risk you use a...
screens.explanation: A wider stop means a smaller size keeps the dollar loss the same.

screens.question: Position size is worked [___] from your dollar risk and stop.
screens.explanation: You start from the risk and stop, then solve for size.

screens.scenario: Someone uses the same fixed position size no matter how far away the stop is.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A fixed size regardless of stop distance makes the dollar risk vary unpredictably between trades.
Stop distance never matters for sizing.
screens.explanation: Consistent dollar risk requires adjusting size to the stop distance.

screens.question: Position size is worked [___] from your dollar risk and stop distance.
screens.explanation: You start from the risk and stop, then solve for the position size.

screens.question: A wider stop distance calls for a larger position size to keep the same dollar risk.
screens.explanation: A wider stop calls for a SMALLER size to keep the dollar risk the same, not larger.

lessons.title: Position Sizing & R Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered position sizing & R!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of risk per trade, dollar risk, R, and position sizing.

screens.question: On a $10,000 account, risking 1% is...
screens.explanation: 1% of $10,000 is $100, that trade's 1R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and gain $300. That's...
screens.explanation: $300 on $100 risk is +3R.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The amount risked on the trade
A gain of twice the risk
Chosen so a stopped-out loss equals the planned risk
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core math.

screens.template: Dollar risk = account size × risk [__1__]; results are measured in multiples of [__2__].
screens.explanation: Percent gives dollar risk; R measures the results.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Risk a small consistent percent, size from the stop, and measure results in R
Bigger size always means bigger profit
options.wrong_explanation: Size sets risk, not guaranteed profit.

options.label: Size randomly and hope
options.wrong_explanation: The unit is about a consistent method.

screens.explanation: Consistent percent risk, stop-based sizing, and R measurement is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together risk per trade, dollar risk, R, and [___].
screens.explanation: All four core ideas from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: R lets you compare trade results across different position sizes.
screens.explanation: Measuring in R (multiples of risk) makes results comparable regardless of size.

lessons.title: Win Rate Isn't Everything
lessons.celebration: You understand why win rate alone misleads!

screens.title: How Often vs. How Much
screens.text: Win rate is how often you win. But it ignores how much you win or lose. A high win rate with tiny wins and huge losses can still lose money overall.

screens.question: Win rate measures...
screens.explanation: Win rate is the frequency of wins, not their size.

screens.question: A high win rate always means a profitable system.
screens.explanation: If wins are tiny and losses are huge, even a high win rate can lose overall.

screens.question: Win rate ignores how [___] you win or lose per trade.
screens.explanation: Win rate is frequency only; it ignores the size of wins and losses.

screens.question: Why isn't win rate enough on its own?

options.label: Because it's always wrong
options.wrong_explanation: Win rate is useful, just incomplete.

options.label: Because it ignores the size of the wins and losses
Because winning never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Both how often and how much matter.

screens.explanation: You need both how often (win rate) and how much (R) to judge results.

screens.question: Win rate measures how [___] you win, not how much.
screens.explanation: Win rate is purely a frequency measure, not a measure of size.

screens.question: A high win rate always means a profitable system.
screens.explanation: Tiny wins and huge losses can still lose money overall, even with a high win rate.

lessons.title: Combining Win Rate and R
lessons.celebration: You can combine win rate and R!

screens.title: Frequency Meets Size
screens.text: The honest picture combines win rate (how often) with average R (how much). A lower win rate can still come out ahead if the average win in R is large enough.

screens.question: To judge a system honestly, combine win rate with...
screens.explanation: Win rate plus average R (size) gives the honest picture.

screens.question: A 40% win rate can still be profitable if the average winner is large in R.
screens.explanation: Big average wins (in R) can outweigh more frequent small losses.

screens.template: Combine how [__1__] you win with how [__2__] you win to judge a system.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) and size (R) together tell the story.

screens.question: A system wins 40% of the time but averages +3R on wins and −1R on losses. This can be...
options: profitable overall, thanks to the large average win.
guaranteed to lose because win rate is under 50%.
screens.explanation: Large average wins can more than offset frequent small losses.

screens.question: Combining win rate with average [___] gives the honest picture.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) plus size (average R) together tell the full story.

screens.question: A 40% win rate can still be profitable if the average win in R is large enough.
screens.explanation: Large average wins can outweigh more frequent, smaller losses.

lessons.title: What Is Expectancy?
lessons.celebration: You understand expectancy!

screens.title: Average Result Per Trade
screens.text: Expectancy is the average result per trade, measured in R, over many trades. A positive expectancy means the average trade gains R over the long run.

screens.question: Expectancy is the...
options: average result per trade (in R) over many trades.
screens.explanation: Expectancy is the long-run average result per trade.

screens.question: A positive expectancy means the average trade, over many trades, gains R.
screens.explanation: Positive expectancy = the average trade comes out ahead in R over the long run.

screens.question: Expectancy is the average result per trade measured in [___].
screens.explanation: Expressed in R, expectancy compares across position sizes.

screens.question: Why is expectancy a long-run idea?

options.label: Because it predicts the next trade exactly
options.wrong_explanation: It says nothing certain about one trade.

options.label: Because it's an average that only holds over many trades, not any single one
Because it ignores wins and losses
options.wrong_explanation: It's built from wins and losses.

screens.explanation: Expectancy is an average over many trades, not a promise about any single one.

screens.question: Expectancy is the average [___] per trade, in R, over many trades.
screens.explanation: Expectancy is a long-run average, measured in R.

screens.question: A positive expectancy means the average trade, over many trades, gains R.
screens.explanation: That's the definition of positive expectancy.

lessons.title: Winning With Under 50% Wins
lessons.celebration: You understand how low win rates can still win!

screens.title: Big Wins, Small Losses
screens.text: A system can be profitable with a win rate below 50% if its winners are much larger (in R) than its losers. Size can outweigh frequency.

screens.question: A system with a 35% win rate can still be profitable if...
options: its winners are much larger in R than its losers.
screens.explanation: Large winners in R can outweigh more frequent, smaller losers.

screens.question: You must win more than half your trades to be profitable.
screens.explanation: With large enough winners in R, a sub-50% win rate can still profit.

screens.question: A low win rate can still win if the [___] are much larger in R.
screens.explanation: Larger winners in R can more than offset frequent small losses.

screens.scenario: Someone dismisses a system purely because its win rate is under 50%, without checking the average R.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Win rate alone isn't enough, a sub-50% system with large winners in R can still have positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: Both win rate and average R matter; ignoring R misjudges the system.

screens.question: A system can be profitable with a win rate below [___]%.
screens.explanation: Sub-50% win rates can still be profitable if the average winner in R is large enough.

screens.question: You must win more than half your trades to be profitable.
screens.explanation: With large enough winners in R, a sub-50% win rate can still profit overall.

lessons.title: Sample Size Matters
lessons.celebration: You understand sample size!

screens.title: A Few Trades Prove Little
screens.text: Expectancy and win rate only mean something over a large enough sample. A handful of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.

screens.question: Expectancy is meaningful only over...
options: a large enough sample of trades.
screens.explanation: Averages need many trades to be meaningful; small samples are noisy.

screens.question: Three winning trades in a row prove a system has positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: A tiny sample can happen by chance; it doesn't prove long-run expectancy.

screens.question: A small [___] of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.
screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, not the true average.

screens.question: Why be careful with a small sample?

options.label: Because small samples are always accurate
options.wrong_explanation: They're the least reliable.

options.label: Because sample size never matters
options.wrong_explanation: It's central to trusting an average.

options.label: Because chance can make a few trades misleading in either direction

screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, so they can badly mislead.

screens.question: Expectancy is meaningful only over a [___] sample of trades.
screens.explanation: A large sample is needed for averages like expectancy to be meaningful.

screens.question: Three winning trades in a row proves a system has positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: A tiny sample can happen by chance; it doesn't prove long-run expectancy.

lessons.title: Expectancy & Edge Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered expectancy & edge!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of win rate, R, expectancy, and sample size.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: How much trades win or lose, in R
The average result per trade over many trades
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What two things must you combine to judge a system honestly?
options: Candle color and time of day.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) plus size (average R) gives the honest picture.

screens.template: A system can profit with a [__1__] win rate if its winners are [__2__] in R.
screens.explanation: Large winners in R can offset a lower win rate.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: A few trades prove everything
options.wrong_explanation: Sample size matters.

options.label: Judge a system by win rate alone
options.wrong_explanation: Win rate alone can mislead.

options: Two wins prove a positive expectancy.

lessons.title: Trending, Ranging, or Volatile?
lessons.celebration: You can classify market conditions!

screens.title: Three Broad Conditions
screens.text: Markets are commonly classified into broad conditions: trending (directional), ranging (sideways between levels), and volatile (large, erratic swings). Reading the condition guides how you read everything else.

screens.question: The chart above makes steady higher highs and higher lows. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Directional progress (higher highs/lows) is a trending condition.

screens.question: The chart above bounces sideways between two levels. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between support and resistance is a ranging condition.

screens.question: The chart above shows large, erratic swings with no clear direction. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Big, erratic swings with no clear direction is a volatile condition.

screens.question: Match each condition to its description.
screens.explanation: These three broad conditions describe most markets.

screens.question: Markets are commonly classified as trending, ranging, or [___].
screens.explanation: Trending, ranging, and volatile are the three broad commonly cited conditions.

screens.question: Reading the market condition first frames how you read everything else.
screens.explanation: Condition is commonly treated as the context for reading levels, patterns, and candles.

lessons.title: Classifying a Trend
lessons.celebration: You can classify a trend!

screens.title: Direction and Structure
screens.text: A trending condition shows directional structure, higher highs and higher lows (up) or lower highs and lower lows (down).

screens.question: The chart above makes lower highs and lower lows. It is a...
screens.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows is a downtrend.

screens.question: An uptrend shows higher highs and higher lows.
screens.explanation: Rising highs and lows define an uptrend.

screens.question: Tap the lower high on this downtrend.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the bounce that made a lower high, confirming the downtrend.

screens.question: Drag to connect the lower highs that confirm this trending condition.
screens.explanation: Candles 1 and 3 mark the falling sequence of lower highs that define a trending condition here.

screens.question: A trending condition has a clear [___] in one direction.
screens.explanation: Directional progression is what makes it a trend.

screens.question: A trending condition shows directional [___] in the swings.
screens.explanation: Directional progression (higher highs/lows or lower highs/lows) defines trending.

screens.question: Higher highs and higher lows describe a trending condition.
screens.explanation: That progression is the defining structure of a trend.

lessons.title: Classifying a Range
lessons.celebration: You can classify a range!

screens.title: Sideways Between Levels
screens.text: A ranging condition moves sideways between a support and resistance, without directional progress.

screens.question: The chart above stays between a floor and ceiling. It is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between two levels is ranging.

screens.question: Drag the line to the range's resistance.
screens.explanation: The ceiling of the range is its resistance.

screens.question: Drag across every candle bounded inside this ranging condition.
screens.explanation: All six candles here stay bounded between support and resistance, the ranging condition itself.

screens.question: A ranging market makes strong directional progress.
screens.explanation: Ranging is sideways, the opposite of directional progress.

screens.question: A range moves [___] between support and resistance.
screens.explanation: Sideways bounded movement is a range.

screens.question: A ranging condition moves [___] between two levels.
screens.explanation: Sideways movement between support and resistance defines a range.

screens.question: A ranging market makes strong directional progress.
screens.explanation: A range is sideways, the opposite of directional progress.

lessons.title: Classifying Volatile
lessons.celebration: You can classify volatile conditions!

screens.title: Big, Erratic Swings
screens.text: A volatile condition shows large, fast swings in both directions, big candles and long wicks, without a clean trend or tidy range.

screens.question: The chart above shows large swings both ways with no clean direction. It is...
screens.explanation: Big erratic two-way swings is a volatile condition.

screens.question: Volatile conditions have larger, faster swings than a calm range.
screens.explanation: Volatility means bigger, faster moves than a calm, tight range.

screens.question: Volatile conditions show large, [___] swings in both directions.
screens.explanation: Large erratic two-way swings define volatility.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a wildly volatile chart as a calm, tidy range.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Big erratic swings are volatile, not a calm range, the condition was misread.
Volatile and calm ranges are the same.
screens.explanation: Volatile conditions have far larger, more erratic swings than a tidy range.

screens.question: A volatile condition shows large, [___] swings.
screens.explanation: Large, erratic two-way swings define a volatile condition.

screens.question: Volatile conditions have larger, faster swings than a calm range.
screens.explanation: Volatility means bigger, faster moves than a calm, tight range.

lessons.title: Why Classification Matters
lessons.celebration: You understand why condition matters!

screens.title: Read the Room First
screens.text: The market condition frames everything else. A level that "holds" in a range may get blown through in a volatile spell. Reading the condition first is a core advanced skill.

screens.question: Why classify the market condition first?
options: Because it changes the candle colors.
Because it has no effect on anything.
Because it frames how you read levels, patterns, and candles.
screens.explanation: The condition sets the context for every other read.

screens.question: The same level can behave differently in a range vs a volatile condition.
screens.explanation: A level that holds calmly in a range can be blown through when volatile.

screens.question: The market condition [___] how you read everything else.
screens.explanation: Condition is the context that frames the rest of the read.

screens.question: Which best captures the role of condition?

options.label: It guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: It frames, it doesn't guarantee.

options.label: It's irrelevant to reading a chart
options.wrong_explanation: It's central context.

options.label: It's the context you read first, before levels and patterns

screens.explanation: Condition is the first-read context that frames every other read.

screens.question: The market condition [___] how you read levels, patterns, and candles.
screens.explanation: Condition sets the context for every other read.

screens.question: The same level can behave differently in a range versus a volatile condition.
screens.explanation: A level that holds calmly in a range can get blown through when volatile.

lessons.title: Classification Drill & Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered market classification!

screens.title: Read the Condition
screens.text: A final round, classify each chart's condition.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows is trending up.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Sideways between levels is ranging.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Large erratic swings is volatile.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows is trending down.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Condition never matters
options.wrong_explanation: It's core context.

options.label: Classify trending, ranging, or volatile first. It frames every other read
Classification guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: It frames, not guarantees.

screens.explanation: Condition-first reading is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together trending, ranging, and [___] classification.
screens.explanation: All three broad conditions from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: Classifying market condition is a first-read step that frames the rest of your analysis.
screens.explanation: This has been the throughline, condition-first reading, framing everything else.

lessons.title: What Is a Moving Average?
lessons.celebration: You understand moving averages!

screens.title: The Average of Recent Prices
screens.text: A moving average (MA) is the average of the last N prices, recalculated each candle. A 20-period MA averages the last 20 closes. It's a smoothed line that follows price.

screens.question: A moving average is the...
options: average of the last N prices, updated each candle.
screens.explanation: An MA averages the most recent N prices and updates as new ones arrive.

screens.question: A 20-period moving average averages the last [___] prices.
screens.explanation: The number is how many recent prices it averages.

screens.question: A moving average updates as each new candle arrives.
screens.explanation: It's "moving" because it recalculates with each new price.

screens.question: What does a moving average give you?

options.label: The exact future value
A smoothed line summarizing recent price
A guarantee of the next price

screens.explanation: An MA smooths recent price into a line; it doesn't predict the future.

screens.question: A moving average is the average of the last [___] prices, updated each candle.
screens.explanation: An MA averages a set number (N) of recent prices, recalculating with each new one.

screens.question: A moving average predicts future prices with certainty.
screens.explanation: An MA summarizes recent price into a smoothed line. It doesn't guarantee the future.

lessons.title: Smoothing Out Noise
lessons.celebration: You understand smoothing!

screens.title: Less Jitter, Clearer Direction
screens.text: Because it averages, a moving average smooths out the candle-to-candle jitter, making the broader direction easier to see.

screens.question: Averaging recent prices makes a moving average...
screens.explanation: Averaging smooths the noise, so the line is steadier than raw price.

screens.question: A moving average [___] out short-term noise.
screens.explanation: Averaging reduces the jitter, smoothing the line.

screens.question: A longer moving average is generally smoother than a shorter one.
screens.explanation: Averaging more prices smooths more, so longer MAs are steadier.

screens.question: Smoothing makes the broader [___] easier to see.
screens.explanation: With less noise, the general direction is clearer.

screens.question: Averaging recent prices makes a moving average [___] than raw candles.
screens.explanation: Averaging reduces candle-to-candle jitter, producing a smoother line.

screens.question: A longer moving average is generally smoother than a shorter one.
screens.explanation: Averaging more prices smooths more, making longer MAs steadier.

lessons.title: The Slope Reflects Trend
lessons.celebration: You can read an MA's slope!

screens.title: Rising, Falling, or Flat
screens.text: A moving average's slope reflects the trend: a rising MA reflects an uptrend, a falling MA a downtrend, and a flat MA a range. It's a smoothed read of direction.

screens.question: On a rising market like the chart above, a moving average would be...
screens.explanation: In an uptrend, the average of recent prices rises, the MA slopes up.

screens.question: A falling moving average reflects a downtrend.
screens.explanation: When recent prices fall, their average falls, the MA slopes down.

screens.question: A flat moving average most likely reflects a...
screens.explanation: Sideways price keeps the average roughly flat, a range.

screens.question: A moving average's [___] reflects the trend direction.
screens.explanation: The slope (up/down/flat) mirrors the trend.

screens.question: A moving average's slope reflects the [___].
screens.explanation: Rising, falling, or flat slope mirrors the underlying trend direction.

screens.question: A flat moving average most likely reflects a strong trend.
screens.explanation: A flat MA more likely reflects a range, not a strong trend.

lessons.title: Price Above vs. Below the MA
lessons.celebration: You can read price against the MA!

screens.title: Which Side Is Price On?
screens.text: Price trading above a rising MA is commonly described as strength; below a falling MA as weakness. It's a descriptive read, not a signal to act.

screens.question: Tap the candle where price crosses above the MA line.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where price closes back above the MA, the crossing point.

screens.question: Price holding above a rising moving average is commonly described as...
screens.explanation: Staying above a rising MA is commonly read as strength, descriptively.

screens.question: Price below a falling MA is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Trading under a falling average is commonly read as weakness.

screens.question: Price vs the MA is a [___] read, not a signal to act.
screens.explanation: It describes strength/weakness; it isn't an automatic buy/sell.

screens.question: Tap the candle where price crosses below the MA line.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where price closes back below the MA, the crossing point.

screens.scenario: Someone treats "price above the MA" as an automatic, guaranteed buy signal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The MA guarantees the next move.
Price above the MA is a descriptive strength read, not a guaranteed signal to act on.
screens.explanation: An MA read is descriptive context, never a guaranteed signal.

screens.question: Price holding above a rising MA is commonly described as relative [___].
screens.explanation: Staying above a rising MA is commonly read as strength.

screens.question: Price vs the MA is a guaranteed signal to act on.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive strength/weakness read, not a guaranteed signal.

lessons.title: Short vs. Long MAs
lessons.celebration: You understand fast vs slow MAs!

screens.title: Fast and Slow
screens.text: A short MA (few periods) reacts quickly to price. It's "fast." A long MA (many periods) reacts slowly. It's "smooth and slow." Each shows a different scale of trend.

screens.question: A short-period MA is...
options: fast. It reacts quickly to price.
screens.explanation: Fewer periods means quicker reaction, a "fast" MA.

screens.question: A long-period MA is...
screens.explanation: More periods means slower reaction, a "slow," smooth MA.

screens.template: A short MA is [__1__]; a long MA is [__2__].
screens.explanation: Short = fast reaction; long = slow, smooth.

screens.question: A short MA hugs price more closely than a long MA.
screens.explanation: Reacting faster, the short MA tracks price more tightly.

screens.question: A short-period MA is [___]. It reacts quickly to price.
screens.explanation: Fewer periods means quicker reaction, making it a "fast" MA.

screens.question: A long-period MA hugs price more closely than a short-period MA.
screens.explanation: A SHORT MA hugs price more closely; a long MA is smoother and slower.

lessons.title: MA Crossovers
lessons.celebration: You understand MA crossovers!

screens.title: When Fast Crosses Slow
screens.text: A "crossover" is when a fast MA crosses a slow MA. It's commonly used as a descriptive trend cue. But MAs are lagging (built from past prices), so crossovers are not guaranteed signals.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses above the slow MA.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where the fast (blue) MA crosses above the slow (amber) MA, a bullish crossover.

screens.question: An MA crossover is when...
options: a fast MA crosses a slow MA.
screens.explanation: A crossover is the fast and slow MAs crossing each other.

screens.question: Moving averages are lagging, since they're built from past prices.
screens.explanation: An MA is an average of past prices, so it lags current price.

screens.question: Because MAs are built from past prices, they are [___].
screens.explanation: Averaging past prices makes MAs lag, not lead.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses below the slow MA.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where the fast (blue) MA crosses below the slow (amber) MA, a bearish crossover.

screens.question: How should a crossover be read?

options.label: As a descriptive, lagging trend cue, not a guaranteed signal
As a guaranteed entry
options.wrong_explanation: Crossovers lag and can whipsaw.

options.label: As a leading predictor of price
options.wrong_explanation: MAs lag; they don't lead.

screens.explanation: A crossover is a lagging, descriptive cue, never a guarantee.

screens.question: Moving averages are [___] because they're built from past prices.
screens.explanation: Averaging past prices makes MAs lag current price, rather than lead it.

screens.question: An MA crossover is a guaranteed trading signal.
screens.explanation: A crossover is a descriptive, lagging cue, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Moving Averages Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered moving averages!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of what an MA is, smoothing, slope, price-vs-MA, and crossovers.

screens.question: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: The average of the last N prices
Fast MA crossing slow MA (a lagging cue)
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What does an MA's slope reflect?
screens.explanation: Slope up/down/flat mirrors the trend.

screens.template: A moving average [__1__] price and [__2__] the current price (it's lagging).
screens.explanation: MAs smooth and lag; they don't predict.

screens.question: Which best summarizes moving averages?

options.label: A smoothed, lagging line whose slope reads the trend, descriptive, not predictive
A predictor of the next price
options.wrong_explanation: MAs lag, they don't predict.

options.label: Unrelated to price
options.wrong_explanation: An MA is built directly from price.

screens.explanation: Smoothed, lagging, descriptive trend reading is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together what an MA is, smoothing, slope, and [___].
screens.explanation: All the core ideas from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: Moving averages are descriptive and lagging, not predictive.
screens.explanation: This has been the throughline, smoothed, lagging, descriptive trend reading.

lessons.title: What Is an Oscillator?
lessons.celebration: You understand oscillators!

screens.title: A Bounded, Derived Measure
screens.text: An oscillator is an indicator derived from price that moves within a bounded range. It summarizes something about price (like the speed of moves) rather than showing price itself.

screens.question: An oscillator is...
options: a price-derived measure that moves in a bounded range.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are derived measures bounded within a range (e.g., 0–100).

screens.question: An oscillator is [___] from price, not the price itself.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are calculated from price data.

screens.question: An oscillator shows the raw price directly.
screens.explanation: It shows a derived measure about price, not the price line itself.

screens.question: An oscillator moves within a [___] range.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are bounded (e.g., 0–100 for RSI).

screens.question: An oscillator is [___] from price and moves within a bounded range.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are calculated from price data, bounded within a fixed range.

screens.question: An oscillator shows the raw price directly.
screens.explanation: It shows a derived measure about price, not the price line itself.

lessons.title: What RSI Measures
lessons.celebration: You understand RSI!

screens.title: Speed and Size of Moves
screens.text: RSI (Relative Strength Index) is an oscillator from 0 to 100 that measures the speed and size of recent price moves. Higher RSI = stronger recent up-moves; lower = stronger down-moves.

screens.question: RSI measures the...
options: speed and size of recent price moves, on a 0–100 scale.
screens.explanation: RSI summarizes recent up vs down move strength from 0 to 100.

screens.question: RSI is bounded between 0 and [___].
screens.explanation: RSI runs from 0 to 100.

screens.question: A higher RSI reflects stronger recent up-moves.
screens.explanation: RSI rises when recent gains dominate recent losses.

screens.question: RSI is an example of a(n)...
screens.explanation: RSI is a bounded, price-derived oscillator.

screens.question: RSI runs from [___] to 100.
screens.explanation: RSI is bounded between 0 and 100.

screens.question: A higher RSI reflects stronger recent up-moves.
screens.explanation: RSI rises when recent gains dominate recent losses.

lessons.title: Overbought & Oversold Zones
lessons.celebration: You can read RSI zones honestly!

screens.title: Labels, Not Signals
screens.text: RSI above ~70 is commonly labeled "overbought" and below ~30 "oversold." These are descriptive labels, not buy/sell signals, a strong trend can stay "overbought" for a long time.

screens.question: RSI above ~70 is commonly labeled...
screens.explanation: High RSI (~70+) is commonly labeled overbought, a description.

screens.question: "Overbought" is a guaranteed sell signal.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive label; a strong uptrend can stay overbought for a long time.

screens.question: "Overbought" and "oversold" are descriptive [___], not signals to act.
screens.explanation: They describe RSI's zone; they aren't automatic trade signals.

screens.scenario: Someone shorts every time RSI hits "overbought," sure it must reverse.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: "Overbought" is a label, not a signal, strong trends can stay overbought a long time.
Overbought always means an immediate reversal.
screens.explanation: Zones describe RSI; they don't guarantee a reversal.

screens.question: "Overbought" and "oversold" are descriptive [___], not signals.
screens.explanation: These are labels describing an RSI zone, not automatic trade signals.

screens.question: "Overbought" is a guaranteed sell signal.
screens.explanation: A strong uptrend can stay overbought a long time. It's a label, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: What MACD Shows
lessons.celebration: You understand MACD!

screens.title: Two Moving Averages' Relationship
screens.text: MACD is built from the relationship between two moving averages (a fast and a slow one). It summarizes momentum, how the fast MA is pulling away from or converging with the slow one.

screens.question: MACD is derived from...
options: the relationship between two moving averages.
screens.explanation: MACD tracks how a fast and slow MA relate, a momentum read.

screens.question: MACD is built from moving averages, so it is also lagging.
screens.explanation: Because it's built from MAs (past prices), MACD lags too.

screens.question: MACD summarizes [___] from two moving averages.
screens.explanation: The gap/relationship between the MAs reads as momentum.

screens.question: Since MACD comes from moving averages, it is...
screens.explanation: MA-based indicators lag price.

screens.question: MACD tracks the relationship between two [___] averages.
screens.explanation: MACD is built from a fast and slow moving average's relationship.

screens.question: Because MACD is built from moving averages, it is also lagging.
screens.explanation: MA-based indicators lag price, and MACD is no exception.

lessons.title: Divergence
lessons.celebration: You understand divergence!

screens.title: When Price and Indicator Disagree
screens.text: Divergence is when price and an oscillator move in different directions, e.g., price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. It's a descriptive "disagreement," not a guaranteed reversal.

screens.question: Divergence is when price and the indicator...
screens.explanation: Divergence is a disagreement between price and the oscillator.

screens.question: Divergence guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive disagreement, a clue, never a guarantee.

screens.question: Divergence is price and an oscillator [___] on direction.
screens.explanation: The two disagreeing on direction is divergence.

screens.question: How should divergence be read?

options.label: As proof the data is broken
options.wrong_explanation: It's a normal, valid reading.

options.label: As a descriptive disagreement worth noting, not a guarantee
As a guaranteed reversal
options.wrong_explanation: Divergence can persist without a reversal.

screens.explanation: Divergence is a descriptive clue, not a guaranteed signal.

screens.question: Divergence is price and an oscillator [___] on direction.
screens.explanation: Divergence specifically describes price and the oscillator moving in different directions.

screens.question: Divergence guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive disagreement, a clue, never a guarantee.

lessons.title: Oscillators Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered oscillators!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of oscillators, RSI, its zones, MACD, and divergence.

screens.question: Match each to its meaning.
pairs: A 0–100 oscillator of recent move strength
A momentum read from two moving averages
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What do RSI and MACD have in common?
options: Both are indicators derived from price (and both lag it).
Both are the raw price line.
screens.explanation: Both are derived, lagging indicators, not guarantees.

screens.template: Oscillators are [__1__] from price and their extreme zones are [__2__], not signals.
screens.explanation: Derived measures with descriptive zones, not automatic signals.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Oscillators are guaranteed signal generators
options.wrong_explanation: They describe, they don't guarantee.

options.label: Oscillators derive momentum reads from price; their zones and divergence are descriptive, not guarantees
Oscillators lead price
options.wrong_explanation: They're derived and lagging.

screens.explanation: Descriptive, derived, lagging, never guaranteed, is the throughline.

screens.question: This review ties together oscillators, RSI, its zones, MACD, and [___].
screens.explanation: All the core ideas from this unit are reviewed together here.

screens.question: RSI and MACD are both derived, lagging indicators, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: This has been the throughline, descriptive, derived, lagging, never guaranteed.

lessons.title: What Is a Trade Plan?
lessons.celebration: You understand trade plans!

screens.title: Decide Before, Not During
screens.text: A trade plan decides the key things in advance: the idea (why), the invalidation (where you're wrong), the target (planned exit), and the size (risk). Planning ahead keeps decisions off the emotional moment.

screens.question: A trade plan is best decided...
options: in the heat of the moment.
screens.explanation: Planning ahead keeps decisions out of the emotional moment.

screens.question: Match each part of a plan to what it defines.
pairs: Where the idea is proven wrong
screens.explanation: Idea, invalidation, target (and size) are the core of a plan.

screens.question: A plan decides the key things [___] entering.
screens.explanation: The point of a plan is deciding in advance.

screens.question: A trade plan includes where the idea would be proven wrong.
screens.explanation: Invalidation, where you're wrong, is a core part of a plan.

screens.question: A trade plan decides the key things [___] entering.
screens.explanation: Planning ahead keeps decisions out of the emotional moment.

screens.question: A trade plan includes where the idea would be proven wrong.
screens.explanation: Invalidation is a core part of a plan.

lessons.title: Invalidation
lessons.celebration: You understand invalidation!

screens.title: Where the Idea Is Wrong
screens.text: Invalidation is the price/level where your trade idea is proven wrong. It's what a stop is commonly based on, not an arbitrary number.

screens.question: Invalidation is the point where...
options: the trade is guaranteed to win.
the trade idea is proven wrong.
screens.explanation: Invalidation marks where the reasoning no longer holds.

screens.question: A stop is commonly based on where the idea is invalidated, not a random number.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to invalidation gives it a clear, reasoned basis.

screens.question: Invalidation is where the trade idea is [___].
screens.explanation: It's the level that disproves the idea.

screens.scenario: Someone enters a trade with no idea of where they'd be wrong.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A trade never needs a wrong-point.
Without an invalidation point, there's no clear place to stop or admit the idea failed.
screens.explanation: A defined invalidation is what makes risk manageable and the idea testable.

screens.question: Invalidation is where the trade idea is proven [___].
screens.explanation: Invalidation marks where the reasoning no longer holds.

screens.question: A stop is commonly based on where the idea is invalidated, not a random number.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to invalidation gives it a clear, reasoned basis.

lessons.title: Process Over Prediction
lessons.celebration: You understand process over prediction!

screens.title: You Control the Process, Not the Outcome
screens.text: You can't control whether one trade wins, only whether you followed your process. Good process with a bad outcome is still good process; the edge shows over many trades.

screens.question: In trading, you directly control...
options: the outcome of any single trade.
screens.explanation: You control the process; outcomes vary trade to trade.

screens.question: A good process can still produce a losing trade.
screens.explanation: Any single outcome is uncertain; process is judged over many trades.

screens.question: You control the [___], not the outcome of one trade.
screens.explanation: Process is the controllable part; outcomes vary.

screens.question: Why focus on process over outcome?

options.label: Because outcomes are fully controllable
options.wrong_explanation: You can't control a single result.

options.label: Because process never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Process is the controllable edge.

options.label: Because the edge shows over many trades, not any single one

screens.explanation: Process is what you control; the edge appears over a large sample.

screens.question: You control the [___], not the outcome of any single trade.
screens.explanation: Process is the controllable part; outcomes vary trade to trade.

screens.question: A good process can still produce a losing trade.
screens.explanation: Any single outcome is uncertain; process is judged over many trades.

lessons.title: A Pre-Trade Checklist
lessons.celebration: You can build a pre-trade checklist!

screens.title: Same Questions Every Time
screens.text: A checklist asks the same questions before every trade: what's the condition, is there a level, is there a signal, and what's the risk? Consistency comes from repeating the process.

screens.question: A simple pre-trade checklist order:
items: Classify the market condition
Identify the key level
Look for a signal at that level
Define the risk (invalidation and size)
correct_order: Classify the market condition
Identify the key level
Look for a signal at that level
Define the risk (invalidation and size)
screens.explanation: Condition, level, signal, risk, a repeatable pre-trade sequence.

screens.question: The point of a checklist is to...
options: ask the same questions consistently every time.
screens.explanation: Consistency, not a guarantee, is the value of a checklist.

screens.question: A checklist brings [___] to the pre-trade process.
screens.explanation: Repeating the same checks each time builds consistency.

screens.question: A checklist guarantees profitable trades.
screens.explanation: It brings consistency to the process; it can't guarantee outcomes.

screens.question: A pre-trade checklist brings [___] to the process.
screens.explanation: Repeating the same checks each time builds consistency.

screens.question: A checklist guarantees profitable trades.
screens.explanation: It brings consistency; it can't guarantee outcomes.

lessons.title: Sticking to the Plan
lessons.celebration: You understand plan discipline!

screens.title: Follow It, Even When Tempted
screens.text: A plan only helps if you follow it. Moving your stop, skipping your checklist, or abandoning the idea mid-trade undoes the plan's whole purpose.

screens.question: A trade plan only helps if you...
screens.explanation: The plan's value comes from following it consistently.

screens.question: Widening your stop mid-trade to avoid a loss undermines the plan.
screens.explanation: Moving the stop breaks the invalidation the plan was built on.

screens.question: A plan helps only if you [___] it.
screens.explanation: Following the plan is what gives it value.

screens.scenario: Someone hits their planned invalidation but moves the stop further away to avoid taking the loss.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Invalidation is optional once you're in.
Moving the stop is following the plan.

lessons.title: What Is VWAP?

screens.title: The Volume-Weighted Average
screens.text: VWAP is the Volume-Weighted Average Price, the average price over a session, weighted by how much volume traded at each price. It's commonly used intraday as a reference "fair value" line.

screens.question: VWAP stands for...
screens.explanation: VWAP is the volume-weighted average price over a session.

screens.question: VWAP weights each price by its [___].
screens.explanation: More volume at a price gives it more weight in the average.

screens.question: VWAP is commonly used as an intraday reference for average price.
screens.explanation: VWAP is a common intraday "fair value" reference line.

screens.question: How does VWAP differ from a simple moving average?
options: It only uses the highest price.
It weights prices by volume, not just by time.
screens.explanation: VWAP weights by volume; a simple MA weights each period equally.

screens.question: VWAP stands for Volume-[___] Average Price.
screens.explanation: VWAP weights each price by the volume traded there.

screens.question: VWAP is commonly used as an intraday reference for average price.
screens.explanation: VWAP is a common intraday "fair value" reference line.

screens.title: Above or Below Fair Value
screens.text: Price trading above VWAP is commonly described as trading above the session's average (relative strength); below as relative weakness. It's descriptive context, not a signal.

screens.question: Price above VWAP is commonly described as...
options: trading above the session average (relative strength).
screens.explanation: Above the volume-weighted average is commonly read as relative strength.

screens.question: Price below VWAP is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Below the session's average price reads as relative weakness.

screens.explanation: VWAP context is descriptive, never a guaranteed signal.

screens.question: Price above VWAP is commonly described as relative [___].
screens.explanation: Trading above the session's volume-weighted average reads as relative strength.

screens.question: Price below VWAP is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Below the session average reads as relative weakness.

lessons.title: What Are Bollinger Bands?

screens.title: A Band Around a Moving Average
screens.text: Bollinger Bands draw a moving average with an upper and lower band set a number of standard deviations away. The bands measure how far price is straying from its average.

options: moving average, with bands set by standard deviation.
screens.explanation: The middle is an MA; the bands are standard deviations from it.

screens.question: The Bollinger band width is based on [___] deviation.
screens.explanation: The bands are placed a number of standard deviations from the MA.

screens.question: The middle Bollinger line is a moving average.
screens.explanation: Bollinger Bands center on a moving average, with bands around it.

screens.question: The bands measure how far price is straying from its...
screens.explanation: The bands quantify deviation from the moving-average center.

screens.question: Bollinger Bands are built around a moving [___].
screens.explanation: The middle line is a moving average, with bands set by standard deviation.

screens.question: The middle Bollinger line is a moving average.
screens.explanation: Bollinger Bands center on a moving average, with bands around it.

lessons.title: Bands Widen and Narrow

screens.title: Width Reflects Volatility
screens.text: When volatility rises, the bands widen; when it's calm, they narrow. Band width is a quick read of how volatile price is right now.

screens.question: Wide Bollinger Bands reflect...
screens.explanation: Bigger deviations (volatility) push the bands wider.

screens.question: Narrow ("squeezing") Bollinger Bands reflect...
screens.explanation: Small deviations (calm) pull the bands narrow.

screens.question: Band width is a quick read of current volatility.
screens.explanation: Width tracks how far price is deviating, i.e., volatility.

screens.question: Narrow ("squeezing") Bollinger Bands reflect low volatility.

lessons.title: Price at the Bands

screens.title: Touching a Band Isn't a Signal
screens.text: Price touching the upper or lower band shows it's stretched far from its average. But in a strong trend, price can "ride" a band for a long time. It's descriptive, not a reversal signal.

screens.explanation: An upper-band touch means price is far above the moving-average center.

screens.question: A band touch is a guaranteed reversal signal.
