screens.explanation: Band touches are descriptive stretch reads, not guaranteed reversals.

lessons.title: What Is a Drawdown?

screens.title: The Drop From a Peak
screens.text: A drawdown is the percentage decline from an account's peak value to a later low. Every account has drawdowns. They're a normal part of the equity curve.

options: peak value to a later low.
screens.explanation: A drawdown is the drop from a prior peak to a subsequent low.

screens.explanation: Drawdowns are commonly expressed as a percent from peak.

screens.explanation: Drawdowns are a normal part of any equity curve.

screens.explanation: Drawdown is measured from the prior peak value.

lessons.title: Recovery Math
lessons.celebration: You understand recovery math!

screens.title: Losses Need Bigger Gains Back
screens.text: A key fact: a loss needs a larger percentage gain to recover. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to break even. This is why limiting drawdowns matters.

screens.question: A 50% loss requires what gain to break even?
screens.explanation: Halving your account means you must double what's left, a 100% gain.

screens.question: A 20% loss requires roughly what gain to break even?
screens.explanation: From 80% of the start, you need +25% (0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00).

screens.question: A loss needs a larger percentage gain than the loss itself to recover.
screens.explanation: You're gaining on a smaller base, so the required percent is larger.

screens.question: The bigger the drawdown, the [___] the gain needed to recover.
screens.explanation: Deeper losses require disproportionately larger recovery gains.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a 50% loss just needs a 50% gain to get back.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover, since you're rebuilding from a smaller base.
screens.explanation: Recovering a loss requires a larger percent gain than the loss itself.

screens.question: A 50% loss requires a [___]% gain to recover.
screens.explanation: Halving your account means you must double what's left to break even.

screens.question: A loss needs a larger percentage gain than the loss itself to recover.
screens.explanation: You're gaining on a smaller base, so the required percent is larger.

screens.text: A string of losses in a row happens even with a positive-expectancy system, purely by chance. A losing streak alone doesn't prove the system is broken.

options: normal. It can happen by chance.
screens.explanation: Even a good system sees losing streaks by chance.

screens.question: A few losses in a row proves a system has negative expectancy.
screens.explanation: Short streaks happen by chance; they don't prove the long-run expectancy.

screens.question: A losing streak alone doesn't prove a system is [___].

Because systems never lose

lessons.title: What Is ATR?

screens.text: ATR (Average True Range) is an indicator that measures the average size of price movement over a recent period. It's expressed in price, not as a bounded 0-100 oscillator.

screens.question: ATR measures...
options: The average size of price movement over a recent period.
The exact direction price will move next.
screens.explanation: ATR is a volatility measure based on the average size of recent price movement.

screens.question: ATR is expressed in price terms, not as a bounded 0-100 scale.
screens.explanation: Unlike RSI, ATR is expressed in the asset's own price units.

screens.question: ATR measures the average [___] of price movement.
screens.explanation: ATR is specifically about size (range) of movement, not direction.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: The broader concept ATR is one way of measuring
screens.explanation: ATR is one specific, price-based way of quantifying volatility.

screens.question: Which best describes what ATR tells you?

screens.explanation: Like volume, ATR is judged relative to what's typical for that specific asset.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a specific ATR number is universally "high" for every single asset.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: ATR is judged relative to that asset's own typical range, not one fixed universal number.
Every asset shares the identical ATR scale.
ATR values never vary between assets.
screens.explanation: ATR readings are relative to each asset's own typical volatility.

lessons.title: ATR and Position Sizing
lessons.celebration: You understand how ATR connects to position sizing!

screens.title: Sizing to Typical Movement
screens.text: Some traders use ATR to help gauge a reasonable stop distance, sizing positions around how much an asset typically moves rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: How might ATR be used alongside position sizing?
options: To help gauge a reasonable stop distance based on typical movement.
To replace the need for any stop-loss at all.
screens.explanation: ATR can inform how far a stop might reasonably need to sit given typical movement, connecting back to the Position Sizing unit.

screens.question: A wider ATR (more typical movement) might call for a wider stop distance to avoid being caught by normal noise.
screens.explanation: A stop set too tight relative to typical movement risks getting triggered by ordinary volatility.

screens.question: Using ATR for stops means basing distance on typical [___], not an arbitrary number.
screens.explanation: ATR-based stops are grounded in the asset's own typical price movement.

screens.question: Match the concept to how it connects to ATR.
pairs: Can be informed by typical movement (ATR)
Still derived from dollar risk and stop distance
Connect back to the Risk Management and Position Sizing units
screens.explanation: ATR is one more input into the same risk-management process covered earlier in the course.

screens.question: Why might a stop based on ATR make sense?

options.label: It guarantees the stop is never hit
options.wrong_explanation: No stop placement guarantees anything.

options.label: It's sized to typical movement, reducing the chance normal noise triggers it
It removes the need for position sizing entirely
options.wrong_explanation: Sizing is still calculated from risk and stop distance.

screens.explanation: ATR-informed stops are grounded in typical movement, not a guarantee against being stopped out.

screens.scenario: Someone sets a stop far tighter than the asset's typical ATR and is surprised it gets hit by normal noise.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Stop distance should never consider typical movement.
ATR has no relationship to stop placement.
A stop set well inside typical movement (ATR) can get triggered by ordinary volatility, not a meaningful shift.
screens.explanation: This connects back to the earlier Stop-Loss Placement Logic lesson — a stop too tight for normal movement risks getting hit by noise.

lessons.title: ATR Across Market Conditions
lessons.celebration: You can read ATR across different conditions!

screens.title: Trending, Ranging, and ATR
screens.text: ATR commonly rises during volatile or strongly trending conditions and commonly falls during quiet ranges or consolidation.

screens.question: ATR commonly does what during a tight, quiet range?
options: Has no relationship to market condition.
screens.explanation: Quiet, range-bound conditions commonly show lower ATR readings.

screens.question: ATR commonly rises during volatile or strongly trending conditions.
screens.explanation: Bigger typical moves during volatile/trending conditions commonly push ATR higher.

screens.question: ATR connects back to the Market Condition Classification unit by [___] typical movement size.
screens.explanation: ATR gives a numeric way to describe how much price typically moves in a given condition.

screens.question: Match the market condition to its commonly cited ATR behavior.
pairs: A way to quantify this difference numerically
screens.explanation: ATR gives numeric texture to the trending/ranging/volatile classifications from earlier in the course.

screens.question: How does ATR add to market condition classification?

options.label: It replaces classifying trending vs. ranging entirely
options.wrong_explanation: ATR adds to, not replaces, that classification.

options.label: It gives a numeric read on how much price is typically moving, reinforcing the classification
It has no relationship to market condition
options.wrong_explanation: ATR commonly shifts with condition.

screens.explanation: ATR is one more piece of confluence alongside the condition classification skill from Advanced.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes ATR always stays exactly the same number no matter the market condition.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: ATR never changes regardless of condition.
ATR commonly rises in volatile/trending conditions and falls in quiet ranges — it isn't fixed.
Market condition has no bearing on ATR.
screens.explanation: ATR moves with the underlying volatility of the current condition.

lessons.title: ATR Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Average True Range unit!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of what ATR measures, comparing readings, ATR and position sizing, and ATR across market conditions.

screens.question: ATR measures typical size of price movement, not direction.
screens.explanation: That's the core, consistent idea across this whole unit.

screens.question: ATR is judged [___] to what's typical for that specific asset.
screens.explanation: Like volume, ATR readings are relative, not a single universal number.

screens.question: How does ATR commonly connect to risk management?
options: It has no relationship to stops or sizing.
It guarantees a specific trade outcome.
It can inform a reasonable stop distance based on typical movement.
screens.explanation: ATR is commonly used as one input into stop placement, connecting back to earlier Risk Management lessons.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Average size of recent price movement
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: ATR guarantees the next price direction
options.wrong_explanation: ATR describes size, not direction or certainty.

options.label: ATR quantifies typical movement size, connecting to stops, sizing, and market condition
ATR is unrelated to risk management
options.wrong_explanation: It connects directly to stop placement and sizing.

screens.explanation: ATR quantifying typical movement, connected to risk concepts already taught, is the throughline of this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts using ATR as a buy/sell signal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: ATR always tells you when to buy or sell.
ATR describes typical movement size, it's not a buy or sell signal.
ATR has no descriptive value at all.
screens.explanation: Like every indicator in this course, ATR is descriptive context, never a trade signal.

lessons.title: What Is Relative Volume?
lessons.celebration: You understand what RVOL measures!

screens.title: Volume Compared to Normal
screens.text: Relative Volume (RVOL) compares today's volume to that same stock's typical volume at this point in the day. It answers "is this unusually active, or a normal day?"

screens.question: RVOL compares today's volume to...
options: The volume of every other stock in the market.
The stock's all-time high volume ever recorded.
That stock's own typical volume at this point in the day.
screens.explanation: RVOL is a same-stock, same-time-of-day comparison, not a cross-market ranking.

screens.question: RVOL is about comparing a stock's volume to its own typical pattern, not to other stocks.
screens.explanation: RVOL is stock-specific and time-of-day-specific.

screens.question: RVOL helps answer whether today's volume is [___] for this stock.
screens.explanation: RVOL flags whether current activity is normal or standout compared to that stock's own history.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: Comparing current volume to typical volume, same stock
Total shares traded, no comparison built in
screens.explanation: RVOL adds context that raw volume alone doesn't provide.

screens.question: Why might RVOL matter more than raw share volume alone?

options.label: Because raw volume alone doesn't say whether that's unusual for this particular stock
Because RVOL replaces the need to look at price at all
options.wrong_explanation: RVOL is one added piece of context, not a replacement for price.

options.label: Because raw volume is always identical across all stocks
options.wrong_explanation: Typical volume varies enormously by stock.

screens.explanation: A million shares might be huge for one stock and tiny for another — RVOL adds that missing context.

screens.scenario: Someone sees "2 million shares traded" and assumes that's automatically a big deal for every stock.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Raw share count means the same thing for every stock.
Whether 2 million shares is unusual depends on that stock's own typical volume, which RVOL captures.
Volume numbers never need any context.
screens.explanation: Without comparing to typical volume, a raw number alone doesn't reveal whether it's unusual.

lessons.title: Reading an RVOL Reading
lessons.celebration: You can interpret RVOL readings!

screens.title: Above and Below "Normal"
screens.text: An RVOL reading is often expressed as a multiple of normal, for example "2x" meaning twice the typical volume for this time of day.

screens.question: An RVOL reading of "3x" commonly means...
options: Volume is roughly three times this stock's typical level.
The stock has three times as many shares outstanding.
screens.explanation: RVOL multiples describe volume relative to typical, not price or share count.

screens.question: An RVOL below 1x commonly reflects quieter-than-usual volume.
screens.explanation: A reading under 1x means volume is running below what's typical for that time.

screens.question: An RVOL reading is often expressed as a [___] of normal volume.
screens.explanation: RVOL is commonly shown as a multiple (like 2x or 0.5x) of typical volume.

screens.question: Match the RVOL reading to its meaning.
screens.explanation: The 1x baseline represents this stock's own normal volume for that time of day.

screens.question: Why compare RVOL to 1x rather than to a fixed universal number?

options.label: Because RVOL has no baseline at all
options.wrong_explanation: 1x serves as the "typical" baseline.

options.label: Because 1x is a fixed number that means the same thing for every stock
options.wrong_explanation: 1x is relative to each stock's own typical volume.

options.label: Because 1x represents this specific stock's own typical volume as the baseline

screens.explanation: The 1x baseline is specific to each stock, which is what makes RVOL a relative measure.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes an RVOL of "1.5x" means the same absolute share count for every stock.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: RVOL has no connection to that stock's own history.
1.5x always equals exactly the same number of shares everywhere.
1.5x is relative to that stock's own typical volume, which differs stock to stock.
screens.explanation: The multiple is anchored to each stock's own typical volume, not a shared absolute number.

lessons.title: RVOL and News or Catalysts
lessons.celebration: You can connect RVOL to catalysts!

screens.title: A Clue, Not a Signal
screens.text: Unusually high RVOL sometimes coincides with news, earnings, or other catalysts, since more participants may be trading around the event. It's descriptive context, not a trade signal.

screens.question: Elevated RVOL alongside news commonly reflects...
options: More participants than usual trading around that event.
Confirmation that the news is accurate.
screens.explanation: Elevated RVOL is a participation clue, not a guarantee of direction or of the news itself.

screens.question: High RVOL around a catalyst is context, not a buy or sell signal.
screens.explanation: Like every indicator in this course, RVOL describes conditions rather than prescribing action.

screens.question: Elevated RVOL near news commonly reflects more [___] than usual.
screens.explanation: More shares changing hands reflects more participation, not certainty of outcome.

screens.question: Match the scenario to what it commonly reflects.
pairs: More participants trading around the event
Unusual activity worth noting as context
screens.explanation: RVOL by itself describes activity level, and pairing it with a known catalyst adds context.

screens.question: How should elevated RVOL near a catalyst be treated?

options.label: As one piece of descriptive context about participation, not a signal
As a guarantee that price will move in a specific direction
options.wrong_explanation: RVOL says nothing about direction.

options.label: As proof the news itself is true
options.wrong_explanation: Volume doesn't verify news accuracy.

screens.explanation: RVOL adds context about participation levels, never a directional or truth guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone sees high RVOL on earnings day and treats it as a guaranteed breakout signal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Earnings always cause identical RVOL patterns.
High RVOL reflects participation, not a guaranteed direction or outcome.
RVOL always predicts a breakout on earnings days.
screens.explanation: RVOL is descriptive context about activity level, never a predictive signal.

lessons.title: RVOL Across the Trading Day
lessons.celebration: You understand how RVOL shifts intraday!

screens.title: Time-of-Day Matters
screens.text: Because RVOL compares to typical volume at that specific time of day, a stock's expected volume in the first ten minutes differs from its expected volume midday, connecting back to the Trading Sessions unit.

screens.question: Why does RVOL account for time of day rather than the whole day at once?
options: Because volume is identical every minute of the day.
Because typical volume itself varies by time of day, like the open being busier than midday.
Because RVOL only applies after the market closes.
screens.explanation: This connects back to earlier lessons on how volume and activity vary across the trading session.

screens.question: Typical volume in the opening minutes commonly differs from typical volume at midday.
screens.explanation: Sessions differ in typical activity level, which is why RVOL compares like-for-like time windows.

screens.question: RVOL compares current volume to what's typical for that same [___] of day.
screens.explanation: The comparison window matters since typical volume itself shifts through the session.

screens.question: Match the session to a commonly cited RVOL consideration.
screens.explanation: This ties RVOL directly back to the Trading Sessions & News unit's session-activity concepts.

screens.question: Why does time-of-day matter for reading RVOL correctly?

options.label: Because every session has identical typical volume
options.wrong_explanation: Sessions commonly differ in typical activity.

options.label: Because comparing to the wrong time window could make normal activity look unusual, or vice versa
Because RVOL ignores time of day entirely
options.wrong_explanation: RVOL's baseline is specifically time-of-day aware.

screens.explanation: A meaningful RVOL reading depends on comparing against the right same-time-of-day baseline.

screens.scenario: Someone compares midday volume directly to the opening-minutes baseline and calls it "quiet."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: RVOL has no relationship to time of day.
Volume is identical at every point in the trading day.
Comparing across mismatched time-of-day baselines can make normal midday volume look artificially low.
screens.explanation: RVOL's comparison should use the typical baseline for that same time window, not a different one.

lessons.title: RVOL Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Relative Volume unit!

screens.text: A final review of what RVOL measures, reading its readings, its relationship to catalysts, and how time of day factors in.

screens.question: RVOL compares current volume to that stock's own typical volume, not to other stocks.
screens.explanation: That's the core, consistent idea across this whole unit.

screens.question: An RVOL reading is commonly expressed as a [___] of typical volume.
screens.explanation: A recap of the "2x," "0.5x" style readings covered in this unit.

screens.question: How should elevated RVOL near a catalyst be treated?
options: As descriptive context about participation, not a trade signal.
As proof the catalyst news is accurate.
screens.explanation: A recap of the descriptive, non-predictive framing used throughout the course.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Volume relative to that stock's own typical level
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: RVOL guarantees the next price direction
options.wrong_explanation: RVOL describes participation, not direction.

options.label: RVOL adds relative, time-aware context to raw volume, without predicting direction
RVOL is unrelated to time of day
options.wrong_explanation: The baseline itself is time-of-day specific.

screens.explanation: RVOL's value is the relative, time-aware context it adds to plain volume figures.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts using RVOL alone as a buy/sell trigger.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: RVOL has no descriptive value at all.
RVOL always tells you when to buy or sell.
RVOL describes relative participation, it's not a buy or sell signal on its own.
screens.explanation: Like every indicator in this course, RVOL is descriptive context, never a trade signal.

lessons.title: What Is the Opening Range?
lessons.celebration: You understand what the opening range is!

screens.title: The First Few Minutes
screens.text: The opening range refers to the high and low price established during a defined early window after the market opens, commonly the first five, fifteen, or thirty minutes.

screens.question: The opening range is defined by...
options: The high and low price during a set early window after the open.
The average price over the entire prior week.
The closing price from the prior day.
screens.explanation: The opening range is specifically about the high/low formed in an early defined window, not prior-day or weekly data.

screens.question: The opening range window is commonly the first five, fifteen, or thirty minutes of the session.
screens.explanation: Different traders use different defined windows, but these are common choices.

screens.question: The opening range is the high and low formed during a [___] early window.
screens.explanation: The window is a specific, defined stretch of time, not an arbitrary or extended one.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: High/low during an early defined window
The top of that early window's range
The bottom of that early window's range
screens.explanation: The opening range establishes a reference high and low from the earliest minutes of trading.

screens.question: Why might traders pay attention to the opening range?

options.label: It guarantees the day's exact high and low
options.wrong_explanation: The opening range is an early reference, not a guarantee of the day's extremes.

options.label: It's an early reference level formed from the session's first activity
It only matters for the last hour of trading
options.wrong_explanation: The opening range is defined by early, not late, price action.

screens.explanation: The opening range gives an early reference level built from the session's first few minutes.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes the opening range guarantees the day's final high and low.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The opening range has no relationship to the rest of the day.
The opening range always matches the day's final high and low exactly.
The opening range is an early reference level, not a guarantee of the full day's eventual high or low.
screens.explanation: Price can move well beyond the opening range as the day continues.

lessons.title: Opening Range Breaks
lessons.celebration: You can describe an opening range break!

screens.title: Trading Above or Below the Range
screens.text: When price moves above the opening range high or below the opening range low, that's commonly described as breaking out of the opening range.

screens.question: Price closing above the opening range high is commonly described as...
options: Breaking out of the opening range to the upside.
Breaking down through support from last week.
screens.explanation: Moving beyond the opening range high is the defining description of an upside break of that range.

screens.question: Price can also break below the opening range low, described as breaking down out of the range.
screens.explanation: Breaks can occur in either direction relative to the established range.

screens.question: Moving beyond the opening range boundary is commonly called [___] the range.
screens.explanation: This is simply the descriptive term for price moving past the established opening range boundary.

screens.question: Match the scenario to its description.
screens.explanation: These are the three basic descriptive states relative to the opening range.

screens.question: What does an opening range break describe, on its own?

options.label: That price has moved beyond an early reference level, nothing more by itself
A guaranteed continuation for the rest of the day
options.wrong_explanation: A break describes a boundary crossing, not a guaranteed continuation.

options.label: Confirmation that a reversal is now impossible
options.wrong_explanation: Price can reverse after any break.

screens.explanation: An opening range break is a descriptive observation about crossing an early reference level, not a guarantee of what follows.

screens.scenario: Someone treats an opening range break as guaranteed to continue trending the rest of the day.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Price never reverses after breaking the opening range.
Every opening range break continues in the same direction all day.
A break describes crossing the range boundary, it doesn't guarantee the rest of the day's direction.
screens.explanation: Like any breakout, a range break can continue, stall, or reverse afterward.

lessons.title: Opening Range and False Breaks
lessons.celebration: You understand opening range false breaks!

screens.title: When a Break Doesn't Hold
screens.text: Sometimes price breaks the opening range briefly and then moves back inside it, commonly described as a false break of the opening range, echoing the false breakout concept from earlier units.

screens.question: Price briefly moving above the opening range high and then falling back inside is commonly described as...
options: Proof the opening range was calculated incorrectly.
A false break of the opening range.
screens.explanation: This is the same false-break/failed-breakout idea covered earlier, applied specifically to the opening range.

screens.question: A false break of the opening range echoes the false breakout concept covered in the Breakouts & Retests unit.
screens.explanation: The underlying idea, price failing to hold beyond a level, is the same concept applied to this specific reference range.

screens.question: A break that doesn't hold and returns inside the range is commonly called a [___] break.
screens.explanation: This mirrors the "false breakout" terminology already established earlier in the course.

screens.question: Match the concept to its connection.
pairs: Echoes the general false breakout concept
The specific reference level being tested
screens.explanation: The opening range is simply one more level that can be broken, held, or falsely broken.

screens.question: Why is it useful to recognize a false break of the opening range?

options.label: Because false breaks of the opening range never happen
options.wrong_explanation: They can and do occur, same as any other breakout.

options.label: Because it reinforces that any break, including this one, can fail to hold
Because it means the opening range concept doesn't apply here
options.wrong_explanation: The opening range concept still applies, it just didn't hold.

screens.explanation: Recognizing false breaks keeps the opening range concept consistent with the broader breakout/retest ideas taught earlier.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every opening range break automatically holds and never fails.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Opening range breaks are a completely different phenomenon from regular breakouts.
Opening range breaks can fail to hold, just like any other breakout covered earlier in the course.
False breaks are impossible once price crosses the opening range boundary.
screens.explanation: The opening range is one more level subject to the same false-breakout dynamics taught earlier.

lessons.title: Opening Range and Volatility
lessons.celebration: You can connect opening range width to volatility!

screens.title: Wide Range vs. Narrow Range
screens.text: A wider opening range commonly reflects more volatile early trading, while a narrower opening range commonly reflects calmer early trading, connecting back to the ATR and volatility concepts.

screens.question: A wider opening range commonly reflects...
options: Lower trading volume for the whole day.
screens.explanation: A wide early range simply reflects larger early price swings, similar to a higher ATR reading.

screens.question: A narrower opening range commonly reflects calmer early trading.
screens.explanation: A tight range in the early minutes reflects smaller early price swings.

screens.question: Opening range width connects to the same idea as [___], covered earlier in this course.
screens.explanation: Both opening range width and ATR describe the size of recent price movement, just over different windows.

screens.question: Match the range width to its commonly cited meaning.
pairs: A volatility descriptor, like ATR but for the open specifically
screens.explanation: This ties the opening range back to volatility concepts taught earlier in the course.

screens.question: How does opening range width add to reading a session?

options.label: It replaces the need for ATR throughout the rest of the day
options.wrong_explanation: Opening range width is one added data point, not a replacement.

options.label: It gives an early descriptive read on volatility, similar to ATR but specific to the open
It has no relationship to volatility
options.wrong_explanation: Range width directly reflects early volatility.

screens.explanation: Opening range width is simply a volatility read specific to the earliest minutes of the session.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a wide opening range guarantees a volatile day for the remaining hours.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A wide opening range describes early volatility, it doesn't guarantee how the rest of the day unfolds.
Opening range width always predicts the entire day's volatility.
Opening range width has no connection to volatility at all.
screens.explanation: The opening range only describes the earliest window, not a guarantee for the rest of the session.

lessons.celebration: You've completed the Opening Range unit!

screens.explanation: A recap of the false-break terminology covered in this unit.

Price moving beyond that range's boundary

lessons.title: Stocks Don't Move Alone
lessons.celebration: You understand sector and index context!

screens.title: The Bigger Picture
screens.text: Individual stocks commonly move alongside their sector (a group of related companies) and the broader market indexes, rather than in complete isolation.

screens.question: Sector and index context describes...
options: A rule that stocks never share any common movement.
A guaranteed prediction of a stock's next move.
How a stock's movement commonly relates to its sector and the broader market.
screens.explanation: Sector and index awareness is about relative context, not a prediction rule.

screens.question: Individual stocks commonly move somewhat alongside their sector and the broader market.
screens.explanation: Shared macro and sector-wide forces commonly influence related stocks together.

screens.question: A sector is a group of companies in the same [___] of business.
screens.explanation: A sector groups companies by the type of business they're in, such as technology or energy.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: A group of related companies by business type
A broader gauge tracking many stocks together
One company, often influenced by both of the above
screens.explanation: These three layers, stock, sector, and index, are related but distinct levels of context.

screens.question: Why consider sector and index context alongside an individual stock?

options.label: Because shared forces commonly move related stocks together, adding useful context
Because sector and index context replaces looking at the individual stock
options.wrong_explanation: It's added context, not a replacement.

options.label: Because every stock always moves in perfect lockstep with its sector
options.wrong_explanation: Correlation is common but not exact or guaranteed.

screens.explanation: Sector and index context adds useful confluence without guaranteeing exact matching movement.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a stock always moves in perfect lockstep with its sector.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Sector context has no relationship to an individual stock at all.
Stocks commonly move somewhat together with their sector, but not in guaranteed lockstep.
Every stock in a sector moves identically at all times.
screens.explanation: Correlation is common, not a guarantee, so individual stocks can diverge from their sector.

lessons.title: Relative Strength and Weakness
lessons.celebration: You can describe relative strength and weakness!

screens.title: Outperforming or Lagging
screens.text: When a stock moves more than its sector or index in the same direction, it's commonly described as showing relative strength; moving less, or opposite, is commonly described as relative weakness.

screens.question: A stock rising more than its sector on an up day is commonly described as showing...
screens.explanation: Outperforming its peer group to the upside is the definition of relative strength in this context.

screens.question: A stock falling more than its sector on a down day, or rising less than its sector on an up day, is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Underperforming the sector, in either direction, fits the relative weakness description.

screens.question: Moving more than the sector/index in the same direction is commonly called relative [___].
screens.explanation: This is simply the descriptive term used for outperformance versus a peer group.

screens.question: Match the scenario to its description.
pairs: Stock moving in line with sector
screens.explanation: Relative strength/weakness describes divergence from the sector's typical movement.

screens.question: What does relative strength describe, on its own?

options.label: That a stock is outperforming its sector or index, nothing more by itself
A guarantee that outperformance will continue
options.wrong_explanation: Relative strength describes current comparison, not a guaranteed future.

options.label: Proof that the stock has better fundamentals
options.wrong_explanation: Relative strength is a price comparison, not a fundamentals judgment.

screens.explanation: Relative strength is a descriptive comparison of price movement, not a guarantee or fundamentals claim.

screens.scenario: Someone treats relative strength today as a guarantee it continues tomorrow.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Relative strength describes current comparative movement, it doesn't guarantee future outperformance.
Relative strength always continues indefinitely once observed.
Relative strength has no meaning beyond a single day.
screens.explanation: Like any descriptive read, relative strength can shift from one period to the next.

lessons.title: Sector Rotation
lessons.celebration: You understand sector rotation as a concept!

screens.title: Money Moving Between Sectors
screens.text: Sector rotation describes a pattern where different sectors take turns showing relative strength or weakness over time, commonly discussed as shifting participation between areas of the market.

screens.question: Sector rotation describes...
options: A guaranteed schedule of which sector rises next.
Different sectors taking turns showing relative strength or weakness over time.
A rule that only one sector ever trades at a time.
screens.explanation: Sector rotation is a descriptive pattern of shifting relative strength, not a fixed schedule.

screens.question: Sector rotation is discussed as a pattern, not a guaranteed or fixed schedule.
screens.explanation: Like most concepts in this course, it's a descriptive pattern rather than a predictive rule.

screens.question: Sector rotation describes sectors taking [___] showing relative strength over time.
screens.explanation: The core idea is that which sector shows strength commonly shifts over time.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: Sectors taking turns showing relative strength
One stock or sector outperforming a comparison
The broader backdrop sectors rotate within
screens.explanation: Sector rotation is really relative strength/weakness applied at the sector level over time.

screens.question: How should sector rotation be treated as a concept?

options.label: As a descriptive pattern of shifting relative strength between sectors, not a fixed schedule
As a concept unrelated to relative strength
options.wrong_explanation: It's relative strength/weakness applied over time at the sector level.

options.label: As a guaranteed calendar of which sector leads each month
options.wrong_explanation: No fixed schedule is guaranteed.

screens.explanation: Sector rotation is best understood as a descriptive, shifting pattern rather than a predictive schedule.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes sector rotation follows a fixed, guaranteed monthly schedule.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Sector rotation has no relationship to relative strength.
Sector rotation always follows an identical, predictable calendar.
Sector rotation describes a shifting pattern over time, not a fixed guaranteed schedule.
screens.explanation: Sector rotation is a descriptive pattern, not a guaranteed timetable.

lessons.title: Confluence With Sector and Index Context
lessons.celebration: You can connect sector context to broader analysis!

screens.title: Adding One More Layer of Confluence
screens.text: Sector and index context can add one more layer of confluence alongside chart patterns, volume, and other concepts covered earlier, echoing the Confluence unit's core idea.

screens.question: Considering sector and index context alongside a chart pattern is an example of...
options: Replacing the need to look at the chart at all.
screens.explanation: This connects directly back to the Confluence unit, where multiple factors are considered together descriptively.

screens.question: Sector and index context is one more descriptive factor to weigh alongside others, not a standalone signal.
screens.explanation: Consistent with how confluence was framed earlier in the course.

screens.question: Weighing sector context alongside chart patterns is an example of building [___].
screens.explanation: This is the same confluence concept from earlier, just adding a sector/index layer.

screens.question: Match the factor to its role in confluence.
pairs: One more descriptive factor, not a replacement for the others
screens.explanation: Confluence means weighing multiple descriptive factors together, none of which alone is a guarantee.

screens.question: How does sector/index context fit alongside other analysis tools from this course?

options.label: As something entirely disconnected from the rest of the course
options.wrong_explanation: It connects directly to the Confluence unit's framing.

options.label: As a replacement for chart patterns and volume analysis
options.wrong_explanation: It's additive context, not a replacement.

options.label: As one more descriptive factor to weigh, consistent with the Confluence unit

screens.explanation: Sector and index context slots into the same multi-factor, descriptive confluence approach taught earlier.

screens.scenario: Someone uses sector strength alone, ignoring every other factor, as a complete trading system.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Sector context has no relationship to the Confluence unit's ideas.
Sector strength alone is sufficient and no other factor matters.
Sector context is one descriptive factor among several, not a complete standalone system.
screens.explanation: This echoes the Confluence unit's core lesson that no single factor should be relied on alone.

lessons.title: Sector & Index Strength Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Sector & Index Strength unit!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of sector and index context, relative strength and weakness, sector rotation, and how it all connects to confluence.

screens.question: Individual stocks commonly move somewhat alongside their sector and the broader market, though not in guaranteed lockstep.
screens.explanation: That's the core, consistent idea across this whole unit.

screens.question: A stock outperforming its sector to the upside is commonly described as relative [___].
screens.explanation: A recap of the relative strength/weakness terminology from this unit.

screens.question: How should sector rotation be understood?
options: As a descriptive pattern of sectors taking turns showing relative strength over time.
As something with no connection to relative strength.
screens.explanation: A recap of sector rotation as a descriptive, non-predictive concept.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Sectors taking turns showing strength over time
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Sector and index context is unrelated to confluence
options.wrong_explanation: It connects directly to the Confluence unit's framing.

options.label: Sector and index context adds descriptive confluence, without guaranteeing any stock's future movement
Sector context guarantees which stocks will outperform going forward
options.wrong_explanation: It's descriptive context, not a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Sector and index context is valuable as one more descriptive layer of confluence, not a predictive guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts trading based on sector strength alone as a complete signal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Sector context has no descriptive value at all.
Sector strength is one descriptive factor among several, not a standalone buy or sell signal.
Sector strength alone is a complete and sufficient trading system.
screens.explanation: Like every concept in this course, sector and index context is descriptive confluence, never a standalone signal.

lessons.title: What Is Level II?
lessons.celebration: You understand what Level II data shows!

screens.title: Beyond the Last Price
screens.text: Level II data displays a list of current buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) at different price levels, sometimes called the order book, rather than just the single last traded price.

screens.question: Level II data displays...
options: A list of current bid and ask orders at different price levels.
Only the single most recent traded price.
screens.explanation: Level II is specifically about the order book, current bids and asks, not a single last-price figure or fundamentals report.

screens.question: Level II data is sometimes called the order book.
screens.explanation: "Order book" and "Level II" commonly refer to the same underlying concept.

screens.question: Level II shows current buy and sell [___] at different price levels.
screens.explanation: Level II is fundamentally a list of orders, not financial statements.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: A current buy order, and its price
A current sell order, and its price
The full list of bids and asks at various levels
screens.explanation: Level II aggregates many individual bid and ask orders into one view.

screens.question: What does Level II data add beyond a simple last-price quote?

options.label: A complete history of the company's past decade of earnings
options.wrong_explanation: Level II is about current orders, not historical financials.

options.label: A guarantee of exactly what price comes next
options.wrong_explanation: Level II shows current orders, not a guaranteed next price.

options.label: Visibility into current buy and sell orders waiting at various price levels

screens.explanation: Level II adds a view of standing orders that a simple last-price quote doesn't show.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes Level II data tells you exactly what price will print next.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Level II shows current standing orders, it doesn't guarantee the exact next traded price.
Level II always predicts the very next trade price precisely.
Level II has no relationship to bids and asks at all.
screens.explanation: Level II is a descriptive snapshot of current orders, not a guaranteed prediction of the next trade.

lessons.title: Bids, Asks, and the Spread
lessons.celebration: You understand bids, asks, and the spread!

screens.title: The Gap Between Buyers and Sellers
screens.text: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay; the ask is the lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. The gap between them is called the spread.

screens.question: The bid represents...
options: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
The average price over the past year.
screens.explanation: The bid and ask represent opposite sides of the current order book, buyers versus sellers.

screens.question: The spread is the gap between the current bid and ask price.
screens.explanation: This is the standard definition of the bid-ask spread.

screens.question: The ask is the lowest price a [___] is currently willing to accept.
screens.explanation: The ask specifically reflects the seller side of the order book.

screens.question: Match the term to its definition.
pairs: Highest price a buyer will currently pay
Lowest price a seller will currently accept
The gap between the bid and ask
screens.explanation: These three terms together describe the basic structure of the order book at any moment.

screens.question: Why might the size of the spread be worth noting descriptively?

options.label: Because the spread guarantees a specific profit on every trade
options.wrong_explanation: Spread size doesn't guarantee any profit outcome.

options.label: A wider or narrower spread can reflect differing levels of current trading activity
Because the spread never changes throughout the day
options.wrong_explanation: Spreads can widen or narrow as conditions change.

screens.explanation: Spread width is simply one more descriptive detail about current market conditions, not a profit guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes the bid-ask spread guarantees a certain profit if crossed.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The spread describes the current gap between buy and sell orders, it doesn't guarantee any profit.
The spread has no relationship to buyers and sellers.
Crossing the spread always guarantees a profitable outcome.
screens.explanation: The spread is a descriptive snapshot of order book conditions, not a profit guarantee.

lessons.title: Order Book Depth
lessons.celebration: You understand order book depth!

screens.title: How Much Is Waiting at Each Level
screens.text: Order book depth refers to the number of shares represented by orders waiting at each price level, giving a descriptive sense of how much buying or selling interest exists nearby.

screens.question: Order book depth describes...
options: A guaranteed direction for the next price move.
How many shares are represented by orders waiting at each price level.
screens.explanation: Depth is specifically about the size of orders waiting at various levels, not company-wide share counts or predictions.

screens.question: Deeper order book levels commonly reflect more resting orders at that price.
screens.explanation: More depth simply means a larger number of shares represented in waiting orders at that level.

screens.question: Order book depth gives a descriptive sense of buying or selling [___] nearby.
screens.explanation: Depth reflects current interest represented by resting orders, not a guarantee of future action.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: Size of orders waiting at each price level
Resting buy orders at various price levels
Resting sell orders at various price levels
screens.explanation: Depth can be considered separately on the buy side and the sell side of the book.

screens.question: How should order book depth be treated conceptually?

options.label: As proof of exactly what will happen to price next
options.wrong_explanation: Depth describes current orders, not a guaranteed outcome.

options.label: As a fixed, permanent measure that never changes
options.wrong_explanation: Resting orders can be added, canceled, or filled at any time.

options.label: As a descriptive snapshot of current resting orders, which can change at any moment

screens.explanation: Order book depth is a constantly shifting descriptive snapshot, not a fixed or predictive figure.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a large order sitting at one price level as a permanent, unchangeable wall.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Resting orders in the book can be modified or canceled at any moment, they aren't necessarily permanent.
Order book depth has no relationship to buying or selling interest.
Orders in the book can never be canceled once placed.
screens.explanation: The order book is a live, constantly shifting snapshot, not a fixed structure.

lessons.title: Limitations of Level II Awareness
lessons.celebration: You understand Level II's limitations!

screens.title: A Snapshot, Not a Crystal Ball
screens.text: Level II shows a real-time snapshot of orders, but those orders can be added, changed, or canceled at any moment, and Level II alone doesn't reveal the intentions behind them.

screens.question: A key limitation of Level II data is that...
options: It replaces the need for any other form of analysis.
It always accurately predicts the next ten trades.
Displayed orders can be added, changed, or canceled at any moment.
screens.explanation: The order book is a live, changeable snapshot, not a locked-in prediction of future trades.

screens.question: Level II alone doesn't reveal the underlying intentions behind any specific order.
screens.explanation: An order's presence in the book doesn't explain the trader's underlying strategy or intent.

screens.question: Level II should be treated as a real-time [___], not a guarantee of what happens next.
screens.explanation: This is the core, consistent framing for order book data throughout this unit.

screens.question: Match the limitation to its description.
pairs: Resting orders may be canceled before they're filled
The book doesn't reveal why an order was placed
A descriptive snapshot, not a predictive tool
screens.explanation: Recognizing these limitations keeps Level II awareness properly descriptive rather than predictive.

screens.question: How should a beginner-level understanding of Level II be framed?

options.label: As a tool that guarantees knowing exactly what happens next
options.wrong_explanation: Level II has real limitations and doesn't guarantee outcomes.

options.label: As descriptive awareness of the order book, with real limitations, not a predictive edge
As something irrelevant to understand at all
options.wrong_explanation: Conceptual awareness of the order book is still useful context.

screens.explanation: This course frames Level II as useful conceptual awareness, with clear limitations, never a predictive guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes Level II removes all uncertainty about what will happen next in a stock.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Level II has no limitations worth understanding.
Level II is a live, changeable snapshot with real limitations, not a tool that removes uncertainty.
Level II guarantees full certainty about every future trade.
screens.explanation: Order book data is descriptive and limited, not a certainty-removing tool.

lessons.title: Level II Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Level II & Order Book Awareness unit!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of what Level II shows, bids/asks/spread, order book depth, and the real limitations of this kind of data.

screens.question: Level II displays current buy and sell orders at various price levels, sometimes called the order book.
screens.explanation: That's the core, consistent idea across this whole unit.

screens.question: The gap between the current bid and ask is called the [___].
screens.explanation: A recap of the spread terminology covered in this unit.

screens.question: How should Level II data be treated conceptually?
options: As something with no descriptive value at all.
As a tool that guarantees the next trade price.
As a real-time, changeable snapshot with real limitations, not a predictive guarantee.
screens.explanation: A recap of the cautious, descriptive framing used throughout this unit.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Size of orders waiting at each level
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Level II offers descriptive awareness of the order book, with real limitations, never a certainty
Level II is unrelated to bids, asks, or depth
options.wrong_explanation: Those are exactly what Level II displays.

options.label: Level II guarantees exact knowledge of every future trade
options.wrong_explanation: Level II has real, acknowledged limitations.

screens.explanation: This unit's throughline is conceptual, descriptive awareness of the order book, with honest limitations.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts treating Level II alone as a complete trading edge.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Level II is descriptive, limited context, it's not a complete standalone trading edge.
Level II has no descriptive value at all.
Level II alone is sufficient for guaranteed success.
screens.explanation: Like every concept in this course, Level II awareness is descriptive context, never a guaranteed edge.

lessons.title: What Is FOMO?
lessons.celebration: You understand FOMO!

screens.title: The Fear of Missing Out
screens.text: FOMO describes the urge to jump into a trade because price is already moving fast, often without a clear plan.

screens.question: FOMO describes jumping into a trade because a plan says it's a good setup.
screens.explanation: FOMO specifically describes acting from urgency about missing a move, not from a planned setup.

screens.question: The urge to jump into a trade purely because price is already moving fast is commonly called [___].
screens.explanation: "FOMO" (fear of missing out) is the standard term for this urge.

screens.question: What commonly characterizes a FOMO-driven trade entry?
options: Entering because of urgency about a fast-moving price, without a clear pre-existing plan.
Entering after carefully calculating position size in advance.
Entering only after a calm, pre-planned checklist is satisfied.
screens.explanation: FOMO entries are commonly described as reactive and plan-less, driven by urgency.

screens.question: Match the trading behavior to its description.
pairs: Jumping in reactively because price is moving fast
Entering after a pre-set plan's conditions are met
Waiting for a planned setup rather than chasing price
screens.explanation: Contrasting FOMO with planned, patient entries highlights what makes FOMO distinct.

screens.template: FOMO is commonly described as an [__1__] response, rather than a [__2__] one.
screens.explanation: FOMO is commonly framed as emotional urgency, in contrast to a calm, planned entry.

screens.question: A commonly cited way to recognize a FOMO impulse before acting on it:
items: Notice the urge to enter immediately because price is moving
Ask whether this matches a pre-existing plan or setup
Recognize if the urge is driven mainly by fear of missing out
Pause instead of acting immediately on the impulse
correct_order: Notice the urge to enter immediately because price is moving
Ask whether this matches a pre-existing plan or setup
Recognize if the urge is driven mainly by fear of missing out
Pause instead of acting immediately on the impulse
screens.explanation: This process gives space to recognize FOMO before automatically acting on it.

screens.question: Which best describes a FOMO-driven trade entry?

options.label: Entering after a pre-set plan's specific conditions are met
options.detail: This describes a planned entry, not FOMO
options.wrong_explanation: A planned entry is the opposite of what FOMO describes.

options.label: A guarantee that the trade will be profitable
options.wrong_explanation: FOMO describes a motivation for entering, not an outcome.

options.label: Entering because of urgency about a fast-moving price, without a clear plan

screens.explanation: FOMO specifically describes an emotionally reactive, plan-less entry driven by urgency.

screens.scenario: Someone sees a stock moving up quickly and buys immediately, without any plan, purely because they're afraid of missing further gains.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Entering purely from urgency about missing a move, without a plan, is a commonly described FOMO reaction.
They should never look at fast-moving prices again.
They should have bought even more, even faster.
screens.explanation: Acting from fear of missing out, without a plan, is the commonly described core of a FOMO-driven mistake.

screens.question: FOMO describes urgency about [___] a fast-moving price.
screens.explanation: FOMO is the urgency to jump in purely because price is already moving.

screens.question: FOMO entries are commonly described as reactive and plan-less.
screens.explanation: FOMO is driven by urgency, not a pre-existing plan.

lessons.title: Revenge Trading
lessons.celebration: You understand revenge trading!

screens.title: Trying to "Win It Back"
screens.text: Revenge trading describes entering a new trade quickly after a loss, driven by the urge to immediately recover it rather than a plan.

screens.question: Revenge trading describes entering a new trade quickly after a loss, driven by the urge to recover it immediately.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of revenge trading.

screens.question: Entering a trade quickly after a loss, mainly to try to "win it back," is commonly called [___] trading.
screens.explanation: "Revenge trading" is the standard term for this reactive pattern.

screens.question: What commonly characterizes a revenge trade?
options: It's driven mainly by the urge to recover a recent loss quickly, rather than a fresh, planned setup.
It's driven by a carefully pre-planned checklist unrelated to the prior loss.
It always uses a smaller position size than usual.
screens.explanation: Revenge trades are commonly described as reactive attempts to immediately recover a loss.

screens.question: Match the behavior to its description.
pairs: Entering quickly after a loss to try to recover it
Entering later, based on a fresh setup unrelated to urgency
Calmly assessing what happened before deciding on next steps
screens.explanation: Contrasting revenge trading with a calm, planned response highlights the distinction.

screens.template: Revenge trading is commonly linked to [__1__] decision-making, rather than a fresh, [__2__] setup.
screens.explanation: The reactive, emotional nature of revenge trading is commonly contrasted with a calm, planned entry.

screens.question: A commonly cited way to respond to a loss without falling into revenge trading:
items: Notice the urge to immediately jump into another trade
Pause instead of acting on that urge right away
Review what happened in the prior trade calmly
Only consider a new trade if a fresh, planned setup appears
correct_order: Notice the urge to immediately jump into another trade
Pause instead of acting on that urge right away
Review what happened in the prior trade calmly
Only consider a new trade if a fresh, planned setup appears
screens.explanation: This process creates space between a loss and the next decision.

screens.question: Which best describes "revenge trading"?

options.label: A guarantee that the next trade will be profitable
options.wrong_explanation: Revenge trading describes a motivation, not a guaranteed outcome.

options.label: Entering a new trade quickly after a loss, driven by the urge to recover it immediately
options.detail: A reactive pattern tied to a recent loss

options.label: Reviewing a loss calmly before deciding what to do next
options.detail: This describes a measured response, not revenge trading
options.wrong_explanation: A calm review is the opposite of revenge trading.

screens.explanation: Revenge trading specifically describes a reactive attempt to immediately recover a recent loss.

screens.scenario: Someone loses on a trade and immediately doubles their position size on the next trade to "make it back fast."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should stop looking at charts entirely from now on.
Increasing size specifically to recover a loss quickly is a commonly described sign of revenge trading, adding risk on top of an emotional reaction.
They should double their size again after the next loss too.
screens.explanation: Sizing decisions driven by the urge to recover a loss quickly are a commonly cited revenge-trading pattern.

screens.question: Revenge trading is driven by the urge to [___] a recent loss quickly.
screens.explanation: The urgency to immediately win back a loss defines revenge trading.

screens.question: Revenge trading is commonly linked to emotional decision-making.
screens.explanation: Reactive, emotional decisions (not a fresh plan) drive revenge trading.

sections.heading: 1. Data Collection & Storage
sections.body: This application operates strictly on a "local-first" architecture. All application states, learning progress, score logs, streak calendars, daily quest data, and checklist metrics are stored locally and exclusively inside the sandboxed hardware storage of your individual physical device. No personal identifiable data, biometric profiles, account credentials, or network logs are collected, stored, tracked, or transmitted by this software or its developers.

sections.heading: 2. Third-Party Disclosures
sections.body: We do not utilize remote server networks, cloud database buckets, advertising analytics, or user behavior tracking pixels. No data is harvested, shared, or sold to third-party entities.

sections.heading: 3. Your Rights & Purging Data
sections.body: Because all application states reside entirely on your personal physical hardware, you maintain total ownership of your information. Deleting the application from your device permanently purges all stored statistics, records, and history from your system memory.
